title: Europe will one day thank Trump for 'shaking' it out of its 'complacency': UK defense chief
excerpt: President Donald Trump, speaking at the NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey, criticizes Spain, Italy and the UK for not offering immediate support to the U.S. in a potential conflict with Iran. Trump descri...
body_text:
President Donald Trump, speaking at the NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey, criticizes Spain, Italy and the UK for not offering immediate support to the U.S. in a potential conflict with Iran. Trump describes their response as a 'bad moment' but later emphasizes the 'tremendous unification' among NATO members, expressing mutual love and respect.

The U.K.'s new defense secretary said Sunday that Europe will ultimately thank President Donald Trump for waking up the continent from its complacency and forcing NATO allies to take responsibility for their own security.

Speaking on Sky News, Wes Streeting also signaled a rebalancing of the U.K. government's transatlantic stance under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham while stating that Britain continued to refuse to back U.S. offensive military action against Iran.

"The first thing you do is you don't suck up, and… my impression is President Trump, his administration… that's not what they're looking for, actually," Streeting told Sky News anchor Trevor Phillips, stating his perspective on Washington.

"He's a straight talker. He says what he means and means what he says."

ANDY BURNHAM TAKES OVER AS UK PRIME MINISTER, CALLS FOR 'NEW POLITICAL MODEL'

British Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting said that Europe will one day thank President Donald Trump for shaking Europe out of its strategic complacency and forcing NATO allies to shoulder more of their own defense. (Carl Court/Getty Images)

"I don't know him, but I do trust the United States," he added.

Streeting took charge of the U.K. Ministry of Defence on July 20, the same day Burnham became prime minister.

"I've not even been in the job a week. I've always been aware that the alliance between the U.S. and the U.K. is unlike any in the world, and of course, that's historic, it's cultural, it's political," Streeting said. "It's driven by self-interest as well as mutual shared interests."

During his first week in office, Streeting also had a call with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to discuss maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz and broader NATO commitments.

"But just in my first week as defense secretary, I have had a unique insight into just how close and integral that relationship is when it comes to defense and security," Streeting explained.

UK DEFENSE SHORTFALLS HIGHLIGHTED AS BRITAIN AVOIDS IRAN OFFENSIVE ROLE AMID TRUMP CRITICISM

Streeting said he was "very keen and pleased" to meet with his American counterpart, War Secretary Pete Hegseth. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

"And it's one of the reasons why I was very keen and pleased in the first week to meet with my U.S. counterpart, Pete Hegseth, where I was clear that we've not supported offensive action in Iran, and we won't support offensive action in Iran," he continued. "But there are plenty of things that we can and should do together when it comes to securing the Strait of Hormuz, in making sure that Iran doesn't develop nuclear weapons, in terms of investing in our capability and NATO's capability."

Trump has long criticized European NATO members for failing to spend enough on defense, arguing they should shoulder a greater share of the alliance's security burden.

WHO IS ANDY BURNHAM? THE TRUMP CRITIC SET TO BECOME THE UK'S NEXT PRIME MINISTER

"And one of the things I'd say about President Trump specifically… we don't always like what he says. We don't always like his methods," Streeting said. (Stoyan Nenov/Reuters)

At July's NATO summit in Turkey, Trump pressed allies to follow through on their commitments to increase defense spending.

"And one of the things I'd say about President Trump specifically: we don't always like what he says, we don't always like his methods," Streeting said. "But I genuinely think when this period of history is written, Europe will thank President Trump for shaking us out of our complacency and forcing us to stand on our own two feet and end the period of overreliance on the United States for defense because what he said about Europe isn't unique to President Trump, the MAGA movement or the Republican Party."

"This has been a longstanding grain of U.S. frustration with Europe under Democratic and Republican presidents, and in the world we live in, it is right that we can act to secure ourselves," he added.

Streeting also said the U.K. could "act with our allies here in Europe and, of course, work with the United States without being overly dependent to the extent that NATO and Europe has been."

Fox News Digital has reached out to 10 Downing Street for further comment.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: YouTube star Ms Rachel gives funds to democratic socialist Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed
excerpt: Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt and Lawrence Jones discuss the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, highlighting the division between moderate Haley Stevens and progressive Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens is ...
body_text:
Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt and Lawrence Jones discuss the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, highlighting the division between moderate Haley Stevens and progressive Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens is backed by Sen. Peters, while El-Sayed has support from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders. Hewitt predicts a Republican win in the general election due to the left's potential dissatisfaction.

Popular children's YouTube educator "Ms. Rachel" faced criticism Sunday after a federal filing showed she gave $3,000 to Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate campaign, supporting the progressive Democrat in a nationally watched primary increasingly divided over Israel.

The donation prompted National Republican Senatorial Committee spokeswoman Samantha Cantrell to warn parents about both figures, The New York Post reported.

"Abdul El-Sayed and Ms. Rachel are one and the same, forcing their socialist, they/them, anti-America agenda on our children," Cantrell told The New York Post. "Parents should be worried when they head to the ballot box."

Children’s YouTube star Ms. Rachel. (Maxine Wallace/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

DAVID MARCUS: IN BOOMING DETROIT, VOTERS SKEPTICAL OF SOCIALISM SNAKE OIL

Rachel Griffin Accurso, who produces children's content under the name, "Ms. Rachel," was listed in a Federal Election Commission 48-hour notice dated July 19, according to the New York Post. The filing did not make clear whether the payment was a contribution or a loan.

The transaction connected Accurso, whose YouTube channel has more than 20 million subscribers, to El-Sayed, who has called for an arms embargo against Israel and accused the country of genocide in Gaza.

El-Sayed, who is backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., was asked during a July appearance on "Inside Politics Sunday" whether the United States should designate the Israeli government as a foreign terrorist organization.

El-Sayed has called Israel a "rogue state" and accused the country of committing genocide in Gaza. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

JEWISH MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS ADMIT THEY WILL VOTE REPUBLICAN IF ABDUL EL-SAYED BECOMES NOMINEE

"It’s certainly a rogue state," El-Sayed said. "I mean, they did a genocide."

Israel has repeatedly rejected genocide allegations, maintaining that its military targets Hamas and works to limit civilian casualties.

El-Sayed also held Michigan rallies in April with far-left streamer Hasan Piker, who previously said "America deserved 9/11" and later apologized. When Fox News host Will Cain pressed El-Sayed about their association in May, the candidate rejected the suggestion that campaigning with Piker meant endorsing all his remarks.

"Because he said something one time, you think I automatically believe that," El-Sayed said.

Ms. Rachel’s contribution comes as El-Sayed faces Rep. Haley Stevens in a Michigan Democratic Senate primary divided over Israel. (Getty Images)

ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK

Accurso has kept her Gaza advocacy largely separate from her children’s programming. During an August PBS NewsHour interview, she defended speaking publicly about Palestinian children while responding to accusations that her advocacy promoted anti-Israel messaging.

"I think it’s sad to take someone’s dedication and love for all children and try and make that wrong," Accurso said.

Accurso previously gave $3,500 each to Brad Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier, two congressional candidates backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani who defeated Democratic incumbents in June, the New York Post reported.

Accurso's husband, Aron Accurso, also gave $1,500 to Chevalier, according to FEC records.

The YouTuber has increasingly entered politics beyond campaign contributions. She told NBC News in March that she was working with lawyers and activists to close the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in South Texas after accusing the facility of "neglect and child abuse," Fox News Digital reported.

She embraced the political label during the interview while explaining her immigration advocacy.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"I am political," Accurso said. "It’s political to believe that children are worthy of love and care, and that every child is equal, and that our care shouldn’t stop at what we look like, our family, at our religion, at a border."

CoreCivic, which operates the Dilley facility, disputed Accurso’s allegations in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying it provides families with "safe, humane and compassionate care."

Accurso continued her immigration advocacy in June by meeting with families outside the Delaney Hall detention facility in Newark, New Jersey, before traveling to Washington with letters and drawings from children in ICE custody to urge lawmakers to end family detention, according to The Washington Post.

The Aug. 4 Michigan primary pits El-Sayed against Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. The pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC has spent nearly $30 million supporting Stevens, according to The Associated Press.

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed and Accurso for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

title: The Indian Army's first woman boxer is now chasing Commonwealth gold
excerpt:
Jaismine Lamboria is one of India's strongest boxing gold-medal prospects at the Glasgow Games

The reigning 57kg world champion boxer Jaismine Lamboria from India throws punches for a living, but whe...
body_text:
Jaismine Lamboria is one of India's strongest boxing gold-medal prospects at the Glasgow Games

The reigning 57kg world champion boxer Jaismine Lamboria from India throws punches for a living, but when it comes to handling pressure, she looks to one of her country's most celebrated cricketing legends for inspiration.

"I really admire MS Dhoni's mindset," says the soft-spoken Lamboria of the former Indian captain. "He is known as 'Captain Cool' for a reason, and I want to be calm like him."

That composure will be particularly valuable for Lamboria over the coming days.

The 24-year-old is one of India's strongest boxing gold-medal prospects at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, looking to improve on the bronze she won at Birmingham 2022.

Coming off a breakout 2025 during which she won World Cup golds in Astana and Delhi before becoming world champion in Liverpool, Lamboria is in Glasgow with an uncomplicated ambition.

"I aim to change the colour of that medal to gold," she says. "That's what I've been training and preparing towards."

At 5ft 8½in, Lamboria is tall by Indian boxing standards. Her Olympic debut in Paris ended in a first-round defeat to Tokyo silver medallist Nesthy Petecio of the Philippines.

But the setback came in the weight class she had only recently returned to. After spending nearly three years boxing at 60kg, Lamboria dropped back to 57kg during the Paris qualification campaign - a move that ultimately paid off when she won the world title by defeating Paris Olympic silver medallist Julia Atena Szeremeta of Poland.

Lamboria (left) is the the first female boxer inducted into the Indian Army

"That Paris 2024 Olympics exit was disappointing but it was an eye-opener," says Lamboria. "It prompted several changes in me - physically and mentally. And a significant part of it has come about at the Army Sports Institute (ASI) in Pune, which is where I train."

Lamboria credits her ASI coaches for improving his physical strength and a motivational coach and sports psychologist for sharpening her mental game.

The Indian Army, however, has provided the wider institutional framework around much of her development.

After winning bronze at the 2022 Commonwealth Games, Lamboria became the first female boxer inducted into the army, joining the Corps of Military Police. She now trains under its Mission Olympics Wing.

"It's a great honour they wanted to begin with me, but I also see it as an opportunity to become a role model for female athletes," says Lamboria of joining a system that has produced Olympians and Paralympians, including Olympic javelin champion Neeraj Chopra.

In early 2024, the Indian Army launched the Girls Sports Company to train girls aged 12 to 16 in four Olympic sports, including boxing, creating a pathway to elite competition and army recruitment.

"These girl athletes are doing very well too," says Lamboria. "One boxer has already won Asian Championships gold, which makes me really happy. I may have been the first female boxer in the Indian Army, but I won't be the last."

Lamboria's relationship with boxing, however, began long before the army entered her story.

Lamboria (right) began boxing seriously when she was around 14 years old

Born in the northern state of Haryana, she grew up in Bhiwani, a city synonymous with Indian boxing and widely nicknamed the country's 'Mini Cuba'.

Her great-grandfather Hawa Singh was one of Indian boxing's early giants. A heavyweight, he won successive Asian Games gold medals in 1966 and 1970 and was among those who established the famed Bhiwani Boxing Club, which would later produce boxers including Olympic medallist Vijender Singh.

Even so, it is not Hawa's medals that feature most prominently in the stories Lamboria remembers hearing about him at home. "He was powerful, but there was also so much humility in him," she says.

Her earliest boxing influences were her uncles, Sandeep Singh and Parvinder Singh. "I grew up watching them compete," she says. "They were the ones who got me started."

Lamboria began boxing seriously around the age of 14, training first at an academy run by Hawa's son, Sanjay Sheoran, before continuing under her uncles.

Though the sport ran through her extended family, Lamboria grew up in a household of modest means. Her father, Jaiveer, works as a home guard, while her mother, Joginder, is a homemaker.

"Their support has been a big reason why I was the first girl in my immediate family to take up sport seriously," she says, "not least as the youngest among the girls in the family."

Her inspirations, meanwhile, extend well beyond her own family.

Lamboria wants to win the gold at the Glasgow games

Lamboria grew up idolising Olympic medallists MC Mary Kom and Vijender Singh. Later, she looked up to Indian Army boxers Amit Panghal and Manish Kaushik, Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, American swimming great Michael Phelps and Indian sprinting legend Milkha Singh.

Closer to home, she credits senior Indian boxers Nikhat Zareen, Lovlina Borgohain and Pooja Rani, not just for their medals but for the encouragement they offer younger athletes.

"When you look at them, you naturally feel that you want to do what they have done," she says.

Now, Lamboria is beginning to occupy that role herself.

"For a long time, boxing has been seen as a male-dominated sport," she says. "Being a woman boxer and an Army athlete, it means a lot to compete on the world stage, prove myself and inspire others through my performances."

That change is reflected in the Commonwealth Games too. Boxing has been part of the event since 1930, but women's competition was introduced only in 2014. In Glasgow, bouts begin on 24 July, with the finals on 31 July and 1 August.

After winning bronze in Birmingham four years ago, Lamboria hopes to leave Glasgow with gold.

"When you're competing overseas and the national anthem plays, it's a completely different feeling," she says.

"I experienced that at the World Championships in Liverpool last year. That's the moment I want to recreate here."

title: Trump’s border czar probes possible vetting failures after ICE shooting
excerpt: United States President Donald Trump’s border czar says the vetting of an immigration officer involved in the deadly shooting of a Colombian native in Maine is under internal review after the officer’...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump’s border czar says the vetting of an immigration officer involved in the deadly shooting of a Colombian native in Maine is under internal review after the officer’s relatives revealed to The Associated Press that he had a history of serious mental health struggles and violent behaviour.

Tom Homan said on Sunday that if the allegations against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer are true, “I don’t think he should ever have cleared vetting.”

“There’s several things under review,” Homan said on CNN about the officer, Army veteran David Brouillette. “The training is under review. I know this specific case, as far as the vetting, is under review by the internal affairs section.”

Questions about the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) rush to hire, train and deploy thousands of new ICE officers to carry out Trump’s immigration crackdown have come into stark focus after back-to-back deadly shootings of immigrants in Maine and Houston.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ordered a pause in vehicle stops after the Maine shooting, but Trump almost immediately reversed course and insisted the stops resume as a necessary tool in his campaign to round up and deport immigrants without current legal status.

DHS did not immediately respond on Sunday to a request for comment about the internal review.

Homan said that “changes have been made” and that acting ICE director David Venturella has issued a new directive that body cameras must be in use if officers make a vehicle stop.

“Right now, on all vehicle stops, there’s at least one body camera on site to record the entire event,” he said.

He said Venturella “sent an instruction out that he wants at least one body camera on those vehicle stops, so we have everything on video”.

It is unclear if the steps the department is taking will be enough to quell the concerns coming from certain Congress lawmakers over DHS training and tactics as it tries to reach Trump’s mass deportation goals.

Lawmakers from both parties have raised concerns.

Democrats pressed ICE officials during a closed-door briefing for the House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee last week, leaving some with more questions than answers.

Lawmakers were told during the briefing that there have been 56 complaints of excessive force against ICE officers – 32 were cleared, and one was referred for disciplinary action.

No discipline had yet been handed out, the lawmakers said they were told. The rest of the incidents are still under investigation.

Meanwhile, Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine, chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has pushed for the use of body cameras and ensured funding for the effort. She had said it was “extremely unfortunate” that the officer involved in the shooting in her home state was not using a camera.

title: Burnham to meet Zelenskyy at UK naval base in show of ‘unwavering’ support
excerpt:
Ukrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime minister

Volodymyr Zelenskyy will become Andy Burnham’s first overseas visitor as prime minister, in a visit that Burnham said...
body_text:
Ukrainian president will be first overseas visitor for new British prime minister

Volodymyr Zelenskyy will become Andy Burnham’s first overseas visitor as prime minister, in a visit that Burnham said underlined Britain’s “unwavering” backing for Ukraine.

Less than two weeks after Keir Starmer travelled to Kyiv for the final foreign visit of his prime ministership, the Ukrainian president will on Monday join Burnham at a naval base where Ukrainian forces have been receiving training.

Zelenskyy was one of the first world leaders Burnham spoke to when he entered No 10 last week, and the prime minister has promised to maintain Starmer’s strong support for the country in pushing back against Russia’s invasion.

On the visit to the base, the pair will speak to Ukrainian and British military personnel who have taken part in Exercise Sea Breeze, a 15-country training deployment based on mine exercises and other maritime operations in the Black Sea.

The second part of this year’s exercise, which took place in Portland, Dorset, finished on Friday and involved more than 200 Ukrainian personnel.

Burnham and Zelenskyy are also due to discuss joint projects including Stone Cloak, an electronic jammer for which the UK has shared the intellectual property, allowing Ukraine to use the system immediately.

Thousands of the jammers, each about the size of a tablet computer, have been sent to Ukraine to be fitted to drones, with the aim of stopping Russian air defence systems from tracking and targeting them.

Ukraine is now able to mass produce the devices itself. After being initially used there, the jammers are due to be fitted to new UK weaponry, including cruise missiles.

Burnham, in a comment released by Downing Street before the visit, said: “Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering. Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve a long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine.

“Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries.”

According to statistics released by No 10, since Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, total UK support for the country has totalled £25bn, including £16bn in military assistance.

Starmer visited Ukraine a number of times, and hosted Zelenskyy regularly. In one of the most telling displays of UK support, after a March 2025 visit to the White House during which the Ukrainian leader was publicly berated by Donald Trump, he then travelled to the UK and met not only Starmer but also King Charles at Sandringham, which is primarily a royal home and rarely used for official events.

During Starmer’s final visit to Ukraine, Zelenskyy presented him with the country’s Order of Freedom, the most prestigious honour that can be given to an overseas national.

During a press conference with Starmer, the Ukrainian president said he hoped to build a strong relationship with Burnham, and to arrange a meeting “as soon as possible”.

title: PM pledges continued support for Ukraine ahead of Zelensky visit
excerpt:
President Zelensky will also meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK

Andy Burnham has pledged to continue the ...
body_text:
President Zelensky will also meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK

Andy Burnham has pledged to continue the UK's "unwavering" support for Ukraine ahead of a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.

Zelensky will become the prime minister's first international visitor since he took office a week ago, which No 10 said "illustrates the strength of the relationship between the two nations".

They will visit a naval base, where Burnham will announce the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale.

The prime minister said: "Britain stands with Ukrain, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering. Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve long lasting and just peace for Ukraine."

He added: "Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries."

The electronic jammers are the size of a tablet computer, and are designed to block the detection of any drones it is fitted to.

The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations.

Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons.

It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons which fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight.

During Monday's visit, the two leaders will also meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK.

Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea.

Watch: Starmer given Order of Freedom medal in final Ukraine trip as PM

Britain's backing of Ukraine has been constant since Russia's invasion four years ago, and the UK has committed £25bn in funding, external for the country's war fight.

In one of his first calls after becoming prime minister last Monday, Burnham spoke to Zelensky and invited him to visit the UK "at the earliest opportunity".

In a post on X shortly afterwards, Zelensky said: "I truly appreciate that the support for Ukraine and our people will remain steadfast."

Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, visited Kyiv on his final full day as Labour leader.

During that trip he announced fresh funding worth £255m (300m Euro) for Ukraine's fight against Russia, and was awarded Ukraine's Order of Freedom.

Asked if he was concerned about changes of leadership in Britain, and in France next year, Zelensky said: "Of course I'm afraid of changes, of course we are afraid because we are in the war each day.

"But again the priority is the relation between nations, not just between just people. I'm sure that these relations will not change, or we have to do our best not to lose such very good relations."

He added: "I hope we will never lose strong relations with the UK during or after the war." Sir Keir replied: "You won't."

Wildfires are ravaging many parts of western and southern Europe, with France and Spain among the hardest hit.

The World Health Organization has warned that climate change is contributing to the frequency and intensity of the fires. title: Israeli government nods to international stabilisation force in Gaza
excerpt:
Israel’s government has approved the entry of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), part of United States President Donald Trump’s 20-point “peace plan,” to Gaza.

An Israeli official reported ...
body_text:
Israel’s government has approved the entry of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), part of United States President Donald Trump’s 20-point “peace plan,” to Gaza.

An Israeli official reported on Sunday that Israel’s security cabinet had approved the key legal measures and that the force would operate “in full coordination with” the Israeli military, according to the Times of Israel.

There was no timeframe given for when the ISF, which will include 200 people from “friendly countries such as Uganda and Morocco”, according to the Reuters news agency, will be deployed.

The cabinet determined that Israel will have the authority to approve which countries can send forces.

Following the implementation of Trump’s deal, Israel dictates who can and cannot enter the Gaza Strip, along with how much aid and food can enter, in the wake of Israel’s two-year, genocidal war on Gaza.

Though a “ceasefire” between Hamas and Israel was agreed in October, reports of killings of Palestinians by the Israeli military occur almost daily.

The Palestinian Ministry of Health reports that 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the deal was implemented, with 3,888 wounded.

The plan also called for an international “Board of Peace” to oversee the administration and reconstruction of the strip, for the creation of a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) technocratic governing body, and for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw from the strip.

Nickolay Mladenov, the director-general of the Gaza Board of Peace – which the vast majority of Western countries refused to join – welcomed the news.

The former Bulgarian foreign minister and defence minister said Israel enabling the deployment was “a critical part of the agreed framework for stabilising Gaza, supporting demilitarisation, and enabling the transition to effective Palestinian transitional administration” under the NCAG.

The cabinet’s approval comes a day before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due to travel to Washington, DC in the United States.

Israel currently occupies close to 70 percent of Gaza. Its population of almost two million has been forced to live in a diminishing fraction of the strip, as Israel continues to move the “Yellow Line” it created to demarcate areas it withdrew to under the first phase of the deal.

The ISF will operate in the areas that are not under Israeli control.

Displaced Palestinians in Gaza cautiously welcome Israel’s approval for an international stabilisation force to enter the territory under the US-backed ceasefire plan. Residents hope the force can help rebuild Gaza and allow them to return home after months of bombardment and displacement.

The Americans who voted for President Donald Trump are seeing a “wholesale violation” ...
body_text:
Democratic lawmaker Sheldon Whitehouse says the US is turning into one of the world’s ‘worst-behaved countries’.

The Americans who voted for President Donald Trump are seeing a “wholesale violation” of his campaign promise to avoid unnecessary wars, especially the United States-Israel war on Iran, US Senator Sheldon Whitehouse argues.

The Democrat tells host Steve Clemons that the Iran war has been “managed just spectacularly incompetently and dishonestly”.

Other countries increasingly see the US as similar to “some of the worst-behaved countries they have to deal with, where bribe requests, side deals, personal favours and ulterior motives are really what’s going on,” Whitehouse says.

He adds that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “hasn’t been a good friend”.

title: Berlin Pride attack believed to be an act of Islamic terror, suspect on the run: German minister
excerpt: Fox News' Chanley Painter reports Berlin police are conducting a manhunt for 21-year-old Abdul B, identified as the suspect in a deadly van attack at a German Pride Festival. One person was killed and...
body_text:
Fox News' Chanley Painter reports Berlin police are conducting a manhunt for 21-year-old Abdul B, identified as the suspect in a deadly van attack at a German Pride Festival. One person was killed and 16 others were injured after the van crashed into a crowd near the parade route. Authorities are investigating reports of additional stab wounds and suspect terrorism, noting the individual's ties to Islamic groups.

A suspect in the attack at Berlin's Pride festival that left one person dead and at least 29 others injured was killed during a confrontation with police in a nearby suburb, The Associated Press reported, citing authorities.

German authorities on Sunday launched an intensive manhunt for Abdul Ballout, a German citizen with Lebanese roots. Ballout was killed following a nearly 24-hour search. Prosecutors said he had previously sought to join the militant Islamic State group.

"Everything we see here points to us dealing with an Islamic terror attack," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said.

AT LEAST 1 DEAD, SEVERAL INJURED AFTER VAN RAMS INTO CROWD AT PRIDE FESTIVAL; SUSPECT 'KNOWN TO POLICE'

Abdul Ballout, a German citizen with Lebanese roots, was killed in a police confrontation after being sought in connection with the attack, authorities said. (Berlin Police)

The minister said the suspect had previously come to the attention of authorities for multiple crimes, as well as his "radicalization and belonging to the Islamist scene."

Dobrindt said Ballout was born in Germany and that his mother became a naturalized German citizen in 2002, three years before he was born. He said the suspect previously received a suspended prison sentence of one year and 10 months but did not disclose what he had been convicted of.

Police officers stand near a vehicle crashed into a tree after driving into a crowd near Berlin's annual Pride event, in Germany, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)

Police said a white van drove into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park around 10 p.m. on Saturday before crashing into a tree. Authorities say the suspect then attacked several people with a machete before fleeing.

WITNESSES RECOUNT 'SCARY' NYC STABBING AFTER SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY YELLED 'ALLAHU AKBAR' DURING ATTACKS

A woman was killed, while three people suffered life-threatening injuries and eight others were seriously hurt, according to Berlin's fire service. Dobrindt said at least 29 people were injured.

Emergency personnel and police gather in Berlin, early Sunday, July 26, 2026, following the cancellation of Christopher Street Day festivities. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi)

The attack happened a few hundred yards from Berlin's annual Christopher Street Day Pride celebration — one of Europe's largest LGBTQ+ events — but not on the parade route or at the festival's closing event near the Brandenburg Gate. Investigators said the victims appeared to include both Pride attendees and other people who were in the park.

Organizers stopped the celebration shortly after the attack, cutting off a live performance and urging people to leave the area.

People stand on 17 June Street following the cancellation of Christopher Street Day in Berlin on Saturday, July 25, 2026. (Fabian Sommer/DPA via AP)

SYNAGOGUE IN LONDON TARGETED IN ATTEMPTED 'ANTISEMITIC HATE CRIME,' UK POLICE SAY

Police spokesman Florian Nath earlier said the suspect was known to investigators because of his alleged ties to Islamic groups in Berlin.

"The suspect is known to police. He is known to us as a member of Islamic circles here in Berlin, and our search for this person is proceeding at full speed," Nath said, according to The Associated Press. "We still have no information whatsoever regarding his specific motives, the exact sequence of events, or his role in the crime itself."

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt speaks to the media near the scene where a car rammed into a crowd at the Pride March in Berlin, Germany, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)

Police searched several locations across Berlin overnight and into Sunday, including an apartment in the Schöneberg district. It was not immediately clear where the confrontation happened.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Self-dressing clothes could help older adults
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Most of us get dressed every day without thinking twice about it. However, a stiff shoulder can make pulling on a shir...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Most of us get dressed every day without thinking twice about it. However, a stiff shoulder can make pulling on a shirt surprisingly difficult, while balance problems can turn a simple pair of pants into a real challenge. That is what makes a new invention from South Korea's KAIST and Stanford University worth watching.

Researchers have created self-dressing clothes with soft, air-powered robots built into the fabric. Once activated, the garment moves along the body and helps guide itself into place, even while the wearer moves. The technology remains an early research project, but it shows how future clothing could help older adults get dressed with less assistance and stay independent at home longer.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL

The self-dressing system uses soft, air-powered robots to guide sleeves, a jacket and pants into place around the body. (KAIST)

Getting dressed ranks among the basic activities that often determine whether someone can live independently. When mobility or dexterity declines, people may need a spouse, family member or professional caregiver to help with a deeply personal routine.

The researchers behind the project say dressing challenges can reduce autonomy and increase reliance on caregivers. They designed the system for people with limited mobility, including older adults and those recovering from injuries. Stanford researchers have also identified dressing assistance as an important use for future home robots. The university says assistive technology could help older adults remain in their homes as caregiving needs increase.

Dressing requires more movement than many people realize. You need to reach behind your body, lift your arms and shift your weight while handling fabric. Arthritis may make gripping or pulling clothing painful. Meanwhile, shoulder problems can limit your reach. Recovery from hip or knee surgery can also make bending difficult.

Balance adds another concern. Pulling on pants often requires someone to stand briefly on one leg or bend toward the floor. For a person who already feels unsteady, that familiar routine can become stressful. Self-dressing clothes could eventually reduce some of that reaching and pulling. However, researchers still need clinical studies to learn how well the system works for people with real mobility limitations.

The researchers call their system SWAG, which stands for Self-Wearing Adaptive Garment. Instead of placing a large robotic arm next to the person, the team built flexible robotic tubes into the clothing. Air pressure causes these soft structures to unfold and grow along the body.

The movement turns the garment inside out as it advances. That approach allows the clothing to follow the person's shape while reducing friction between the fabric and skin. Think of ivy growing around a wall or tree. The plant advances from its tip rather than dragging its entire length forward. The soft robot uses a similar motion, which helps it follow curves and move across different surfaces.

In this demonstration, the robotic garment unfurls over the legs while the wearer remains seated. (KAIST)

The idea began when KAIST postdoctoral researcher Nam Gyun Kim was riding his bike when it began to rain. As he kept moving, he wondered how helpful it would be if a raincoat could put itself on.

That simple idea led to a much bigger thought. Instead of making your body do all the pulling, reaching and twisting, what if the clothing could move into place on its own? From there, Kim and the research team began developing garments that use soft robotics to help dress the person wearing them.

Kim says putting on a full suit takes about 10 seconds. The published paper provides additional timing from individual demonstrations. A jacket moved into place in about 13 seconds, while the pants demonstration took roughly 21 seconds. A sleeve prototype took about 14 seconds.

The researchers tested sleeves, jackets and pants. Their results showed that the garments could unfold along the body while keeping contact forces within the team's safety limits. The system also relies on its physical design instead of a complicated control program. That could eventually help simplify the hardware needed for dressing assistance.

Many existing dressing robots use rigid mechanical arms. Those systems must handle loose fabric while carefully avoiding uncomfortable contact with the person. They may also require the person to hold a fixed pose while the robot completes the task. That setup could feel awkward inside a bedroom or bathroom.

The KAIST and Stanford design takes a different approach by placing the robotic mechanism inside the garment. The clothing becomes the helper. Because the system uses soft materials, it can bend around the body rather than approaching it with a hard mechanical structure. KAIST says this design reduces physical strain and supports safer contact.

COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

Flexible robotic tubes built into the jacket help pull the sleeves and fabric into position with less effort from the wearer. (KAIST)

Older adults and people with disabilities represent a major potential use for the technology. KAIST also sees possibilities for rehabilitation patients who need temporary assistance after an injury or medical procedure. However, industrial workplaces may adopt the idea sooner.

Semiconductor employees frequently put on protective cleanroom clothing. Emergency workers may also need to suit up quickly while carrying other equipment. The researchers believe air-powered garments could help people put on protective clothing without relying heavily on their hands. The published study also discusses possible medical uses, such as helping healthcare workers apply protective coverings or compression bandages. Those applications remain potential future directions.

The current system remains a research prototype connected to a pneumatic base station. Researchers have yet to announce a consumer price or release date. Several everyday questions remain unanswered. The garments would need to fit different body shapes and movement patterns. Designers would also need to address washing, storage and portable air power.

The research team says future versions may use adjustable sheaths or elastic materials to fit a wider range of bodies. The researchers also want to automate the garment-loading process and improve the controls.

Most importantly, the team says clinical trials involving people with mobility impairments will be essential. Those tests could show whether the clothing feels comfortable and works reliably outside the lab. Researchers also need to explore how the garment comes off. The current work concentrates mainly on dressing, while automated removal remains a future possibility.

You probably will not find robotic clothing hanging in a local store anytime soon. Yet this research gives us a useful preview of where assistive technology may be heading. For you or someone you care about, the biggest benefit could be control over a private daily routine. Clothing that handles part of the pulling and positioning could make mornings less tiring.

It could also delay the point when someone needs another person present simply to get dressed. That possibility still depends on testing, affordability and a design people feel comfortable wearing.

Self-dressing clothes may sound unusual, but the need behind them is easy to understand. Arthritis, limited mobility or recovery from surgery can make getting dressed frustrating and exhausting. For older adults, a garment that helps guide itself into place could mean more privacy, less reliance on a caregiver and more confidence starting the day. The KAIST and Stanford system still has a long way to go. Researchers need to make it portable, test it with people who have mobility challenges and prove it can work safely in a home. Even so, the idea shows how technology could support independence through something as familiar as the clothes you already wear.

Would you or someone you care about use self-dressing clothes to stay independent? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com
