title: Cape Verde World Cup star Vozinha agrees deal with Chile’s Colo Colo
excerpt:
Cape Verde’s heroic World Cup goalkeeper, Vozinha, has reached an agreement to join Chilean club side Colo Colo.

The 40-year-old stopper, who made headlines around the world after starring in a goall...
body_text:
Cape Verde’s heroic World Cup goalkeeper, Vozinha, has reached an agreement to join Chilean club side Colo Colo.

The 40-year-old stopper, who made headlines around the world after starring in a goalless draw with Spain, will travel to Chile for a medical before being unveiled, Colo Colo’s president, Anibal Mosa, announced on Saturday.

Vozinha became one of the most talked-about players at the World Cup with a string of remarkable saves against top teams, including defending champions Argentina.

The goalkeeper, who left Portuguese second-tier side Chaves before the summer, was voted into FIFA’s fan-selected World Cup dream team.

“Vozinha will be a Colo Colo player. In the coming days, he will travel to Chile, undergo the usual medical examinations and then be presented here at the Estadio Monumental,” Mosa said.

He added that Vozinha’s World Cup performance showed he deserved the move, while acknowledging the signing also carried marketing appeal for the Chilean side.

Colo Colo teased the signing on social media with an image appearing to show the veteran goalkeeper’s trademark curly hair.

Vozinha, whose full name is Josimar Jose Evora Dias, has also become a social media star, with help from Brazilian influencer Casimiro. The goalkeeper’s Instagram following has soared from 50,000 to nearly 30 million.

He also made headlines after revealing that his mother, Ana Candida Evora, was unable to travel to watch her son due to the cost of a bond payment for a visa to enter the US.

She was eventually granted a visa with all travel fees waived after lobbying from US House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.

Colo Colo, who are based in the Chilean capital Santiago, are currently top of the Liga de Primera.

They are the most successful side in Chile and the only club from the country to win the Copa Libertadores.

title: Joshua comes back twice to knock out Prenga and set up Fury showdown
excerpt:
Former two-time world champion Anthony Joshua recovered from two knockdowns to knock out Kristian Prenga in the second round of a dramatic non-title heavyweight fight in Saudi Arabia.

The fight in Je...
body_text:
Former two-time world champion Anthony Joshua recovered from two knockdowns to knock out Kristian Prenga in the second round of a dramatic non-title heavyweight fight in Saudi Arabia.

The fight in Jeddah on Saturday was seen as the British boxer’s final step before setting up a long-awaited showdown against his compatriot Tyson Fury.

It also marked his return to the ring for the first time since a horrific car crash in Nigeria in December, during which Joshua lost two of his best friends and sustained injuries.

Back inside the ring, Joshua was floored by an uppercut inside 30 seconds. He beat the count but looked seriously shaken.

Then Prenga knocked Joshua down again, but the former heavyweight champion rose before the end of the count and survived until the bell in the first round.

A quick end to the fight was expected, but nobody thought it would be Prenga’s.

In the second round, Joshua unleashed a flurry of punches and finished Prenga with a right hook, sending the Albanian through the bottom of the ropes.

The turnaround shocked even heavyweight king Oleksandr Usyk, whose face was caught by TV cameras as he watched from ringside.

The comeback kept alive the possibility of an all-British fight between Joshua and Fury.

Joshua’s manager Eddie Hearn claims his fighter and Fury have signed a contract to meet for the first time later this year, but on the condition that they come through warm-up bouts this weekend.

“I hope the fans will be in for a lovely treat,” Joshua told the crowd about fighting Fury following his win over Prenga.

Fury played his part by coming out of retirement this year and, on Friday, forcing 46-year-old Polish journeyman Mariusz Wach to retire in round seven in Pattaya, Thailand.

Joshua almost blew his part of the claimed contract before showcasing his champion’s fightback spirit.

Prenga brought a 20-1 fight record with 20 KOs into the match-up with Joshua and looked every bit the knockout artist.

Joshua, fighting for the first time since surviving the car crash that killed his friends Sina Ghami and Latif ‘Latz’ Ayodele, acknowledged them straight after improving his fight record to 30-4 (27 KOs).

“It’s more than punch power,” Joshua said of his knockout punch. “That was spirit. That was Latz and Sina. That was the family. You know what I mean? That hurts even talking about it.

“He [Prenga] gave me a good test, but this is what champions do: we rise. We get knocked down and stand up. That is life; that is life’s motto.”

title: Family of former Vodafone manager found drowned call for ‘Adrian’s law’ to protect franchisees
excerpt:
Adrian Howe’s family believe that fears his deal would be financially ruinous led him to kill himself

The family of a former mobile phone store manager who was found drowned days before his new Vodaf...
body_text:
Adrian Howe’s family believe that fears his deal would be financially ruinous led him to kill himself

The family of a former mobile phone store manager who was found drowned days before his new Vodafone franchise was to open its doors is pressing the government to introduce a new franchising law in his name.

The call comes a week after Vodafone settled a long-running legal claim filed by 62 of its former franchisees who alleged that the company “unjustly enriched” itself at their expense by up to £85m.

The confidential agreement was reached 19 months after the claim was originally filed at the high court “without any admission of liability”, the parties said in a joint statement.

The plight of the 62 claimants – who represented almost 40% of the total 167 Vodafone franchisees – was first reported by the Guardian in December 2024, after which Vodafone apologised to claimants, who blamed pressure from the telecoms group for triggering suicidal thoughts.

However, their number did not include Adrian Howe, a former Vodafone employee, whose family he say killed himself in 2018 after becoming convinced his new franchising deal with the telecoms group would prove financially ruinous.

His case was raised in parliament in January, prompting Keir Starmer, then prime minister, to pledge to review laws governing franchising agreements.

“There is no protection for franchisees in the UK – that needs to change,” said Howe’s daughter, Kirsty-Anne Holmes. “There needs to be some governing body to oversee these contracts. The fact that franchisors ​like Vodafone can put anything into a contract, ​such as personal guarantees, is really bad behaviour. If these protections had been in place previously, my dad taking his own life might not have happened.”

Holmes met a representative of the then Department for Business and Trade earlier this month to discuss her father’s case, and raised the prospect of new franchising regulations under the banner of “Adrian’s law”.

“I don’t want it to be forgotten and brushed under the carpet just because someone else takes over [as prime minister],” she said. “I want justice for Dad.”

Howe’s case, which was revealed by the Guardian in December, raised further questions about how the telecoms company treated its franchisees who, a 2020 survey revealed, were overwhelmingly critical about the effects its actions had had on their mental health.

Howe, 58, had been preparing to open a single Vodafone franchise in Irvine, North Ayrshire, but was then told by the company that he needed to take on a second franchise in Kilmarnock, his family recall being told.

He had previously worked in the Kilmarnock store and knew it had struggled. If its performance could not be turned around, the Howe’s family home would have been put at risk by a personal guarantee given to Vodafone as part of its franchising contracts.

Howe’s youngest son, Nathan, recalled his father telling him “Vodafone has me by the balls” when they met for a drink at a local pub shortly before his death. He said his father then added: “This pint might have saved me.”

The store manager was found drowned a short walk from his home on 27 August 2018, days before his franchising business was to open on 2 September.

That looming date appeared to have prompted an entry in a notepad discovered at his home: “1st September nice to have death,” Howe wrote, according to the postmortem report.

The pathologist’s document also hinted at other potential factors such as heart disease and stated that Howe had a “history of anxiety and depression (1995)”, though his relatives said that that specific mental health episode had been short-lived and never recurred. The forensic pathologist went on to state that Howe had “been ‘a bit stressed’ due to setting up a new business” as she concluded that his death was “consistent with drowning”.

Vodafone did not provide any fresh comment on Howe’s case this week.

The company said last year it “wholly rejects” any suggestion that it had “knowingly or recklessly or negligently” put anybody involved with its franchise stores under unreasonable pressure.

Mental health experts emphasise that suicide is usually complex and can often involve many triggers.

A Vodafone UK spokesperson has said previously: “While we are sorry if any partners have had a difficult experience, we reject any suggestion that our franchisees were put under undue pressure. We continue to run a successful franchise operation, and many of our existing franchisees have expanded their business with us by taking on additional stores. We encourage everyone to raise issues, and we will always seek to resolve them.”

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123, or email jo@samaritans.org or jo@samaritans.ie. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: ‘Socialist’ teachers target eight Victorian Labor MPs including education minister – as it happened
excerpt:
A group of self-described “rebel teachers” in Victoria are running a campaign to target eight sitting Labor MPs, including the minister for education, Ben Carroll, in November’s state election.

The c...
body_text:
A group of self-described “rebel teachers” in Victoria are running a campaign to target eight sitting Labor MPs, including the minister for education, Ben Carroll, in November’s state election.

The candidates are members of the “Socialists in Schools” group, in opposition to the department of education. Victorian Socialists have announced they are aiming to contest every lower house seat in Victoria.

Brendan Laws is going up against Carroll in his formerly safe seat of Niddrie, calling for the ending of public funding to high-fee private schools, the abolition of Naplan and full funding for uniforms, excursions, materials and lunches.

Laws said the Victorian school system had been underfunded for years.

double quotation markThere’s a consensus that public education deserves better. On the issue of education, the ALP is not just out of touch – they’re on the other side of the picket line, with the Liberals and One Nation.

Economic segregation is increasing, as working-class students are more and isolated while high-fee private schools get more and more funding each year. This must end immediately.

With that, we will wrap the blog for the afternoon. We’ll be back first thing tomorrow morning but until then, enjoy the rest of your Sundays.

Here’s a recap of the major developments of the day:

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, told Insiders the government isn’t planning to extend the fuel excise relief, due to lapse on 2 August, as the war in the Middle East drags on.

Albanese also said he was a supporter of voluntary euthanasia but opposed allowing patients to use telehealth to access it, as the Greens and independent Kate Chaney plan to introduce legislation based on changes to Labor’s national platform.

Australia is leading the top of the Commonwealth Games table at the pared-back event in Glasgow, with 12 gold and 23 medals overall.

An internal police investigation has been launched after a bystander was shot during a tense standoff between officers and an armed offender in Cairns.

And a group of self-described “rebel teachers” in Victoria are running a campaign to target eight sitting Labor MPs, including the minister for education, Ben Carroll, in November’s state election.

Ex-commandos behind army chopper crash memorial

The memorial for the four aviators who died in a helicopter crash was spearheaded by Operation Pilgrimage, an organisation of former commandos.

“The actual anniversary is only two days off. I selected this weekend for that very purpose,” the Operation Pilgrimage chair, Allan Miles, told AAP.

“It’s been a real privilege to be involved in the planning and then doing the hard yards to get it up and running.”

“I was quite lifted that there’s a sense of sadness, of course, but also acknowledgment amongst themselves that something has moved forward,” Miles said.

A Defence Flight Safety Bureau report into the Taipan tragedy found the primary cause of the crash was “spatial disorientation”, which happens when a pilot misperceives the position of an aircraft in relation to the environment.

It concluded the pilots were likely experiencing fatigue levels shown to “impede optimal performance” and increase susceptibility to spatial disorientation.

Earlier in July, a Senate inquiry examining the crash was told regulator Comcare had referred two briefs of evidence to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions relating to fatigue management and the TopOwl helmet-mounted display system worn by the pilots.

The regulator was informed by federal prosecutors a year earlier they did not intend to prosecute the defence force because they did not consider there were reasonable prospects of obtaining a conviction.

Comcare’s chief executive, Colin Radford, told the inquiry the regulator believed prosecution should proceed.

The inquiry is due to report in September.

Separate probes are being held by the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force and the Queensland coroner.

Memorial unveiled for army chopper crash victims

A memorial for aviators who died in an army helicopter crash is being unveiled almost three years on from the tragedy, AAP reports.

Capt Danniel Lyon, Lt Maxwell Nugent, WO Class Two Joseph Laycock and Cpl Alexander Naggs were killed when their MRH-90 Taipan chopper crashed into waters off Queensland’s Whitsunday Islands during Exercise Talisman Sabre on 28 July 2023.

Their loved ones joined Queensland’s governor, Jeannette Young, at Airlie Beach’s Shute harbour on Sunday for the official unveiling of a memorial commemorating the men’s lives. The project was spearheaded by Operation Pilgrimage, an organisation of former commandos. Whitsundays regional council supported the initiative and successfully lobbied for a Queensland government grant.

The crew, from the Sydney-based 6th Aviation Regiment, were flying in a helicopter given the call-sign Bushman 83 when it crashed during a training exercise. Nineteen family members of the Bushman 83 crew have flown in from Melbourne, Sydney, Canberra and other parts of the country for the event and gathered for a group dinner on Saturday night.

It is estimated almost 50 Australian Defence Force members have died in training activities in the past 30 years.

The US-Israeli war with Iran will probably drive petrol prices above $ 2 a litre in the coming weeks, but the government has no plans to extend its fuel excise relief when it ends in a week.

Fuel excise relief for motorists is unlikely to be extended despite the war in the Middle East flaring up.

The Labor government halved the fuel excise for three months from April in response to rising prices as a result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, saving drivers 32 cents a litre on fuel.

The measure was extended for a further month in July, but at a reduced rate of 16 cents per litre.

The extension is due to lapse on 2 August.

Fresh tensions between the US and Iran have caused Brent crude oil prices to rise to more than $US100 a barrel, but Anthony Albanese has indicated continued excise relief is not on the cards.

“That’s not in our planning at this point in time,” the prime minister told ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday.

“(Fuel) usage has come down and is indeed lower than it was a year ago as well, but importantly as well, we have kept supply going.”

Albanese indicated some fuel-related measures were in the pipeline.

“We’ll have some more announcements about fuel in the coming days and weeks as well,” he said.

“We’ll continue to examine things that were in that process in the budget.”

Drivers have been warned petrol prices could reach more than $2 a litre as the excise discount is wound back.

Average prices for unleaded petrol have climbed to more than $1.80 per litre in all state capitals in recent days, up from about $1.50 at the end of June.

The jump in oil prices comes as Iran-aligned Houthi militants fired on Saudi oil installations on the coast of the Red Sea and Tehran attempted to shut down shipments through the strait of Hormuz again.

US strikes have recommenced in response to Iranian attacks on vessels travelling through the strait, a key oil transit route.

Albanese said a continuation of the conflict would lead to economic pressure.

“The war is having an impact here in Australia and the longer it goes, the bigger the impact will be,” he said.

“This is a war on the other side of the world.

“We are not protagonists in it, but we are impacted by it, and we’ve consistently called for a de-escalation.”

‘Awkward’ selection drama won’t derail Aussie sprinters

Rohan Browning has put the Commonwealth Games track selection drama in the rear vision mirror as he seeks to spearhead Australia’s sprint charge in Glasgow.

The 28-year-old former national champion was picked alongside the current title holder, Lachie Kennedy, and Kiwi defector Eddie Nketia in a three-pronged 100m assault.

It begins on Monday at Scotstoun Stadium, with the men’s 100m heats among the first events on the Games athletics program before nine finals are contested in the evening session. Australia’s 100m selection call sparked a challenge from Josh Azzopardi, whose appeal, heard by the National Sports Tribunal, was ultimately unsuccessful.

Azzopardi said he felt “absolutely robbed” by the decision, but hoped it wouldn’t dent the mood in an Australian camp eyeing unprecedented track success at the Games. It appears there are no hard feelings from Browning, who is adamant the saga hasn’t dampened his relationship with Azzopardi.

The pair are both part of Australia’s five-man 4x100m relay squad in Glasgow, and worked together at training camps in Italy and Spain in the lead-up to the Games. “The nature of going through an appeal process can make this feel a little personal, but ultimately it’s not,” Browning told AAP.

Labor under pressure to allow telehealth for euthanasia but PM opposed

Labor will come under pressure to implement changes to its national policy platform and allow Australians to access voluntary assisted dying through telehealth services, with the Greens and independent MP Kate Chaney to introduce legislation.

This week’s Labor national conference in Adelaide changed the party’s platform and committed to overturn a Howard-era law banning people from having medical appointments regarding euthanasia via telehealth services.

New language added to the platform suggests Labor MPs would have a conscience vote on the issue, but the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said on Sunday the government might not progress laws through parliament.

Rate watchers eye inflation data and RBA chief’s speech

Economists are awaiting key quarterly inflation data but expect the Reserve Bank to hold interest rates despite renewed fighting in the Middle East sending oil prices up again. The Australian Bureau of Statistics will publish the consumer price index’s second quarter on Wednesday, which shows household inflation.

The Reserve Bank governor, Michele Bullock, will also speak in Sydney on Tuesday, with her speech to be closely watched for indicators on how the central bank intends to approach inflation risks.

Taylor Nugent, a NAB senior economist, says the bank does not believe another rate rise is likely in 2026 despite oil prices rising again due to tensions between the US and Iran.

double quotation markOur position is there will be enough confidence in growth slowing in the labour market so that rates don’t need to be tightened further.

That’s despite risks such as elevated inflation, renewed cost pressures and new oil price levels. The Reserve Bank’s board will next meet in more than two weeks, with the Commonwealth Bank noting the “backdrop shifting rapidly”.

double quotation markThe housing market has deteriorated, household spending is slowing from the elevated pace seen earlier this year and businesses’ capacity to pass on higher costs is likely weaker following three interest rate hikes.

The Reserve Bank was expected to keep rates on hold for the remainder of 2026, the CBA said.

An internal police investigation has been launched after a bystander was allegedly shot during a tense standoff between officers and an armed offender, AAP reports.

The woman was one of two people allegedly shot by police in Cairns, in north Queensland, on Saturday night. Ethical standards are investigating the incident after a woman was allegedly hit by a stray bullet when officers opened fire on an armed offender.

Police had been called to Benjamina Street in the southern Cairns suburb of Mount Sheridan, about 5.10pm on Saturday after reports of a man armed with knives and an attempted armed robbery. They found the 28-year-old man at a roundabout and shot him.

The state’s police minister, Dan Purdie, was reluctant to comment in detail on the shooting as it was under investigation, but said he had seen footage. He told reporters on Sunday:

double quotation markThey are highly trained. They do have equipment, and I’m sure some of those operational matters have probably all been answered by the police this morning. I acknowledge the situations, the dangerous situations, police have put themselves in.

It’s the second high-profile Queensland police shooting in three days. It follows the shooting of a police officer and the death of a man after a domestic dispute at Yengarie, near Maryborough, on the state’s Fraser Coast, on Friday evening.

The ethical standards command is investigating the incident, with oversight from the Crime and Corruption Commission, and it will be reported to the coroner.

Homicide police investigating after woman found dead in Melbourne home

In Victoria, homicide squad detectives are investigating the death of a woman whose body was found at a home in Melbourne yesterday.

In a statement, Victoria police said the 73-year-old woman was found dead inside a Fitzroy North home about 1am.

double quotation markThe cause of death is yet to be determined. An investigation into the suspicious death is ongoing.

Why are Labor women overlooked as Albanese’s potential successor?

On Thursday, Kate Ellis was elevated to become Labor’s national president, leading for the first time an all-female team at the top of the party’s organisational wing, with two female vice-presidents.

The former Rudd and Gillard government minister joins the Australian Council of Trade Unions president, Sally McManus, and its secretary, Michele O’Neill, as some of the most powerful members of the labour movement.

But as the federal caucus, again for the first time, has more women than men, they barely get a mention in discussions about who will succeed Anthony Albanese.

Read the piece from Krishani Dhanji here:

Albanese dodges questions on Point Piper dinner with donors hosted by billionaire’s son

Anthony Albanese has tried to avoid answering questions about a Labor fundraising dinner hosted by the son of a Chinese billionaire under scrutiny from the tax office.

Felix Lee, the son of Chinese billionaire high roller Phillip Dong Fang Lee, hosted the prime minister at a dinner at a Sydney mansion, reportedly attended by the Commonwealth Bank boss, Matt Comyn, the former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews, the former Asic chair James Shipton and former Future Fund boss David Murray.

Asked directly by the ABC’s David Speers if he attended the Point Piper event, Albanese said: “I attend lots of functions.”

The Sydney Morning Herald reported last week that Phillip Lee had been investigated by the ATO over large sums of money coming from China to Australia.

Speers eventually asked the PM: “Why don’t you want to answer that?”

Albanese, talking in Adelaide on Saturday night, replied: “Well, I do, you just said that that occurred. You know, that’s fine. I attend lots of dinners, in lots of places, and I don’t talk about private dinners. I have held a number this week here in Adelaide as well.”

Asked whether it was appropriate for Labor to fundraise from families under scrutiny by authorities, Albanese said he was “not aware of those issues”.

double quotation markI attend a lot of meetings, functions, with lots of people. I mean, talking about people’s relatives, even removed from that.

title: One killed and 16 injured after van crashes into crowd at Berlin Pride
excerpt:
Authorities ask for help finding 21-year-old, identified only as Abdul B, after van ramming in German capital

German authorities have issued a wanted notice for a fugitive suspect in the van ramming ...
body_text:
Authorities ask for help finding 21-year-old, identified only as Abdul B, after van ramming in German capital

German authorities have issued a wanted notice for a fugitive suspect in the van ramming near Berlin’s Pride festival that left one person dead and injured at least 16 others.

Police and prosecutors asked for help in finding the 21-year-old, whom they identified as Abdul B. They said he was believed to have injured several people with a moving vehicle on Saturday night, and that one or more people apparently then left that vehicle. Several people were also apparently stabbed, they added.

Sunday’s notice warned the public to avoid “direct contact” with the suspect, saying that he may be armed and dangerous.

Police had said earlier that they had identified a suspect with ties to Islamist groups in the German capital.

“The suspect is known to police. He is known to us as a member of Islamist circles here in Berlin, and our search for this person is proceeding at full speed,” police spokesperson Florian Nath said.

Nath added that “we still have no information whatsoever regarding his specific motives, the exact sequence of events, or his role in the crime itself”.

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, vowed to punish those responsible.

The attack forced organisers to cut short one of Europe’s largest Pride events and comes as Germany remains on edge after a series of deadly vehicle and knife attacks in recent years.

Hours after the apparent attack many details remained unclear, but police said the vehicle struck multiple ⁠people after charging into the city’s central Tiergarten park close to the Brandenburg Gate.

Police said those hurt “included several with life-threatening injuries”.

The driver of a white van had swerved shortly before 10pm into the Tiergarten park, close to the route of the Pride march held earlier in the day, hitting people on a path and crashing into a tree, police said.

“[The vehicle] was empty, which is why we are currently working intensively to track ​down the perpetrator or perpetrators,” police said. Tabloid newspaper Bild cited a witness as saying that a man emerged from the vehicle and fled on foot.

A manhunt involving helicopters and officers from several German states was under way across the capital on Sunday.

A Berlin fire department spokesperson, Dominik Pretz, said one person died and at least 16 others were injured.

Emergency workers set up a helicopter landing pad near the Reichstag parliament building to transport the injured to hospitals.

Merz said in a statement that he and the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, would “push to make sure this horrific act is fully investigated and punished”.

Julian Methig, who attended the event, described it as a terrible day. “It’s one of the worst days for the queer community and a day I personally hoped I’d never have to experience … I’m shocked.”

Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in the German capital in warm summer sunshine to celebrate the pride parade.

It is known in Germany as Christopher Street Day (CSD), named after the site of the Stonewall Inn in New York City where riots against police raids touched off the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. CSD was first held in West Berlin in 1979.

Berlin mayor, Kai Wegner, called the deadly assault “an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society”.

“Following a peaceful and colourful CSD, the rally for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal manner,” he said on X. “Berlin is the city of freedom – and our freedom has today been attacked in the most appalling way. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and friends.”

For the first time in its history, CSD began on Friday night this year with a pro-democracy political rally. Berlin will hold a state election in September.

The parade on Saturday ran under the motto “Taking a stand is hot” which organisers said was “in response to increasing hostility” to queer people in Germany.

More than 80 floats and 50 groups on foot joined the procession through the city centre past Potsdamer Platz and the Victory Column monument in the Tiergarten, culminating in a rally at the Brandenburg Gate.

Earlier in the day one person was arrested for resisting police orders at a far-right counterprotest against the event.

Before last year’s pride parade, Berlin LGBTQ+ organisations sounded the alarm that attacks had become more frequent while hard-won rights were under threat.

Campaigners said a rise in hostility has accompanied the surge in support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, now the most popular party in national opinion polls, as well as an increase in Islamist-inspired attacks.

title: House of Hope: New film follows a Waldorf-inspired school in the West Bank
excerpt: At one point in the documentary, House of Hope, the protagonist, Manar Wahhab, breaks down in a classroom corner in the school she founded with her husband in the occupied West Bank. The cameras keep ...
body_text:
At one point in the documentary, House of Hope, the protagonist, Manar Wahhab, breaks down in a classroom corner in the school she founded with her husband in the occupied West Bank. The cameras keep rolling.

“To step into someone’s life with a camera at the moment when they’re really down, it feels a little bit uncomfortable, but we made the choice together to keep filming during these moments. I wanted the audience to be there with them,” director Marjolein Busstra told Al Jazeera.

The film follows Wahhab, a Palestinian woman who established a Waldorf school with her husband, Milad Vosgueritchian, in al-Eizariya in the occupied West Bank.

House of Hope Vision Kindergarten & School teaches the Waldorf philosophy of non-violent resistance and offers children a space to express their emotions and cope with the trauma and difficulty of living under occupation.

“The school protects the children’s dignity in the present moment. It’s more about refusing to let occupation shape their inner world, so that they can actually be children and have agency,” Busstra said. “It’s in Waldorf philosophy that they make space to express the feelings.”

Working with a Palestinian crew, Busstra spent three years with Wahhab, travelling to the occupied West Bank nine times throughout the course of the documentary. She first met Wahhab 18 years ago during a film workshop in the West Bank.

Although the documentary centres around the elementary school, Wahhab is the story’s driving force. The story follows Wahhab and Vosgueritchian, both at the school and at home with their children.

“I started filming the school, but right away, I knew I wanted to do it about Manar’s inner life,” Busstra said. “I think hope is a difficult word at the moment, but I have a deep awe for Manar, who keeps creating and teaching even while carrying so much herself.”

For Wahhab, her respect for Busstra and their existing friendship helped her trust the film crew during vulnerable moments.

“We both believe deeply in education, in children’s creativity and freedom and in seeing the human being as something whole and beautiful in mind, soul and spirit. Those shared values created openness and trust between us and helped shape a film that is not only about events but also about humanity,” Wahhab told Al Jazeera.

The film was produced by Think-Film, the company behind The Voice of Hind Rajab, which tells the story of the five-year-old Hind killed by Israeli forces in 2024. Soldiers fired 335 bullets into the car carrying the girl and six of her family members – a story that became a symbol for the system failure to protect children in Gaza.

Although sometimes difficult, Wahhab said she made an effort to let the crew document multiple facets of her life.

“Over those three years, the crew met many versions of Manar. Sometimes they arrived, and I was fresh, energetic and cooperative. Other times, they found me exhausted, angry, overwhelmed, or ill,” she said. “I understood that I had to be as authentic as possible, because I was representing not only myself, but also my community, hope, peace and the voice of Palestinians.”

Wahhab and Vosgueritchian founded the school out of a desire to offer a different kind of education to Palestinian children and to provide a place where they felt safe and could share their emotions.

“The school was born many years ago when we saw the hardships surrounding our community and wanted to create something different, a space of love, safety, creativity and healing,” Wahhab said. “House of Hope is an idea, a mission and an energy that we carry wherever we go.”

In an increasingly violent Israeli occupation, Wahhab considers the Waldorf philosophy essential.

“I do not see nonviolence as weakness. Actually, I believe the opposite. Violence is easy. Nonviolence requires courage, awareness, patience and inner work. It asks us to see beyond our own pain and ego and to hold on to our humility even when circumstances are trying to pull us away from it,” she said.

“The world absorbs the energy that we create, and right now, there is so much fear, anger and violence in our world. I think we need more peace within ourselves, peace with one another and peace with nature,” Wahhab added.

After Hamas’s incursion into southern Israel on October 7, 2023, came Israel’s brutal military response. Life became increasingly difficult for Wahhab, Vosgueritchian and the children at House of Hope, but the crew continued to document their realities.

“The story I wanted to create with Manar stayed the same, but after October 7, everything became heavier. They were so down for a while. They were like different people, like they lost all hope,” Busstra said. “The school built this safe haven, but the occupation is always rattling at the door.”

Israel’s intensified military actions in the West Bank, including the shooting and killing of children, are a constant spectre. In another scene, Wahhab watches her son leave for school and checks to see if he has a phone charger and spare clothes in case he is held at a checkpoint for hours.

“The energy is so heavy now. I hope people understand that we are not asking for something extraordinary. We are asking for basic human rights, the right to live with dignity and freedom, the right to safety and the right to be fully human beings,” Manar said.

Busstra, who closely followed Wahhab for three years, said she wants audiences to go “beyond the framing of us vs them”.

“I hope that this stays with people, not as something distant that happens to others, but something they can locate within their own understanding of what it means to love someone in an unsafe world.”

Wahhab believes the film offers a more nuanced perspective of Palestinians.

“I think that in the West, many people see a very limited picture of Palestine and the Middle East. Sometimes they see us through stereotypes as terrorists, as people who are undeveloped or somehow less than themselves,” she said. “I hope this film helps people look beyond those images. The news does not tell the full reality. It often shows only violence and people killing one another. It doesn’t show the essence of people’s lives. It shows negativity,” she said.

Wahhab encouraged people to consider the documentary through a lens of shared humanity.

House of Hope won the best international feature documentary prize at the Hot Docs Canadian International Documentary Festival in May 2026 and was recently screened at UNESCO in Paris. It will soon be screened at the Jerusalem Arab Film Festival.

“Even though our story is deeply rooted in the West Bank, its message is universal. Our hope is that people everywhere can see our story and take something meaningful from it.”

title: Typhoon Noul makes landfall in China, with hundreds of thousands evacuated
excerpt:
Typhoon Noul has hit southern China, including Hong Kong, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to the region and prompting the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people in Guangdong province.

Chi...
body_text:
Typhoon Noul has hit southern China, including Hong Kong, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to the region and prompting the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people in Guangdong province.

China’s national weather centre said Noul made landfall on the coast of Huidong county in Huizhou, southern Guangdong province, at approximately 3:50am local time on Sunday (19:50 GMT on Saturday).

China’s official Xinhua News Agency said Noul was the strongest typhoon to make landfall in China so far this year.

Hong Kong’s Observatory said Noul, with maximum sustained winds of 110 kilometres per hour (68 miles per hour) near its centre, was moving Sunday into inland Guangdong and weakening progressively, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to parts of the region.

More than 715,000 people had been relocated for safety by early Sunday in Guangdong province, according to state-owned China National Radio. On Saturday, authorities said some 340,000 people were evacuated.

China’s National Meteorological Centre expected parts of southern Guangdong and southeastern Fujian provinces to experience heavy rain and strong winds over the weekend.

Many trees were seen uprooted in Huilai county, located on the coast of Guangdong province, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

Hong Kong’s airport authority said about 350 flights were cancelled on Sunday. At least nine people were injured across the city during the typhoon period, according to Hong Kong authorities.

As Noul approached Hong Kong, parts of a large scaffolding on a high-rise building collapsed on Saturday afternoon, local police said, although initial reports indicated there were no injuries.

Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration said Noul was bringing rainfall to parts of southern and eastern Taiwan. It was passing over waters south of Taiwan and was moving away from the island Saturday.

Earlier this month, Typhoon Bavi brought strong winds and rain to eastern China, leading to the evacuation of more than two million people. It made landfall on July 11. Another, Maysak, made landfall in southern China on July 3.

title: A third of UK journalists have changed how or what they report over fears for safety, study finds
excerpt:
Government-backed investigation finds risks are normalised amid ‘a narrowing of the public conversation’

Journalists are self-censoring their reporting on rightwing protests, Donald Trump’s administr...
body_text:
Government-backed investigation finds risks are normalised amid ‘a narrowing of the public conversation’

Journalists are self-censoring their reporting on rightwing protests, Donald Trump’s administration and trans issues because of growing concerns about their personal safety, with newsrooms accused of “normalising” the risks they face.

Hundreds of journalists from across the UK have anonymously disclosed increasing nervousness over their security. Some have reported avoiding or altering coverage on certain topics due to intimidation, leading to self-censorship and “a narrowing of the public conversation”.

The findings are revealed in a government-backed investigation into the safety of journalists, ordered amid growing hostility to traditional media across the west.

“There have definitely been times where there’s been a story that’s maybe in the public interest, maybe worth reporting on, where we have had frank discussions about whether it’s ‘worth it’,” said one journalist.

Another said: “I was definitely looking over my shoulder and making sure I wasn’t being followed and making sure that people weren’t going to start shouting things at me.”

Investigators found a widespread belief that abuse linked to reporting has increased, especially online. They also reported newsroom cultures that treated the increase as inevitable given the polarised political environment – with journalists expected to be “thick-skinned”.

Female journalists faced the brunt of abuse, describing gendered and sexualised harassment, explicit threats, inappropriate messages and online comments focused on appearance.

Common topics raised by journalists as causing safety concerns were rightwing anti-immigration protests, the Trump administration, including protests against US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), as well as trans issues.

“Anti-immigration protests were most widely referenced by journalists, both regarding the in-person risks of attending the marches and the backlash to any subsequent reporting,” the investigation found.

Similar findings have been recorded in the US, where the International Women’s Media Foundation found journalists were working in heightened political polarisation, declining public trust in the media and increasing exposure to physical and psychological risks.

There are numerous accounts of journalists in Northern Ireland facing intimidation from masked men while covering anti-immigration riots, disclosed to the UK’s National Union of Journalists.

In another case, footage of a journalist covering an anti-immigration protest was circulated in a Facebook group, with people working together to identify and locate them.

One respondent described seeing a female journalist subjected to misogynistic heckling at a “unite the kingdom” rally, with the footage later uploaded to social media.

With debates about the personal safety of reporters now a regular discussion point in newsrooms, ministers ordered an investigation by Alma Economics. It amounts to one of the most comprehensive assessments of journalist safety ever produced in the UK, surveying 531 journalists, alongside 55 in-depth interviews.

Almost half of those surveyed said safety concerns influenced their willingness to report on certain stories, while about a third had changed how or what they covered.

The investigation found the shift to online and video journalism had made journalists more identifiable.

“Journalists used to be much more anonymous,” said one reporter. “Now, you’re expected to be live, presenting TikToks all the time … People talk about all sorts of things about like: ‘What’s the future of journalism?’ and ‘How can we adapt?’ But very rarely is it discussed, ‘What does that take from us?’ And especially from female journalists.”

Participants acknowledged that the UK still remained a safe place to work as a journalist compared with other parts of the world.

However, reporters said the risks had intensified over time, driven by “declining public trust, narratives portraying the media as ‘fake news’, and blurred boundaries between journalists and the public” – meaning the rise of “citizen journalists” who have no journalistic training but have access to large online audiences.

“The research findings make for grim reading,” said Laura Davison, the NUJ’s general secretary. “Abuse should never be viewed as part of a journalist’s job. Not only does this behaviour have a hugely detrimental impact on people’s lives, it also has a chilling effect on journalists’ ability to do their jobs and freedom of the press.

“It’s also time for social media companies to finally recognise their responsibility in preventing the abuse and harassment.”

A Department for Culture, Media and Sport spokesperson said the government was working with the National Committee for the Safety of Journalists to tackle harassment and threats.

“It is crucial to create the conditions in which reporters feel supported and protected so that they can focus on telling the stories that matter most,” they said.

title: How Trump could undermine the midterms
excerpt:
The president really has no power over elections – but that hasn’t stopped Trump from laying the groundwork to challenge results in November

When Donald Trump commandeered primetime US television las...
body_text:
The president really has no power over elections – but that hasn’t stopped Trump from laying the groundwork to challenge results in November

When Donald Trump commandeered primetime US television last Friday, he delivered a familiar, but still extraordinary, message. The president argued once again that the results of the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden, were illegitimate.

US elections are “vulnerable to being rigged and stolen”, Trump alleged, claiming that “the trust of the American people was lost” when he was defeated.

Historically, incumbent parties underperform in midterm elections and with the president’s popularity sagging – he has an approval rating of just 37% – Republicans appear on course to lose seats in the US Senate and House of Representatives, as well as in state and local elections, in November.

Trump’s latest intervention, in which he accused China of interfering with the 2020 election, is viewed by US voting rights activists as just the latest escalation of a bid by the White House to influence, and potentially alter, the results of the 2026 midterm elections.

“The number one threat facing American elections is the continued lies coming out of the White House,” said the Arizona secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, the official responsible for overseeing the state’s elections.

The president is fighting to persuade Congress to approve legislation, the Save Act, that would allow the US federal government greater control over elections. Trump has also called for the federal government to take direct control of elections in some states, falsely claiming that his defeats there in 2020 were illegitimate.

There’s just one snag. “We have an election system that is not run by the federal government,” said Ben Berwick, who leads Protect Democracy’s election law and litigation team. “It’s run by states and local jurisdictions.”

The president, he added, “really has no power over elections”. So what can Trump actually do?

Republicans in a handful of states have already scrambled, at Trump’s urging, to redraw their congressional maps in the wake of a landmark decision by the US supreme court – controlled by a conservative supermajority – that effectively gutted a major section of the Voting Rights Act.

Louisiana led the way, tearing up its old map of four Republican and two Democratic districts in favor of a new one, which will probably give Republicans five of the state’s six congressional seats. Such efforts are designed to shift the outcome of future elections.

And with threats to mail-in voting, sowing fears about voting machines, as well as a steady stream of unfounded allegations of election fraud, many fear Trump appears to be laying the groundwork to challenge results that don’t go his way in November.

The memory of the deadly 6 January attack on the US Capitol in 2021, fueled by Trump’s denial of his election defeat, looms large.

“It’s reckless that the president will continue to do what he’s doing, and that the folks around him will continue to let him do what he’s doing, and potentially trigger that sort of behavior that could cost lives,” added Fontes. “This is a powder keg out there, and there’s a lot of folks who just just want to get on with their lives, who just want to get on to solving their own problems.”

Trump has repeatedly tried to restrict voting by mail, and likened it to cheating, despite doing so himself. It is a key focus of his administration’s efforts. In November, the administration could use the US Postal Service (USPS) to “control the flow of mail-in ballots, and potentially not send ballots to certain voters”, Berwick said.

Democratic voters are deemed more likely to cast their ballots by mail than Republicans: about one in four registered Democrats did so in 2024, according to the States United Democracy Center, alongside 1 in 5 registered Republicans.

Eight states and the District of Columbia rely almost exclusively on postal ballots. The USPS, at Trump’s direction, proposed a rule that would require states to turn over their voter roll information to the federal government, which would then tell states which voters were ineligible.

That proposal, enforced by an executive order in March, faces a wall of legal challenges and was ruled unconstitutional by a judge. Cases pursued by the civil rights group NAACP in Washington DC and the League of Women’s Voters in Massachusetts have challenged the plan in court.

Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters, said the organization intervened to ensure the bid to restrict mail-in voting was “shut down” in time for state primary elections, taking place in the months ahead of November’s general election. “And so I think that was really important for us,” she said, “just to make sure that voters knew how that was going to work, and make sure that they understood what their rights were, and how they could execute their ballot effectively”.

At polling stations, Trump is also pointing to electronic voting machines, which he suggested in his 16 July TV address could be compromised by foreign actors. “China carried out what is believed to be the largest compromise of election data in history, resulting in China’s illicit acquisition of 220 million US voter files,” he said.

Declassified files from US investigators show that China downloaded publicly-available election data in 2022. Those same investigators concluded that China did not interfere in the election.

Voting rights advocates believe Trump may have been telegraphing his intent to try to block the use of some voting machines in a late-day election gambit, invoking national security as a rationale.

“The thing that maybe worries me the most is what we saw in Fulton county and elsewhere,” Berwick said, referring to an FBI raid in January that resulted in the seizure of 2020 ballots and election material in Georgia. The administration “may try to do something similar in the immediate post-election period under the sort of pretext of investigating ineligible voting, or votes cast by ineligible voters”, he suggested, “in a way that, if done in the immediate post-election period, would be designed to disrupt the ability of states to count votes and certify elections”.

In the meantime, the White House has actively undermined safeguards to the election system. The Election Assistance Commission, a US federal agency designed to help states overcome technical challenges in election administration, which currently has no commissioners. Trump fired the Democrat members, and allowed the Republicans to resign. More than a third of the staff of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency was meanwhile cut by Trump’s so-called “Department of Government Efficiency”, the cost-cutting drive fleetingly led by Elon Musk, including the entire team looking at cybersecurity threats in elections.

“One cannot help but notice the irony of the administration’s purported interest in securing our election systems, and yet gutting the very agency responsible for that,” said Hannah Fried, co-founder and CEO of All Voting is Local.

The Save Act, which is stalled in Congress, would require voters to present their passport or birth certificate to register to vote, and then to provide photo ID from a narrow list of valid identifications to vote in person. Campaigners argue such restrictions would disproportionately impact Black, Native, elderly and student voters.

The legislation would also sharply constrain voting by mail, too. And it would require states to turn over their voter rolls to the federal government.

Absent that legislation – which is constitutionally questionable – federal agencies under Trump may still try to pressure states to purge voter rolls using unreliable or unverified federal data sets. Courts have consistently blocked attempts by the federal government to force unvetted voter purges.

Some states – led by Republican officials – have already turned over voter rolls, when requested by the federal government.

Berwick highlighted the prospect of federal agencies like the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security seeking voter lists from states, “presumably to then send to states lists of voters they believe are ineligible, which are very likely to be inaccurate”.

While far-right figures like Steve Bannon, an ally and former adviser of Trump, have called for the deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents or federal law enforcement at voting sites, and the president himself has explicitly raised the prospect, it is considered remote because federal law plainly outlaws the presence of troops or federal agents at polling places.

Voter intimidation has already manifested at early voting sites and drop boxes, said Stewart, of the League of Women Voters, who cited an incident in Arizona where armed contractors confronted voters. “The president in particular is pushing for increased ICE funding,” she said. “So you have to ask: for what?”

Stewart highlighted how her organization successfully sued to stop armed drop-box intimidation in 2022, securing a court order within 24 hours. The incident was a demonstration of “how quickly things like that can happen” she said, “but equally as quickly … how we can shut that down”.

Trump’s increasingly inflammatory rhetoric is itself a threat to the integrity of the 2026 election, said Georgia state senator Saira Draper, a leading voting administration expert, who warned that narrative attacks are designed to undermine outcomes, regardless of who wins.

“By sowing distrust in elections, no matter what the outcome is, he continues on the division, whether his party wins or not into the next term,” said Draper, who suggested that such constant rhetoric turns followers into “foot soldiers for the cause”.

Some of those foot soldiers sit on county boards of elections, which are required to certify elections. And some are running for office, successfully winning the Republican nomination, like Alex Kolodin, who helped lead failed legal efforts to overturn Arizona’s 2020 and 2022 election results, who is now the Republican candidate for Arizonan secretary of state: its top elections official.

After the 2020 election, some Republican elections board members refused to certify fair elections, threatening to disrupt the process. A mass refusal could cast doubt on the results in conservative states that have taken a Democratic turn in a swing year.

“This federal interference led by the president isn’t helping anybody,” said Fontes. “It’s not good for, in my view, any circumstance across the country, and it’s got everybody on pins and needles for no really good reason.

“I mean, what’s the really good reason why folks are afraid, that there’s something wrong with our elections? The only explanation is that Donald Trump can’t get over getting his butt kicked in 2020.”

title: Venezuela men sue aviation firms who flew them to notorious Salvadorian jail
excerpt:
Exclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdown

Venezuelan men sent last year to a notorious Salvadorian terrorism prison by the Trump adm...
body_text:
Exclusive: CSI Aviation and GlobalX accused of violating civil rights as part of Trump immigration crackdown

Venezuelan men sent last year to a notorious Salvadorian terrorism prison by the Trump administration are suing the US aviation companies that transported them there.

A lawsuit filed this week in federal court in Washington DC accuses the companies CSI Aviation and GlobalX of violating the Venezuelans’ civil rights, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, negligence and other violations, for their role in flying the three planes that took the men to El Salvador.

CSI and GlobalX “went to great lengths” to undertake the “rendition flights” to El Salvador, “in concert with the US government, in flagrant violation of US and international law”, the lawsuit reads.

Last year, in March, the Trump administration expelled more than 230 Venezuelan men held in US immigration custody to El Salvador, where they were detained for four months in a maximum security terrorism prison and tortured.

The lawsuit accuses CSI and GlobalX of deliberately transporting the men to El Salvador, despite a federal judge ordering the flights to return and despite knowing they would probably be tortured inside the country’s Terrorism Confinement Center (known as “Cecot” by its acronym in Spanish).

Without CSI and GlobalX’s complicity, “neither Plaintiffs nor the Class would have been rendered to CECOT”, the lawsuit reads.

The suit was filed by a team of human rights attorneys on 17 July and is being reported first by the Guardian. It is one of the latest attempts by rights groups to hold private contractors accountable for their role in alleged abuses stemming from the administration’s aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown.

“Many people might not be aware of the degree to which private companies are intertwined with the human rights abuses occurring under the Trump administration through the detention and unlawful deportation schemes that are occurring,” said Anthony Enriquez, the vice-president of advocacy and litigation for the Kennedy Human Rights Center, in an interview with the Guardian. Enriquez is one of the attorneys representing the Venezuelan men.

CSI and GlobalX, which were hired by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), have “enjoyed unprecedented financial profits from the scheme”, while the Venezuelans “continue to experience severe emotional suffering from the humiliation, terror, and cruelty that they endured”, the lawsuit says.

The DHS did not respond to specific claims in the lawsuit and instead referred all questions to the Salvadorian government. CSI and GlobalX did not respond to a detailed request for comment by time of publication.

El Salvador’s government does not make efforts to publicly rebut allegations of brutal treatment inside Cecot. Online influencers are invited in to make videos of the harsh conditions.

CSI Aviation Inc is incorporated in Texas and GlobalX is headquartered in Florida, with both companies playing a significant role in the administration’s mass deportation campaign. The lawsuit says that the American companies were hired by the US government to conduct the El Salvador-bound deportation flights.

CSI has helped broker “nearly all” deportation flights, the lawsuit says, via a multimillion-dollar contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the main agency within the DHS carrying out deportations. CSI is the single highest-value recipient of ICE contracts, the lawsuit adds, with revenue from ICE in 2025 totaling $1.23bn.

For the three flights to El Salvador, CSI sub-contracted with GlobalX, with CSI working as the “intermediary” between ICE and GlobalX, according to the lawsuit.

On 15 March last year, Donald Trump stepped outside government norms to invoke the Alien Enemies Act as a strategy to expel hundreds of Venezuelan immigrants from the US. The US president accused the Venezuelan government, at the time run by Nicolás Maduro, who is now facing trial in the US, of instructing members of the South American gang Tren de Aragua to “invade” the US.

After invoking the Alien Enemies Act, the administration rounded up 252 Venezuelan and Salvadorian men in ICE detention and expelled them to El Salvador. This came after the US and El Salvador struck a controversial and opaque deal, in which the US would pay millions of dollars to El Salvador to detain deportees from the US in Cecot. The administration never proved, and has still not proved, the Venezuelan men were members of Tren de Aragua.

The same day that the Alien Enemies Act was invoked, GlobalX, “working at the behest of CSI”, positioned three planes at an airport in Texas in preparation for the expulsion, the lawsuit says.

After the flights had taken off to Central America, a federal judge in Washington DC ordered they return to the US. The administration and airline companies ignored the court order and eventually arrived in El Salvador.

“Despite knowing that El Salvador’s Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo (‘CECOT’) mega-prison was a notorious blacksite, from which no detainee had ever left alive, Defendants went to great lengths to transport Plaintiffs and Class Members there, in concert with the US government, in flagrant violation of U.S. and international law,” the lawsuit reads. “Defendants evaded or ignored judicial oversight and the foreseeable risk of torture and successfully delivered Plaintiffs and the Class to El Salvador for imprisonment at CECOT.”

The real horror began for the men once they landed in El Salvador, with many thinking they had at least arrived home to Venezuela. Salvadorian security forces boarded the planes, beat the deportees, many later said, and transported them to Cecot.

According to a November 2025 report from Human Rights Watch, the men were “subjected to what amounts to arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance under international human rights law”.

The HRW report and lawsuit also detail brutal conditions and torture inside Cecot, accusing guards of beating, pepper-spraying, firing rubber bullets and sexually assaulting detainees.

Lawmakers, families and members of the public protested against the immigrants’ detention in Cecot. News reports revealed the identities of some of the men, showing that some were falsely accused of being gang members.

Four months later, in July 2025, the group of Venezuelans were returned to their home country after a prisoner exchange deal involving the three countries. The group of Salvadorians, also sent to Cecot in those flights, are still presumably detained there. To this date, the US government has not released the entire list of deportees sent to Cecot.

The Venezuelan men continue to struggle with long-lasting health effects and mental health trauma, the lawsuit says. The three main plaintiffs in the case experience daily headaches, difficulty sleeping and emotional distress from the experience.

CSI and GlobalX “have enjoyed unprecedented financial profits from the scheme and their relationship with the Administration”, the lawsuit says, while the Venezuelan men “continue to experience severe emotional suffering from the humiliation, terror, and cruelty that they endured”.

The companies have not yet responded to the lawsuit. Federal judge James Boasberg, who is presiding over the original Cecot deportation case, will be overseeing the lawsuit’s proceedings and determine whether the entire class of Venezuelans can sue.

title: ‘Scandalous, irrational and irresponsible’: French beekeepers’ fury at lifting of pesticides ban
excerpt:
Allowing use of two neonicotinoids to combat crop-ruining disease will kill bees and reduce harvests, union says

Beekeepers and environmentalists in France have reacted furiously after parliament app...
body_text:
Allowing use of two neonicotinoids to combat crop-ruining disease will kill bees and reduce harvests, union says

Beekeepers and environmentalists in France have reacted furiously after parliament approved a bill reauthorising two banned pesticides scientists say can poison bees.

“There are no words to describe the frustration,” said Carolyn Bouguet, a beekeeper in Essonne, greater Paris. “Bee populations have already been badly compromised by climate change, new parasites and loss of habitat. And now this.”

Henri Clément, a beekeeper in the southern Lozère department and spokesperson for the French beekeeping association, UNAF, said the measure was “an absolute disaster for our sector, and for biodiversity as a whole”.

For bees, the risk was “very high mortality rates and reduced harvests”, Clément told local media. “It’s just incomprehensible these pesticides have been reauthorised. We’ve been fighting them for 30 years. It’s scandalous, irrational and irresponsible.”

The law, passed on Tuesday, allows France’s food and environmental safety agency, Anses, to grant waivers authorising the use of the pesticides acetamiprid and flupyradifurone in struggling farm sectors and under exceptional circumstances.

The use of the pesticides, allowed in the EU but banned in France, will be authorised to combat aphid-borne diseases that can ruin crops of sugar beet, apples, hazelnuts and cherries, which has led producers to claim they can no longer compete with European rivals.

Scientific studies have established that acetamiprid, a neonicotinoid with powerful neurotoxic effects, can poison bees, affecting their foraging capacity and memory. A 2024 study suggested flupyradifurone could be lethal to some honeybees.

Greenpeace France said the country’s centrist government and its rightwing allies in parliament were “trampling on science, health, the environment and the clear will of the people”, describing the legislation as “deeply concerning” and “a disgrace”.

France’s environment minister, Monique Barbut, said the legislation was “one environmental setback too many” and submitted her resignation on Wednesday, but was later persuaded to stay on after meeting President Emmanuel Macron.

However, France’s largest farmers’ union, the FNSEA, welcomed the bill’s approval as “a major milestone and a victory for French farmers”, while the agriculture minister, Annie Genevard, said it brought “real and tangible solutions” to growers.

According to agriculture ministry figures, honey production in France halved between the mid-1990s, when neonicotinoids were introduced, and the mid-2010s, although habitat loss and climate breakdown were also contributing factors.

Bouguet said France had been “a model” for other countries when it banned neonicotinoids. Scientific research showed the pesticides harmed not just insects but soil ecosystems, and could have an impact on human health, she noted.

“Bees are the canary in the environmental coalmine,” she said. “Their health is a huge indicator of what’s happening in the natural world. Protecting bees means protecting life. Protecting life means protecting our future.”

Christian Pons, the UNAF president, told reporters the law “claims to defend French food sovereignty, but since when is it acceptable to destroy one sector – that of beekeepers – in order to save another, for example that of hazelnut trees?”

Yves Delaunay, a beekeeper from the western Vendée department, said that after neonicotinoids were introduced in the 1990s, his honey production “went from 80kg per hive to 5kg” and the colonies “collapsed”.

“In just a few days, we went from 70,000 bees to 20,000,” he told local media. “They were disoriented, unable to return to the hive. We found them dead everywhere. It was a huge loss.”

The senate backed the bill by 214 votes to 111 on Tuesday after it received lower house approval. The proposal to authorise the two pesticides was included in the bill late in the legislative process to help ensure it cleared the right-leaning upper house.

The French parliament last year passed a bill reauthorising acetamiprid despite a petition against it that gathered more than 2m signatures. That bill was annulled by the constitutional council, which said it did not abide by France’s environmental charter.

Barbut, who previously headed the conservation charity WWF France, said after the vote that she had sought to defend “the silence of our forests, the quality of our water, the purity of our air, the richness of our soils and the diversity of life”.

She said she was resigning because “the forces opposing these goals have become so powerful that I can no longer carry this ambition through”, but reversed her decision after Macron gave her “guarantees” on climate action goals.

Genevard, the agriculture minister, has said the health agency would only allow the pesticides’ use in certain areas for limited periods and when there was “no impact on human health or the environment, an emergency situation … and no alternative”.

The beekeeping union , environmental groups and left-leaning members of parliament have said they will refer the new law to the constitutional council on the grounds that its fails to provide adequate safeguards for human health and the environment.

title: New front in US-Iran war escalates as Houthis fire at Saudi oil facilities
excerpt: Tehran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen have fired missiles and drones at two of Saudi Arabia’s most strategically important oil facilities on the Red Sea, in a major escalation of the latest simmering r...
body_text:
Tehran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen have fired missiles and drones at two of Saudi Arabia’s most strategically important oil facilities on the Red Sea, in a major escalation of the latest simmering regional conflict to be reignited by the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran.

But the skies over the country at the epicentre of the widening war were quiet for a second successive night, with no new US attacks on Iran reported by Sunday morning.

Iran had been pounded by 13 consecutive waves of overnight US air strikes since July 11, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attacked tankers trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz. As hostilities escalated, both sides declared that an interim peace agreement signed in June was dead, and a second phase of talks to finalise a comprehensive peace deal appeared doomed.

But there have been no US air strikes since Friday, and tentative signs are emerging that Washington and Tehran are still talking via mediators and might return to more meaningful discussions.

Even if another fragile truce is agreed, however, the cascade of consequences unleashed by the war is still stoking conflict and confrontation elsewhere.

Iran’s attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have put a stranglehold on exports of oil and raw materials for fertiliser, sending energy prices soaring and raising the risk of a food security crisis in some of the world’s most vulnerable countries.

In March, in response to attacks on Iran, the Tehran-backed Hezbollah movement in Lebanon resumed missile attacks on Israel, which then launched a devastating invasion of southern Lebanon that has displaced 1.2 million people.

Now, another smouldering regional conflict has erupted again, between US-allied Saudi Arabia and the Houthi movement which controls most of northern and western Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia and its regional allies joined a brutal civil war against the Houthis in 2015, until a truce was agreed in 2022.

The truce collapsed this month after an attack on Sanaa airport to stop an Iranian plane landing provoked the Houthis to fire ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia. Last Monday, the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, and late on Friday the Saudis launched air strikes on the Houthi-held city of Hodeidah.

In retaliation, Houthi forces launched Sunday’s attacks on facilities belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco in the coastal cities of Jizan and Yanbu, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.

There has been no comment from Saudi Arabia on the extent of any damage to Aramco’s refinery in Jizan, but a large column of smoke was seen rising after the attack.

In Yanbu, Saudi Arabia’s principal west coast export gateway, two ballistic missiles aimed at oil installations were intercepted by a Patriot battery operated in Saudi Arabia by the Greek military under an agreement ‌with Riyadh.

The escalating conflict has raised fears that the Houthis could block the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. If both the Bab al-Mandeb and Hormuz straits were blocked, the resulting supply chain crisis would cause major economic damage across the world.

Besides spreading to the Red Sea, the US-Iran war has become entangled with the deadliest active conflict in the world – Russia’s attempted conquest of Ukraine.

A long-range strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea on Saturday caused an explosion that killed one sailor and wounded another, according to Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which blamed the attack on Ukraine and summoned Kyiv’s charge d’affaires in Tehran to convey its condemnation of the “hostile and criminal” act.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X that Kyiv had achieved “very strong results” with long-range strikes in the Caspian Sea, hitting “vessels used in military cargo shipments involving Iran, as well as a warship”.

Zelenskyy claimed in further comments on X on Saturday that since the start of July, Kyiv had detected “active Russian satellite ⁠surveillance of the Gulf states and US military facilities located there”. He said the satellite images were passed to Tehran to help the IRGC identify targets for ballistic missile and drone attacks.

US President Donald Trump has not given a reason for the sudden cessation in air strikes on Iran, but a senior administration official told the Reuters news agency that Trump “has always been clear that his preference is diplomacy, but he has shown Iran what will happen if they fail to come to the table in a serious way”.

Trump said on Friday that there was still some communication with Iran.

“They are talking to us right now; they’d love to make a deal,” he said. “I don’t think they’re ready to … but I’m willing to listen.”

Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, said Iranian officials had confirmed the two sides were exchanging messages.

“There have been proposals conveyed by the mediators, and Tehran is still reviewing them,” Serdar said, adding there was “not much progress yet” due to “fundamental differences” in their positions and deep mistrust.
