title: Reform councillors told to call donations inquiry ‘establishment stitch-up’
excerpt:
Party briefing notes say: ‘Daily routine of hit jobs and smears will not deter us from winning next general election’

Reform UK has instructed its councillors to describe a police investigation into ...
body_text:
Party briefing notes say: ‘Daily routine of hit jobs and smears will not deter us from winning next general election’

Reform UK has instructed its councillors to describe a police investigation into donations from the mother of George Cottrell as an establishment stitch-up, as polling showed the party’s popularity plummeting.

Internal briefing documents circulated to the party’s councillors included instructions to respond to questions about a Metropolitan police investigation into party donations with: “It is now clear that the establishment will try anything to stop us”, the Times revealed on Thursday.

Local government representatives were also instructed to respond to questions with: “The British people are tired of the establishment media doing anything they can to stop Reform. A daily routine of hit jobs and smears will not deter us from winning the next general election and fixing broken Britain.”

Police are investigating donations worth £500,000 made to Reform UK by Fiona Cottrell, the mother of the crypto-gambler and convicted fraudster “Posh George”, who is a close friend of Farage.

The Guardian revealed in April that the Reform UK leader had received a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election, which is currently subject to standards inquiry. The Conservatives have also asked HMRC to investigate whether Farage should have paid tax on the £5m gift. Farage is also subject to another inquiry over allegations that he breached parliamentary rules by being financially supported by Cottrell.

New polling by YouGov shows that Nigel Farage’s popularity has plummeted, falling to the joint lowest level in the decade it has been tracked by the pollster. Only 22% of people have a positive view of Farage, while 68% see him in a negative light – a net favourability rating of -46.

YouGov said the figure was on a par with figures recorded by Boris Johnson after the first “partygate” revelations had broken (-42 in early December 2021) and Keir Starmer just before his resignation (-45).

On -11%, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, is also enjoying popularity levels higher than those of any Conservative leader for more than five years, according to the survey. It has Burnham on +3%.

Separate polling by More in Common indicated that Burnham’s personal approval rating is already higher after a week in office than Starmer ever achieved. The new prime minister has a net approval rating of +13, with a blitz of voter-pleasing policies appearing to have given a boost to the former mayor of Greater Manchester.

In addition, YouGov’s latest voting-intention poll fo the Times and Sky News showed that Labour and the Tories are now within touching distance of Reform UK. Labour appears to be enjoying a “Burnham bounce”, with the party at its most popular since January.

It shows Labour just two points behind Reform – with Farage’s party on 23% of the vote, Labour on 21% and the Conservatives on 20%.

YouGov gives Labour its highest figure recorded by the pollsters since January, up five points from the 16% low recorded for the party four times between March and early May this year.

The polling continues to show a tightening between the three parties. In the aftermath of May’s local elections, Reform UK polled a 28% vote share, giving them an 11-point lead over any other party.

In his first cabinet meeting, Burnham promised to lead a “cost of living government”, and has used a string of early morning announcements this morning to grab the public’s attention.

His first major announcement since taking office was a cut to VAT on electricity bills from October, before capping bus fares at £2 and giving pubs, clubs and live music venues a 20% discount on their business rates bills as part of a £100m aid package. Burnham has faced questions about how these measures will be paid for, but the new administration insists all measures are fully funded.

title: Life without refrigerators: Gaza residents fight heat and food spoilage
excerpt: Gaza City — Inside the tent Malak al-Zaanin has lived in since being displaced from her home in Gaza, the mother of four holds a tray of rice her family received that afternoon from a nearby community...
body_text:
Gaza City — Inside the tent Malak al-Zaanin has lived in since being displaced from her home in Gaza, the mother of four holds a tray of rice her family received that afternoon from a nearby community kitchen.

She has already shared the meal with her husband and children, but her next worry is how to keep the valued leftovers from spoiling in the sweltering heat.

Before the war, her refrigerator kept food fresh for days, but due to a lack of electricity caused by Israel’s siege on Gaza, it now sits unused inside the tent.

She placed the remaining rice on metal shelves inside the tent, knowing what will inevitably happen amid Gaza’s endemic food crisis.

“The children will be hungry again soon and ask for food,” she says.

“By then, it will probably have spoiled because we don’t have a refrigerator, and the tent feels like an oven.”

UN agencies have previously warned that extreme heat, prolonged power cuts and the lack of refrigeration in Gaza are increasing risks of food spoilage and food-borne illnesses, especially among displaced families.

Fuel supplies remain critically low, and the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimates that just 1 million litres (265,000 gallons) of diesel entered Gaza in early June 2026, falling far short of the amount required to keep life-saving operations running.

Continued shortages are likely to further disrupt electricity, water systems and other essential services, but many families in Gaza are already feeling the impact of the energy crisis.

Malak’s struggle is the same as countless mothers across Gaza, who now face the dual challenge of not only finding food, but in the absence of electricity and refrigeration, also preserving it.

“We barely manage to secure food for our children,” she says. “Imagine watching it spoil in front of you while being unable to save it.”

Besides the heat, stored food is also vulnerable to flies, insects and rodents that have become increasingly common in the crowded displacement camps with little sanitation.

“I’ve turned [the fridge] into a table and storage shelves,” she says, lifting a cloth covering the appliance, showing it filled with aid boxes and supplies for the family’s small kiosk.

The only other options, refrigeration services, are costly or simply unavailable.

She remembers one time receiving trays of rice and meat, only to find no space to store the leftovers after her children had eaten.

“We ate the meat and threw away the rice. What else could we do? That’s our life now.”

When a cool bag of water is available, Malak sometimes buys one for two shekels ($0.35-$0.70), but often the family has nothing available but water from a storage tank heated by the summer sun.

A short walk away, 43-year-old Manal Hamad shares the same modest dream: a glass of cold water.

“I need to keep my medicine in a refrigerator,” she said.

“Cold water is a dream for me. When I drink the hot water from the tank, it feels like my heart is boiling, and my blood pressure immediately drops.”

Manal, a mother of three who lives with diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, needs life-saving medicine that requires constant refrigeration.

She sometimes has to pay people with a refrigerator to keep her medicine cool or preserve leftover food, but even those temporary solutions frequently fall short.

One time she had to pay 10 shekels ($3) to refrigerate meat, only to discover later that it had spoiled.

She constantly has to move vegetables from one shaded corner of her scorching tent to another, trying to delay their spoilage.

What hurts her most is watching her children endure the heat without being able to offer them cold fruit, juice or chilled water.

Instead, she fills a bucket with water so they can cool themselves.

“There’s nothing else I can do,” she said.

In Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood, 40-year-old Nidal Rafeeh has found another use for the refrigerator that has sat idle during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – it has become a cupboard for canned food and personal belongings.

“Things that were once necessities have become things we pay extra for,” he says. “I pay for water, phone charging, and now cooling food or drinking water.”

As Israel’s siege on Gaza leads to massive inflation due to a shortage of goods and energy, small expenses accumulate, forcing Nidal and his wife to cook only single meals to avoid leftovers spoiling.

“We do everything we can to avoid wasting food, like thousands of families across Gaza trying to survive,” he said.

Near a makeshift camp in central Gaza, 34-year-old Mohammed al-Zaanin, displaced from Beit Hanoon, turned a small freezer into his only source of income after losing his job as a driver.

He now runs a wartime survival business, charging phones and selling chilled drinks and water – services that emerged as prolonged power cuts due to the Israeli embargo created new daily needs.

Mohammed relies on a diesel generator to operate the freezer and charging station, but the costs are high.

Running the freezer alone costs about 1,500 shekels a month ($488), while electricity bills reach 1,300–1,400 ($423-$456) shekels every 10 days, with power costing about 35 shekels ($11.39) per kilowatt. Despite the huge costs, which inevitably must fall on the customer, he has no shortage of people using his services.

“People come every day, asking me to chill a bottle of water, cool their food … but I simply can’t meet everyone’s needs,” he said.

He remembers one time a deaf man arrived carrying a single mango, using sign language, pleading with Mohammed to keep it cool in his refrigerator.

“It broke my heart. We’ve reached the point where people bring just one mango to cool,” he said.

“Nobody would have imagined coming to someone else just to charge a phone or chill a bottle of water. Today, these have become luxuries.”

title: Plus-size models and £5 tickets: Sinéad O’Dwyer’s runway show puts inclusivity first
excerpt:
V&A event celebrates all shapes and sizes as wider fashion industry stalls on body diversity

Visitors to London’s Victoria and Albert Museum on Friday afternoon to watch Sinéad O’Dwyer’s Fashion in M...
body_text:
V&A event celebrates all shapes and sizes as wider fashion industry stalls on body diversity

Visitors to London’s Victoria and Albert Museum on Friday afternoon to watch Sinéad O’Dwyer’s Fashion in Motion show would have encountered something a little different. The cast of performers and models wore everything from underwear to skirt suits and sequins, and sometimes danced interpretively on the catwalk to a performance by the band Jeanie and The White Boys, but most notably came in all shapes and sizes.

O’Dwyer’s work has pushed against fashion’s insistence on a thin body type since she appeared at London fashion week in 2021. If most brands make the samples for clothes shown on the catwalk based on a size 4-8, she uses a size 18. She has won awards for her work, as well as celebrity fans including Cardi B and Björk.

Friday’s event – unlike a lot of fashion shows – was open to the public, who could buy a ticket for £5. O’Dwyer says this more inclusive attitude suits her brand. “In terms of the ethos [of the brand], it’s a lot more appropriate for everyone than the luxury fashion system, which actually doesn’t really want everyone.”

For a few years, O’Dwyer was part of a wider shift towards body diversity in fashion – with Paloma Elsesser the first plus-size model of the year at the Fashion Awards in 2023, for example – but progress has stalled. The Size Inclusivity Report, produced by Vogue Business every season since 2023, found that for autumn/winter 2026, 97.6% of models were “straight-size”, or a UK 4-8.

Fashion’s focus on the thin has been controversial since the early 20th century, with women’s bodies long subject to trends – slight with a small bust as an ideal in the flapper 20s, slender and leggy in the youth-obsessed 60s, athletic and curvy in the aerobicised 80s. The current rollback to thinness can be seen as part of a wider trend away from diversity.

“It coincided with Trump coming into power,” says Jeanie Annan-Lewin, a stylist. “There are fewer people of any minority across the board and that’s the same thing that’s happening in fashion.”

Emma Matell, the casting director who worked on O’Dwyer’s show and has also worked for Lueder and Tolu Coker, agrees. “It’s becoming more and more apparent that we’re back to wanting women to both metaphorically and physically take up less space,” she says.

The impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs is also part of the story. “[They] mean cultural figures are shrinking, the general population, in many respects, is shrinking,” says Lucy Maguire, the features director at Vogue Business. “It’s brought back a reverence for thinness that was always underlying in fashion.”

London remains the one fashion week that consistently features more body diversity – even if straight-size models still made up 92.7%, according to the Size Inclusivity Report. As well as O’Dwyer, Mark Fast and Chopova Lowena will probably have a more diverse range at their shows in September.

“Sinéad and a few other young designers are carrying a huge amount of effort that the rest of the industry seems unwilling to make,” says Matell. “But I think that also comes down to the rebellious spirit of London. To me, being inclusive is the most punk thing you can do.”

The difficulty and cost of changing long-established manufacturing methods to make clothes in bigger sizes is central to the problem of body diversity in fashion. But O’Dwyer believes even just seeing models of all sizes on the luxury stage has power. “Luxury is very deeply embedded in everything, even if you don’t know anything about luxury,” she says. “That’s what I definitely experienced as a young person. I didn’t know why I wanted to be size 6, but I really wanted to be size 6.”

Friends Elenor Rowland and Orla McEvoy, both 14, watched Friday’s show – their first interaction with fashion. Rowland said she was glad for the diverse casting “because a lot of the time there’s not much representation for different body types … It probably makes lots of people think: ‘Oh, I’m not that size. Maybe I should be.’”

In the UK, size 16 is the average. Annan-Lewin sees fashion’s continued focus on the very thin to be a missed commercial opportunity. “I find it really strange that we just go ‘no, if you’re plus-size, you don’t have any disposable income, you don’t want to buy anything luxury. You just need to go and get fast fashion,’” she says.

Maguire points to a survey conducted by Vogue Business that found “34% of mid-size and 68% of plus-size respondents felt alienated by the fashion industry due to their size, compared to 17% of straight-size respondents … Brands need to represent different bodies in order to not alienate this consumer who has really huge spending power.”

To change things, all argue that financial support for brands trying to increase size diversity is needed. Annan-Lewin is clear it’s time for action. “I feel like I talk about things all the time, and it’s great, but water is wet,” she says. “What are we going to do about this? If we can’t get that fatphobia out of here, then nothing is going to move forward in any way, shape or form.”

title: White House Correspondents' Association president previews upcoming dinner, 'not gonna be intimidated'
excerpt:
Criminal defense attorney Joshua Ritter discusses the state of the evidence in WHCA Dinner shooting on The Story.

White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) President and CBS News correspondent W...
body_text:
Criminal defense attorney Joshua Ritter discusses the state of the evidence in WHCA Dinner shooting on The Story.

White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) President and CBS News correspondent Weijia Jiang previewed on Thursday what to expect from the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner after an armed suspect stormed the April event.

"I don’t want images of my colleagues hiding under a table to be the last images from this year, of all years," Jiang told People magazine.

She added, "I want us to stand together and to show that we are not gonna be intimidated — that we are going to come back stronger, and we are going to recognize all the people who have done such hard work."

WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' ASSOCIATION PRESIDENT ANNOUNCES EVENT BEING RESCHEDULED AFTER SHOOTING

White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) President and CBS News correspondent Weijia Jiang spoke to People magazine about the upcoming White House Correspondents’ Dinner. (Al Drago/Getty Images)

Since then, Jiang described several security measures taken ahead of Friday's dinner in partnership with the Secret Service and a private security firm hired by the WHCA. These measures include moving the location from the Washington Hilton to the Waldorf Astoria ballroom, shrinking the guest list from 2600 attendees to approximately 680 and allowing only one access point through a private entrance.

"I do feel very good about the measures that we’ve taken and really thought through," Jiang said.

Despite the tight schedule to put together a new dinner, Jiang emphasized the importance of celebrating the press during America's 250th anniversary.

TRUMP PRAISES PRESS AFTER WHCD SHOOTING, SAYS UNITY AT DINNER WAS 'BEAUTIFUL'

"Maybe if it wasn’t this year, 2026, it would’ve been easier just to say, ‘Let’s just wait until next year’s dinner,’" Jiang said. "But especially at that time leading up to July 4th, all the country was talking about, all Washington was talking about, was America 250. And the First Amendment is such an important part of that fabric that this year of all years, we have to show the importance of recognizing those freedoms in the First Amendment."

The White House Correspondents' Dinner was interrupted after an armed suspect stormed the scene. (Jessica Koscielniak/Reuters)

The dinner is largely expected to feature the same speakers and performers scheduled for the original event, such as mentalist Oz Pearlman and President Donald Trump, marking his first time attending the dinner as president.

In addition to honoring journalists and scholarship recipients, the WHCA will award the Secret Service member who survived the April shooting the service award for his efforts. Jiang revealed that the original Washington Hilton staff will also be honored at the dinner.

Though Trump is expected to appear, not all the members of his administration will make a reappearance. First lady Melania Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio will not be there due to prior commitments.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Trump's appearance at the White House Correspondents' Dinner has drawn backlash from journalists who demanded that WHCA members use their position to "speak truth to power" against the president.

President Donald Trump is expected to give remarks at the rescheduled WHCA dinner. (Mandel Ngan / AFP via Getty Images)

Jiang emphasized that the dinner would be an effort to "normalize relations" between the Trump administration and journalists rather than exacerbate tensions.

"The Correspondents’ Dinner is our most visible event, but we do so much all year round," Jiang said. "We’ve really been able to course correct, because there was so much friction last year between our association and the administration. And my goal coming back was just to normalize relations so that we could find compromises so that we could work together."

The White House Correspondents' Dinner will take place on Friday.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

title: ‘Extremely disappointing’: US trade partners respond to Trump’s new tariffs
excerpt:
Countries across the world have responded to the latest round of tariffs imposed by the administration of United States President Donald Trump.

The reactions on Friday came the day after Washington i...
body_text:
Countries across the world have responded to the latest round of tariffs imposed by the administration of United States President Donald Trump.

The reactions on Friday came the day after Washington imposed the new measures, targeting more than 80 countries with rates ranging from 10 percent to 12.5 percent on goods.

The administration justified the levies under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, saying that the countries in question failed to adequately restrict imported goods made with forced labour. Many of the countries targeted have rejected the allegation.

Trump has aggressively pursued tariffs as part of a wider strategy to jumpstart US manufacturing and address what he has described as uneven trade relations. But he has regularly faced major setbacks, with his signature reciprocal tariffs eventually deemed unconstitutional by the US Supreme Court.

The latest duties were imposed as another 10 percent global tariff reached its legal time limit on Thursday night, provoking accusations that Trump was again misusing US law.

Here’s how allies and adversaries alike have responded:

Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell rejected any claims linking Australia, a major exporter of beef, gold and copper, to forced labour.

“We believe that amongst all of the countries in the world, Australia does take the issue of slavery, modern slavery, seriously, and will continue to do that,” Farrell told reporters in Adelaide.

Australia will “continue to lobby the United States” to remove the tariffs.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon called the new tariffs “extremely disappointing to see”.

“The US investigation did not provide meaningful evidence to support claims in relation to forced labour,” he wrote on social media.

A British government spokesman said the latest tariffs will have “no negative change” on exports, despite being targeted by the new US policy.

Previous US/UK trade agreements have exempted several industries from further tariffs.

“We take forced labour very ‌‌seriously to ensure that in global supply chains UK businesses are not complicit,” the spokesman said.

“The US ‌‌has recognised the steps the UK is taking, which is why there are no additional tariffs ‌‌for the UK under this announcement.”

The Chief Cabinet Secretary of Japan, Minoru Kihara, objected to the administration’s claims.

“It is regrettable that tariffs have been imposed on the grounds that Japan does not have a system prohibiting the import of forced labour products, even though Japanese industry and trade operate in accordance with international norms,” he said at a news conference on Friday.

However, he added that Japan has “confirmed with the US” that the total tariffs would not exceed a 15 percent rate set in a trade agreement reached between the countries last year.

The European Commission, the chief executive body of the EU, responded to the announcement of the tariffs with cautious optimism.

It said the new policy did not appear to stray from a previous trade agreement between the US and EU.

“The EU notes positively the fact that this outcome is in line with the US tariff commitments agreed under the EU-US Joint Statement,” a European Commission spokesperson said.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs rebuked the new 12.5 percent levy and reiterated the country’s longstanding rejection of unilateral tariffs.

“Tariff wars and trade wars do not serve any parties’ interests,” ministry spokesman Lin Jian said in a news conference on Friday.

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet again in September, following previous talks in Beijing that set new trade agreements in May.

Textile and clothing exporters in India responded with concern to the new tariffs.

A top trade association noted that India had not been included in a list of countries whose exports of some products, particularly those made from US cotton, would be subject to tariff exemptions.

“The differential treatment risks diverting sourcing orders for textile and apparel items away from India,” said Ashwin Chandran, Chairman of the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry.

title: Abdul El-Sayed scores Sen Tina Smith's endorsement in Democratic primary that exposes party divide

Sen....
body_text:
Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan Abdul El-Sayed speaks one-on-one with Fox News about the battle between the far-left and center-left establishment for the future of the Democratic Party.

Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., has endorsed Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate primary candidate Abdul El-Sayed, describing him as "a fighter."

El-Sayed expressed his gratitude Thursday for the senator's backing.

"Senator Tina Smith has been a fighter for working people in the US Senate," he said in a statement. "She’s fought for and delivered on an economy that works for all of us. I hope to build on her leadership on women’s health and reproductive rights and access which has paved the way for the future I want for my daughters and every American. I’m deeply grateful for her support."

TOP DEM HOPEFUL FLIPS SCRIPT AFTER YEARS IN SOCIALIST ORBIT WITH PUZZLING CLAIM

FILE - Senator Tina Smith, D-Minn., endorsed Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan U.S. Senate primary race. (Tierney L. Cross/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., are some of the figures who have endorsed El-Sayed.

"In all due respect to Haley Stevens, everybody knows that this is not an election between her and Abdul," Sanders said during an event last week in support of El-Sayed. "This is an election between Abdul and the billionaire class. That is what this election is about."

The Senate hopeful is running against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., in the Aug. 4 Democratic primary contest.

WARREN DEFIES SCHUMER AS DEM CIVIL WAR EXPLODES OVER MUST-WIN SENATE RACE

FILE - U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate primary candidate Abdul El-Sayed and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt, greet the crowd after El-Sayed spoke at The People V. The Powerful rally at the Detroit Opera House on July 18, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. He was recently endorsed by Michigan Democratic Sen. Tina Smith. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., who announced last year that he would not seek re-election, is supporting Stevens to succeed him in the Senate seat.

"Over the last eighteen years, while serving the people of Michigan, I have been surrounded by many extremely talented and dedicated partners who work tirelessly for our state. Haley Stevens has been that partner in Congress," Peters wrote in a statement. "Haley Stevens will be ready on day 1 to fight for Michigan, which is why I am excited to announce I am all in for Haley Stevens."

Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., is also among those backing Stevens.

DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN

FILE - Following his endorsement, Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said he will fight for women’s health and reproductive rights and access. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, who is backed by President Donald Trump, does not face any competition heading into the Michigan Republican U.S. Senate primary.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump says Iran will pay — what it takes to end the war remains unclear
excerpt: President Donald Trump delivers a strong warning to Iran, stating the U.S. will bomb bridges or power plants if Iranian forces attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz. This follows ongoing U.S. strikes o...
body_text:
President Donald Trump delivers a strong warning to Iran, stating the U.S. will bomb bridges or power plants if Iranian forces attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz. This follows ongoing U.S. strikes on Iranian military sites.

Nearly five months after launching a sweeping campaign against Iran’s nuclear, missile, naval and proxy capabilities, the Trump administration is now fighting to reopen the Strait of Hormuz while negotiations have yet to produce a permanent settlement.

The administration says its renewed strikes have a clear immediate objective: "making Iran pay." Less clear is what Iran must do to end the strikes — or what conditions would allow the U.S. to step back from a growing military commitment in the region.

President Donald Trump has threatened to expand the campaign to Iran’s nuclear sites, bridges, power plants and other infrastructure.

ARMY IDS 2 VICTIMS KILLED IN JORDAN AIR BASE ATTACK; TRUMP: IRAN WILL PAY 'MANY TIMES OVER'

In response to questioning on the end goals in Iran, a U.S. official said: "Right now, the President is focused on making Iran pay for their violations of the MOU and their continued acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz," referring to the memorandum of understanding between Iran and the United States.

"In addition, the president will make Iran pay for the recent deaths of U.S. soldiers," the official said.

The Trump administration says its renewed strikes have a clear immediate objective: "making Iran pay." (Morteza Akhoundi via Getty Images)

"These devastating blows will continue until the president deems otherwise, but talks between our countries are continuing," the official said. "President Trump has all of the cards and all options at his disposal, and Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon."

The response defined the immediate campaign as punishment for Iran’s actions but did not identify any condition Tehran could meet to halt the strikes beyond Trump deciding that the punishment had been sufficient. Follow-up questioning by Fox News Digital went unanswered.

STEVE FORBES URGES TRUMP TO KEEP THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ OPEN AT ALL COSTS

When Trump launched its military Operation Epic Fury mission on February 28, the White House laid out four sweeping objectives: preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, destroying its ballistic missiles and production capacity, annihilating its navy and severing its support for terrorist proxies.

The administration declared those military objectives achieved in April. But Iran retained enough capability to close the Strait of Hormuz, attack commercial shipping and target U.S. forces and allies across the region.

The administration’s immediate focus is now the strait.

U.S. Central Command said Thursday that its latest strikes targeted Iranian maritime capabilities, coastal surveillance sites, air defenses and missile and drone facilities to degrade Iran’s ability to attack commercial vessels.

TRUMP SEEKS $672M TO STOP IRANIAN NUKES AS NEGOTIATORS WEIGH FATE OF URANIUM STOCKPILE

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has framed the current campaign as an effort to prevent Iran from establishing a "dangerous precedent" by controlling an international waterway, while maintaining that Washington remains open to diplomacy. He said Iran must stop attacking commercial ships and reopen the strait before the United States changes its behavior.

Mourners gather around a vehicle transporting the coffin of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed on February 28 in Israeli and U.S. airstrikes, and coffins of his family members, on the day of his burial, in the culmination of a mass funeral, in Mashhad, Iran, July 9, 2026. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency, via REUTERS)

"Their behavior has to change in order for ours to change," Rubio said Sunday.

Yet recent strikes have expanded beyond Iran's maritime capabilities to include bridges and other infrastructure as Trump continues threatening nuclear facilities, raising new questions about how the widening target set fits into the administration's broader strategy.

Meanwhile, the final nuclear agreement envisioned under the June memorandum of understanding has not materialized, even as the White House says talks between Washington and Iran are continuing. The memorandum had envisioned an agreement within 60 days, but renewed fighting has left its timing and prospects uncertain.

Trump has continued threatening Iran’s nuclear infrastructure, including the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain facility. But he has also appeared to soften one of the administration’s original demands, saying in June that Iran could retain some ballistic missiles in proportion to neighboring countries.

The administration has not clarified whether the original missile objective was achieved, relaxed as part of negotiations or remains part of a future settlement, nor whether ending Iran’s support for proxies remains a condition for victory.

Publicly, the renewed campaign has a clear immediate military task — protecting shipping and preventing Iran from asserting control over Hormuz — but the connection between that mission, the stalled nuclear process and Trump’s threats to widen the war remains unexplained.

Eighteen U.S. service members have been killed since the war began, while Secretary of War Pete Hegseth told lawmakers Tuesday that the campaign has cost an estimated $37.5 billion.

Retired Air Force Brig. Gen. Robert Spalding, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute conservative think tank, who served as a senior strategy official in the first Trump White House, argued that the campaign can still be understood around one overriding objective.

"I think the end goal is to prevent them from having a nuclear weapon," Spalding told Fox News Digital. "The goal is very clear. It is: How do you want to go about getting to those goals, and then what are you willing to pay to achieve them? That’s the decision that has to be made."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has framed the current campaign as an effort to prevent Iran from establishing a "dangerous precedent" by controlling an international waterway, while maintaining that Washington remains open to diplomacy. (Brendan Smialowski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

On Hormuz, Spalding predicted that protecting commercial shipping could require a prolonged U.S. presence, comparing it to Operations Northern and Southern Watch, the yearslong U.S.-led enforcement of no-fly zones over Iraq.

"I don’t think that we’re leaving the area anytime soon," Spalding said.

He described that potential mission as "almost an airborne and seaborne occupation of the strait and the Gulf" intended to preserve the free flow of international shipping.

Such a mission could give the current strikes a defined military purpose, but it would not necessarily resolve the nuclear negotiations, eliminate Iran's remaining leverage or produce a political settlement. It could instead leave American forces enforcing access to Hormuz for an extended period while the broader conflict remains unresolved.

Ali Vaez, Iran project director at the International Crisis Group, said the administration’s changing public emphasis reflects the absence of a coherent strategy connecting its military actions to an achievable end state.

"The administration does not seem to have a clear strategy," Vaez told Fox News Digital. "It’s been a moving goalpost."

Vaez also argued that the conflict has given Iran a potent new form of leverage: the demonstrated ability to choke shipping through Hormuz and impose economic pain on the United States. He described Iran’s control over the strait as a "weapon of mass destruction."

"For more than four decades, the United States has been able to coerce the Iranian regime economically," Vaez said. "The Iranians never had the possibility of retaliating in kind, of putting pressure on the pocketbook of every American citizen."

The U.S. is now trying to inflict enough pain on Iran that it abandons its insistence on controlling the strait, according to Vaez. But Iran views that control as its most valuable remaining source of leverage and one it cannot surrender without weakening its position in any future negotiations, he argued.

President Donald Trump confirmed the U.S. launched strikes on Iran on Saturday, Feb. 28, 2026. (The White House via X Account/Anadolu via Getty Images/Contributor/Getty Images)

"We are in a zero-sum situation," Vaez said. "The U.S. is trying to remove a tool of leverage from the hands of the Iranians that they believe is essential to their survival."

Although the United States retains overwhelming military superiority, Vaez argued that neither side has been able to deliver a decisive blow. Washington can continue inflicting damage, he said, while Tehran has a greater willingness to absorb it because it views the conflict as a struggle for the regime’s survival.

"There is no military solution to resolving the problem in the strait," Vaez said. "After much more death and destruction, I think both sides would return to the same logic that led them to agree to the MOU in the first place — which is that neither side is really able to deliver a knockout blow to the other."

title: Jon Bon Jovi abruptly ends Madison Square Garden show after health setback
excerpt:
Jon Bon Jovi was singing "Living on a Prayer" at his Madison Square Garden concert when he had Pat Monahan take over the vocals before ending the concert early.

Jon Bon Jovi unexpectedly cut his Madi...
body_text:
Jon Bon Jovi was singing "Living on a Prayer" at his Madison Square Garden concert when he had Pat Monahan take over the vocals before ending the concert early.

Jon Bon Jovi unexpectedly cut his Madison Square Garden concert short Thursday night after appearing to have difficulty getting through the performance – forcing Train frontman Pat Monahan to step in and help carry the show across the finish line.

A representative for Bon Jovi confirmed to Fox News Digital that the concert ended early, saying the singer told fans from the stage he had been battling a health setback.

"Jon Bon Jovi spoke from stage and told fans he has been battling a sinus infection which led to the show's early ending," the representative said in a statement.

ROD STEWART CANCELS LAS VEGAS CONCERT HOURS BEFORE SHOWTIME ON DOCTOR'S ORDERS

The shortened show marks a setback in Jon Bon Jovi's comeback following 2022 vocal cord surgery that nearly ended his performing career permanently. (John Nacion/Getty Images)

"As part of the Bon Jovi residency at Madison Square Garden, Jon has said numerous times that it has been a joy to return to live shows for the band. Updated information will be available shortly."

An insider who attended the concert told Fox News Digital Bon Jovi performed for roughly 90 minutes.

Bon Jovi's previous Madison Square Garden residency shows have lasted over two hours, the insider noted. Thursday's performance wrapped after approximately 15 songs, ending far earlier than fans had come to expect.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Jon Bon Jovi performs onstage during Bon Jovi's Forever Tour at Madison Square Garden on July 21, 2026, in New York City. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Bon Jovi)

Monahan was in the arena as a fan Thursday night and was not part of the scheduled show, according to the insider.

WATCH: JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY CUTS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN CONCERT SHORT

The 64-year-old rocker was performing on night eight of his nine-show residency when he stopped the show early. Monahan joined him for "Livin' on a Prayer," taking over the vocals midway through the song.

The shortened performance comes as Bon Jovi continues his comeback following vocal cord surgery in 2022. This is his first major tour since undergoing the career-saving procedure.

Just months before launching the "Forever Tour," Bon Jovi admitted he had been prepared to walk away from music after a vocal cord injury left him fearing he could never perform at the level fans expected.

Jon Bon Jovi cut his performance short after battling a sinus infection. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Bon Jovi)

In October 2025, Bon Jovi recalled realizing something was wrong after a 15-show run.

At the end of the final show, he told his wife he thought it was "pretty good," but his wife disagreed, Bon Jovi recalled on the "How to Fail" podcast.

"I don't think I could do this anymore. I don't know why, but I'm OK with walking away from this because there's no way I'm dragging down the legacy," Bon Jovi said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Doctors later discovered the source of the problem.

"I sought out a surgeon who explained to me that one of my vocal cords had literally atrophied," Bon Jovi said. "It was dying."

He underwent surgery and received an implant designed to help his vocal cords close properly.

Jon Bon Jovi abruptly ended his Madison Square Garden residency. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)

"If I worked hard, he promised me nothing other than I would be better than I was that night in Nashville," Bon Jovi explained.

"Had I known that it was going to be a three-and-a-half-year recovery, I very well might have said thank you, good night," he said. "But the process and the progress was steady enough that I didn't lose faith."

By the time he announced the "Forever Tour," Bon Jovi said he felt "close enough to fully recovered" to return to the stage.

"I'm not doing this for the applause. I'm not doing it for the money. I'm not doing it the fame," he said. "I've had enough of all of it.

"But I would like to feel that joy and the resonance, even if it were only one last time. I don't think this is anywhere near a farewell tour or anything like that. But if it were, you could trust that these few shows that I've announced are gonna be joy-filled."

The "Forever Tour" began July 7 with a nine-show residency at Madison Square Garden and is scheduled to wrap Sept. 9 at London's Wembley Stadium.

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Illinois worker spent over six hours trapped in gas station sign too tall for fire truck ladders to reach
excerpt:
The worker was trapped after his lift malfunctioned, leading to a massive emergency response. (Credit: WFLD)

An Illinois maintenance worker was trapped for more than six hours in a 130-foot-tall gas ...
body_text:
The worker was trapped after his lift malfunctioned, leading to a massive emergency response. (Credit: WFLD)

An Illinois maintenance worker was trapped for more than six hours in a 130-foot-tall gas station sign after his lift malfunctioned.

The worker, who identified himself as AJ Gow, was doing repair work Tuesday on the towering sign, which is located along Lorenzo Road off Interstate 55 in Wilmington.

At 1:55 p.m., the Wilmington Fire District was called to this area on a report of a worker stuck inside one of the enclosed signs atop the sign pole.

"The telescopic boom lift used by the worker had malfunctioned and Fire District personnel were told he had been at the elevated position for around 3 hours," officials with the fire district said in a statement on social media.

EIGHT RIDERS LEFT DANGLING ATOP 100-FOOT ROLLER COASTER FOR OVER THREE HOURS AT TEXAS AMUSEMENT PARK

Fire crews with the Wilmington Fire District in Illinois ascend a boom lift to rescue a maintenance worker, AJ Gow, who was trapped inside one of the signs atop the 130-foot pole for hours on Tuesday. (Wilmington Fire District)

"The telescopic boom lift used by the worker had malfunctioned and Fire District personnel were told he had been at the elevated position for around 3 hours," officials with the fire district said in a statement on social media.

Additionally, the sign pole had no stairs or ladders built into it, making it impossible for rescue teams to climb up without another lift, officials said.

Another problem was that the Wilmington Fire District's trucks have ladders that only go 100 feet in the air, which meant Gow was 30 feet out of reach.

Eventually fire officials located another boom lift in the Joliet area, which is roughly 20 miles north of the rest stop. The lift was brought to the sign with an Illinois State Police escort, officials said.

AJ Gow, the worker, said he spent over six hours trapped in the interior of the sign after his lift malfunctioned. (Wilmington Fire District)

FAMILY'S SPRING BREAK HIKE TURNS INTO LIFE-OR-DEATH RESCUE AFTER PARENT FALLS 70 FEET OFF UTAH CLIFF

After the new lift was in place, firefighters were able to reach Gow and get him back to the ground, the fire district said.

Gow thanked all the first responders from different departments that came to his aid, saying that "seeing that lift roll up with police escorts was the highlight of my day for sure!!"

Gow later said on social media that he spent over six hours in a cramped position within the interior of the sign.

An aerial view of the sign AJ Gow was trapped in for more than six hours this week. (WFLD)

"I was too hot and thirsty to be anxious. I was moreso nauseous and dizzy. And incredibly uncomfortable to be in for over 6 hours. It was only 16" wide and wasn't even tall enough to stand fully upright either," Gow wrote in response to someone commenting on the fire district's post.

In another comment, Gow said the sign "kept swaying with the wind."

Gow said that after he got down, he went to the hospital to be treated for dehydration. Fox News Digital reached out to Gow for comment.

James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Newsom says film tax incentives are bringing Hollywood home but industry experts warn it may be 'too late'
excerpt: Film industry experts told Fox News Digital California Gov. Gavin Newsom's film and television tax credit is "too late" after years of Hollywood studios outsourcing film production for cheaper locatio...
body_text:
Film industry experts told Fox News Digital California Gov. Gavin Newsom's film and television tax credit is "too late" after years of Hollywood studios outsourcing film production for cheaper locations including Canada.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom says Hollywood is returning to its glory after years of production fleeing Los Angeles for cheaper filming locations, but industry experts tell Fox News Digital the sector is still reeling from production "decimation."

"We need a major rescue, like, immediately," Shadowcast Pictures owner Jay Ellison said.

Major studios are increasingly opting to film television shows and movies outside California, such as Canada and overseas in the United Kingdom, Ireland and Australia, as well as to domestic production hubs in Georgia and New Mexico.

Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is also reportedly considering relocating Paramount’s headquarters — which could divert billions of production dollars from California — while production of scripted television shows in Los Angeles is down nearly 30% since 2019, according to Luminate data.

JOE ROGAN MOCKS GAVIN NEWSOM FOR DISMISSING GROWING STATE PROBLEMS AS LA FILM PRODUCTION CRATERS

Experts say production work has been hemorrhaging at a rapid pace for decades and that Los Angeles has lost tens of thousands of film and television jobs over the years.

"Why did it take so long for the political establishment to take this seriously? Because Hollywood's business has been leeching away for the last three decades," entertainment lawyer Jonathan Handel told Fox News Digital.

StageRunner founder and CEO Jason Fisher, formerly head of production at Disney, Paramount and AMC, said he began noticing the rise of runaway production over two decades ago.

"Production has been slowly and then speeding up really over the last two years, leaving California for other states and other countries and really nothing was done until it was almost too late," he told Fox News Digital.

Several popular episodic television series were filmed outside of California, including Paramount’s "Landman" in Fort Worth, Texas and Netflix’s "Stranger Things" in Atlanta, Georgia.

Despite LA-based studios’ efforts to film locally, the substantial savings available outside of California made production in the Golden State increasingly difficult to justify.

"When I worked at the studios, we talked about a lot. ‘What could we do to keep the show here?’ And when you get to that place where you're just saving millions of dollars by going to some place other than California, they're just aren't any other levers to pull," Fisher said.

FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA

Jason Fisher (left), Jay Ellison (middle) and Jonathan Handel (right) spoke with Fox News Digital about the state of Hollywood given Gov. Gavin Newsom's Film and Television Tax credit program, which is expected to bring $6.6 billion in direct production spending back to the Golden State. (Nora Moriarty)

The decline in production has sent ripple effects across California’s economy, with more than 80 production service businesses closing in Los Angeles since 2022 became of a lack of work and industry strikes, according to CBS News.

Experts say production work has been hemorrhaging for decades and that Los Angeles has lost tens of thousands of film and television jobs over the years.

"It is decimation, and it's not just like the film rental companies, the production companies — it trickles down to the restaurants, the people supported by the industry here," Ellison said.

Ellison’s camera rental house, Shadowcast Pictures, provided cameras, lighting and other filmmaking gear to production crews for nearly two decades before becoming one of the businesses forced to close.

"We've been injecting our own money to keep the company going, I know lots of others are doing that and it came to the point where we finally had to say enough because we've had three years of downturn," Ellison told Fox News Digital.

Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is reportedly considering relocating Paramount’s headquarters, which could divert billions of production dollars from California. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Industry workers who once spent 15 to 20 days a month on set are now working as few as one to 10 days, if they are "lucky," Ellison said. He added that many are hoping to secure jobs on long-running television series in search of greater stability.

"I have networks of friends who are actors, who are crew members, who are directors, who are writers trying to get scripts sold. And if you ask one of them, ‘Have you worked lately?’ You get looked at like you're crazy," Handel said.

"Because we all know the answer, which is … in most cases, no," he added.

The production downturn comes amid major turmoil within Los Angeles' entertainment space. Television City, an iconic Los Angeles studio lot where "The Sonny and Cher Show" and "The Price Is Right" were filmed could be up for sale as its owners struggle with all-time low production levels and $357 million worth of debt.

DANNY MCBRIDE SAYS DITCHING LA WAS THE BEST MOVE FOR HIS CAREER AND FAMILY

CBS Television City pictured on July 16, 1990, in Los Angeles, California. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"I don't know if in a year, two years from now, we're going to be able to call it an industry because so much has left," Jay Ellison said.

"We have Quixote Studios closing their stages here. Then we're going to have possibly this major merger between Paramount and Warner Brothers, are they going to keep two massive studio lots? A lot of questions being raised about that right now," he added.

Meanwhile, Gov. Newsom recently touted California’s Film and Television Tax Credit Program, which he said is on track to generate $6.6 billion in direct production spending back to the Golden State.

"The world we invented is now competing against us ... We've got to step up our game," Newsom said last year when discussing the incentive.

Ellison and Fisher agreed that state leaders were "too late" in recognizing the production problem plaguing the birthplace of entertainment, questioning whether Hollywood could ever fully reclaim its former dominance, even with Newsom’s expanded tax credit.

While blame is being placed on California’s political leadership over Hollywood’s production decimation, others are also pointing fingers at the studios themselves. (Getty Images)

"The incentive has brought back some production. It's keeping things going," Ellison said. "It's just not nearly enough when you're competing with so many other foreign countries."

"I think it's a start, but I don't think it is enough," said Fisher. "Everyone who works in the industry understands California is the most expensive place to shoot, and it's the most challenging place to shoot. Getting those incentives is still a real challenge."

Experts said financial incentives are not the only factor luring studios elsewhere. Rival production hubs, most notably Atlanta, have developed extensive infrastructure, experienced local crews and vendor networks.

Ellison said that those investments have put Los Angeles in a position where it no longer has a competitive edge against other cities in production resources.

"Other jurisdictions around the world have built up their own capabilities, and they are now attractive places to shoot. And there's only so much that you can stretch the California budget in terms of tax incentives," Handel said.

Now that studios have access to well-established and less expensive production centers elsewhere, Handel said, California will face difficulty winning business back.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

A production crew prepares to shoot a scene for the film "San Andreas" on Hyde Street in San Francisco, Calif., on Tuesday, July 22, 2014. Actor Dwayne Johnson starred in the earthquake disaster movie. (Paul Chinn/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)

"All of that is now what California is fighting against, and it's a tough uphill climb," the entertainment lawyer told Fox News Digital. "It would have been easier to keep the business here than it will be to claw it back with improved tax incentives in California."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Gavin Newsom’s office said California remains the nation’s top destination for film and television despite "unprecedented competition."

"That’s exactly why Governor Newsom took historic action to more than double California's Film & Television Tax Credit Program, strengthening California's competitive edge by keeping jobs and investment where the industry's unmatched workforce, infrastructure and creative talent have made it the epicenter of the world's entertainment industry for more than a century," the statement said.

"In its first year, the expanded program is projected to generate $6.6 billion in direct production spending across 170 projects, bringing nearly 35,000 cast and crew jobs to communities across the state," it continued.

The Hollywood sign stands in the Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, Calif., on May 29, 2025. (Eric Thayer/Bloomberg)

While some blame California’s political leadership over Hollywood’s production decimation, others are also pointing fingers at the studios themselves.

"Not nearly enough has been done, but at the same time, it's also not up to our elected officials entirely to bring production back to California," Ellison said. "The studios are the ones deciding where they're going to ultimately film, and they're choosing to film overseas because it's cheaper in the end."

Fisher, who held executive roles at major studios, defended the corporations, saying they ultimately bear a "fiduciary responsibility" to shareholders.

"We have a very sharp-edged capitalist system, and the studios are doing what businesses frequently do," Handel said.

Fox News Digital asked the industry experts whether Los Angeles could reclaim its position as the world’s dominant film and television production hub.

"I think that it's not too late. I think it can get rebuilt, but action needs to happen immediately," Ellison said. "It needed to happen months ago."

Nora Moriarty is a Writer at Fox News Digital.

title: US cyclosporiasis outbreak expands to nine states as CDC investigates over 7,400 cases
excerpt:
Over 11,500 people this summer are suspected to have been sickened by disease that can cause explosive diarrhea, CDC says

Investigations into the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak on record expanded to...
body_text:
Over 11,500 people this summer are suspected to have been sickened by disease that can cause explosive diarrhea, CDC says

Investigations into the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak on record expanded to nine states this week, as more than 11,500 people are suspected to have been sickened this summer, according to reports and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Data released by the CDC this week said the agency is looking into 4,173 laboratory-confirmed domestic cases of the disease and investigating an additional 7,400.

Additionally, the Washington Post reported that the CDC’s five-state investigation into cyclosporiasis cases – already the largest on record – had expanded to four more states for a total of nine.

Iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants was linked to cyclospora cases in the first five states – including in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia. More states now included in the investigation include Illinois, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania.

The Kansas department of health and environment independently reported that it was investigating cases “related” to the multistate outbreak. The CDC said 41 states across the US are reporting cyclosporiasis cases, which normally occur in the summer. Investigators are still working on identifying how many of those states are part of the nine-state outbreak connected to the shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants and which are separate cases entirely.

The iceberg lettuce was linked to a single supplier, Taylor Farms de Mexico, which has issued a voluntary recall.

Cyclosporiasis is the illness caused by the parasite cyclospora, a microscopic protozoa that is known to contaminate raw produce that comes into contact with feces. Symptoms of the disease include explosive and watery relapsing diarrhea that can last weeks.

In addition to expanding the search for contaminated produce to more states, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) updated its website on Thursday to reflect a separate investigation into 72 cyclosporiasis cases. It has not yet linked the cases to a specific product or products.

Smaller outbreaks across the country, for example in North Carolina, have linked cyclosporiasis cases to parsley and cilantro, both of which are commonly served raw.

title: Could this African nation become Trump's next terror target as jihadists close in on power?
excerpt: Africa Command Gen. Dagvin Anderson tells lawmakers that shrinking U.S. presence in Africa has weakened intelligence capabilities as Russia, China and terrorist groups expand influence across the cont...
body_text:
Africa Command Gen. Dagvin Anderson tells lawmakers that shrinking U.S. presence in Africa has weakened intelligence capabilities as Russia, China and terrorist groups expand influence across the continent.

JOHANNESBURG: The U.S. is reportedly considering airstrikes against al Qaeda-linked terrorists in Mali, according to regional analysts and recent media reports.

The military junta that has been running this West African country in the Sahel region since coups in both 2020 and 2021 turned away from France and the U.S. to get military protection from Russia and its Africa Corps mercenaries against jihadist groups.

But now the largest of these groups, Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which has Mali’s capital under siege, is credited, along with another group, for killing 50 Malian soldiers this month, for the death of the country’s defense minister earlier this year and has reportedly sent battalions of Russian soldiers retreating on at least two occasions this year.

ISIS POISED TO EXPLOIT HISTORIC US IRAQ EXIT, TERROR GROUP 'ACTIVELY WAITING IN THE GAPS,' EXPERT WARNS

Malian troops parade during the country's 65th anniversary of the African nation's independence. (Habib Kouyate/Xinhua via Getty Images)

JNIM is said to want to change the country into an Islamist Jihadist state. If they succeed, Mali would be the first country in the world to be run by a jihadist group. The organization was designated officially as a Foreign Terrorist Organization during the first Trump administration in 2018.

Islamic State (ISIS) jihadist groups are also operating freely in Mali, and are linked to terror groups in neighboring Nigeria.

A State Department official didn’t respond to a Washington Post report that the U.S. is considering strikes against JNIM in Mali, but used strong language Thursday when talking to Fox News Digital, leading analysts to suggest the time for talking may be over.

"The United States unequivocally condemns the terrorist activity in Mali," the official said, adding, "in the Sahel, the United States is committed to promoting regional ownership and cooperation against terrorist threats, and monitoring indicators and warnings of threats to our homeland."

This undated photograph handed out by French military shows three Russian mercenaries, right, in northern Mali. Russia has engaged in under-the-radar military operations in at least half a dozen countries in Africa in the last five years using a shadowy mercenary force analysts say is loyal to President Vladimir Putin. The analysts say the Wagner Group of mercenaries is also key to Putin's ambitions to re-impose Russian influence on a global scale.  (French Army via AP)

Edmund Fitton-Brown, a former British and United Nations diplomat, said the U.S. could order military action, to primarily try and stop jihadists becoming entrenched in Mali. Fitton-Brown, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital, "Mali is mainly important to the U.S. because, as a failed state becoming a safe haven for al Qaeda and ISIS, it looks like the first of several African dominoes likely to fall."

Retired U.S. Air Force Maj. Gen. Kenneth P. Ekman, who until last year, served as the Department of War’s West Africa Coordination Element lead, said that with strike action the administration may be able to persuade Mali’s rulers to turn away from Russia, and towards the U.S. for protection – and purchases of military equipment.

RESOURCE-RICH NATION PRAISES US TIES AMID WASHINGTON-BEIJING CRITICAL MINERALS RACE

A column of black smoke rises above buildings as traffic passes the Africa Tower monument in Bamako on April 26, 2026. April 25, 2026's shock attacks, synchronized by Tuareg rebels of the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) coalition and the jihadist Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM), targeted several areas in the vast arid country. Fighting resumed on April 26 in several areas, including Kita near Bamako, Kidal, Gao and Severe.Tuareg rebels meanwhile announced an agreement allowing Russian forces backing Mali's army to withdraw from the northern city of Kidal, which they claimed was "totally" under their control. (AFP via Getty Images)

Ekman told Fox News Digital, "JNIM has a stranglehold on the government and much of the population. The Russians are woefully ineffective and extractive. Cooperation with U.S. forces offers a disproportionate and positive impact."

Ekman said that U.S. forces have supported partner-led operations against JNIM before, as recently as 2022, adding "⁠recent proposals amount to returning to similar cooperation against a mutual threat."

The administration may also be in a minerals frame of mind. Mali is one of Africa’s largest gold-producing nations. It also has substantial deposits of lithium, used extensively in rechargeable batteries.

Fitton-Brown said that "President Trump may be less reluctant than his predecessor to work with the juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, if they are losing faith in their Russian friends."

Vehicle turned up following brutal ambush on Russian Wagner fighters in Mali on July 27, 2024. (East2West)

He continued, "The U.S. is certainly a more capable partner. France has already been displaced so all three countries might accept U.S. help if it comes only with strings attached that don’t offend or disadvantage them. Whether even the U.S. is capable of stopping the political decline of these countries, and the rise of militant Islam, is another matter. That cannot be achieved by military force alone."

The FDD’s Fitton-Brown said U.S. assets such as aircraft may not be directly involved if there is a strike, "The U.S. might work with French and other intelligence services to develop local intelligence for strikes on JNIM leadership, but this is unlikely to achieve much. The organization is resilient and will be able to replace those killed."

A former senior Department of War official told Fox News Digital the U.S. has at its disposal cruise missiles and long-range bombers. Attack drones would probably not come into play, and the U.S. Naval Institute’s Fleet Tracker shows no American aircraft carriers anywhere near African waters, effectively ruling out carrier operations.

However, Ekman believes airstrikes are under consideration, noting "JNIM and ISIS are a threat to U.S. interests, and are ascendant in West Africa."

Paul Tilsley is a veteran correspondent who has reported from four continents for more than three decades. Based in Johannesburg, South Africa, he can be followed on X @paultilsley.

title: Australian households face prospect of interest rate hike and petrol prices rising above $2 a litre
excerpt:
Economists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrel

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian households face t...
body_text:
Economists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrel

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian households face the prospect of a Reserve Bank interest rate hike and petrol prices above $2 a litre over the coming weeks, economists warn, as the escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude back above $US100 a barrel.

Financial markets now see an even chance the RBA board will deliver a fourth cash rate increase at the next meeting on 11 August.

Warwick McKibbin, the director of the ANU’s Centre for Applied Macroeconomic Analysis, said crude oil prices were likely to stay elevated for “at least a year” as the US-Iran war entered a new and more dangerous phase.

The Houthis’ blockade of Saudi Arabian oil through the Red Sea and the Ukrainians’ increasingly successful destruction of Russian energy infrastructure had heaped further pressure on global oil supply, McKibbin said.

“Getting access to supplies looks different now than it did a few months ago. All the reserves have been run down, particularly in the US. It’s quite a serious situation for the world to be in.”

The phasing down of the government’s fuel tax relief to 16 cents per litre and this month’s 37% jump in the international Brent crude benchmark has pushed the cost of unleaded to $1.80 a litre, up from a recent low of about $1.50 at the beginning of the month, according to Motormouth.

Johnathan McMenamin, a senior economist at Barrenjoey, said higher global prices and the end of the remaining fuel excise discount after 2 August meant unleaded would march back above $2 a litre over coming weeks.

“That is an uncomfortable level for households, but it isn’t something we are too unfamiliar with,” McMenamin said.

Diesel prices are up by about 50 cents in July to about $2.20 a litre in the major East Coast cities.

Climbing fuel prices will be another blow to the Reserve Bank’s efforts to bring inflation down while managing the damage to the economy from high energy costs.

McMenamin believes the central bank will pull the trigger next month – a view he had even before the latest developments in the Middle East.

“People will start to see fuel prices go up again, and the concern will be that inflation expectations will once again lift among households and businesses,” he said.

“It does matter for how long the oil price is $US100 a barrel – if it’s here for only a couple of days and quickly reverses, then that will provide some relief.

“But, clearly, we’ve all lost confidence in where it [the oil price] will be in six months.”

With the economy already slowing sharply, not all economists are convinced that the RBA needs to hike again.

Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, said she had never assumed the sharp drop in oil prices during the ceasefire was sustainable, even without a major escalation in the conflict.

“But we did think it was going to be just one big spike around March and April, before it settled down. Now it looks like it will be more of a grind, or maybe rolling mini-spikes,” Auld said.

Inflation remains too high but is tracking a little below where the RBA had forecast, Auld said, while unemployment was running a little higher. That combination would be enough to keep the RBA on hold while they waited for a slowing economy to take the steam out of price pressures, she said.

Auld warned that not all Australians will be able to cope with higher borrowing costs and climbing fuel costs.

“If you get an intensification of cost of living pressures plus another rate hike, for a certain segment of households that would be a pretty challenging situation and you would start to worry the economic adjustment won’t be so benign.”

title: Pauline Hanson’s domestic violence comments were no stumble
excerpt:
The One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violence

Follow our Australia news live blog for late...
body_text:
The One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violence

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

For a decade, Pauline Hanson has been beating the same drum.

Her comments this week – suggesting domestic violence was a “two-way street” and questioning why women did not simply leave abusive relationships – have caused significant concern and been labelled “dangerous” by experts and other commentators.

But they are not, as they’ve been portrayed, another “gaffe” by the stumbling One Nation leader as she attempts to stabilise her party’s polls that show it might become a new electoral force in Australia.

The comments make plain something that has been a driving force for the populist leader since her return to parliament in 2016.

One Nation’s political ascendancy in recent months has been built on replicating anti-immigrant and hard right pivots in the United States and the UK. Hanson’s own second coming was built on an allyship with groups of anti-feminist men and heavily influenced by domestic violence allegations against her son, Adam Hanson, which she says were false.

In 2019, Hanson used parliamentary privilege to call her former daughter-in-law “nasty” and accuse her of making false claims about her son. She has consistently – inside and outside parliament – made claims, rejected by experts and evidence, that suggest women routinely make false allegations of violence for advantage in the family law system.

Speaking in 2017, on domestic violence orders, Hanson said: “Women, mostly women, are going around throwing them around left, right and centre.”

In 2021 on Sky News, Hanson said: “There are men who have been accused of these things that didn’t, it didn’t happen.

“It shows you how lies and perjury are leading to the failure of Australia’s family law system and contributing to the death of 21 men by suicide and the murder of one woman each week.”

The “21 men” figure has been repeatedly cited by Hanson, her colleague Malcolm Roberts, and others in One Nation as a campaigning point. The figure comes from a men’s rights organisation, the Australian Brotherhood of Fathers (ABF), and has been debunked by factcheckers.

The ABF have been among Hanson’s biggest cheerleaders since her re-election. Roberts has been particularly close to the group, visiting several times, and recording a special video message for a gathering.

One of the first things Roberts did after a federal parliament hearing in 2019 – when he claimed without evidence there were “many instances” of women making up domestic violence allegations – was to phone the ABF’s founder, Leith Erikson.

The ABF has claimed in Facebook posts to have received donations from One Nation, and the political party has held community barbecues in support of the men’s group.

The trope that women fabricate violence claims against men is a common grievance of men’s rights groups, but experts say there is no evidence to support this.

After the 2019 election, Hanson’s return to the senate became more than a political curiosity. The Morrison government, four seats short of a senate majority, suddenly needed her support to pass legislation.

The government’s sop to Hanson was to accede to her request for a family law inquiry, and to make her the deputy chair (she introduced herself at hearings as the “co-chair”). 
 It is particularly instructive, for all those playing along at home and wondering what One Nation might do with newfound political influence, to understand that the last time Hanson was in a position to ask for something, she chose an inquiry that became a formal platform for misogynists and groups pushing unsupported claims that the system is loaded against men.

Hanson livestreamed the hearings to her Facebook page. Commenters called expert witnesses and MPs things like “man-hater” and “dirty snake”.

The hearings in March 2020 took place less than a month after the murders of Hannah Clarke and her children.

When an expert witness, the Griffith University law professor Zoe Rathus, mentioned the case, Hanson responded:

“I totally agree that what happened to Hannah and her children was horrendous and should never happen. But it’s on both sides. I have read your report, and it’s all about women. Do you agree that there are men who are aggrieved, men who face domestic violence, men who are taking their own lives?

“Do you admit that there are men facing domestic violence?”
 Rathus responded: “I would prefer if you didn’t ask me whether I ‘admit’ things. I’m not really here to admit things. I’m here to present my research.

“The statistics are very clear that domestic violence is something that is very gendered and that violence in the home happens more often by men towards women.”

Her comments this week, in the shadow of four more alleged domestic violence homicides, have understandably triggered more backlash because of One Nation’s political ascendancy.

As a fringe politician needing only to win a senate quota every six years, Hanson’s views only needed to appeal to a small, angry cohort.

The common wisdom is that as One Nation heads for the mainstream – its founder will need to temper her more extreme ideas to keep her coalition of disengaged and aggrieved voters together.

Ben Smee is Guardian Australia’s Queensland state correspondent

title: Middle East crisis latest: US carries out strikes across Iran as Tehran targets American bases in region
excerpt:
Latest attacks come after Trump vowed ‘major military punishment’ for Tehran and its Houthi allies

Benjamin Netanyahu will meet Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, the Israeli prime minister’...
body_text:
Latest attacks come after Trump vowed ‘major military punishment’ for Tehran and its Houthi allies

Benjamin Netanyahu will meet Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, the Israeli prime minister’s office said.

“As part of the visit, the prime minister will meet with President Trump at the White House on Tuesday and attend the funeral service for Senator Lindsey Graham, a friend of Israel,” Netanyahu’s office said, adding that he will depart for Washington on Monday.

Netanyahu’s visit comes at a time when tensions have mounted between the two leaders over the handling of the war with Iran and as Trump threatens to escalate US military action.

Since Trump’s return to the White House last year, the two have already met six times, but this will be the first such meeting in five months. At the last one in February, Netanyahu made the case for the joint offensive against Iran that Trump launched with him weeks later.

Iran has pushed back on a New York Times (paywall) report from Thursday that Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire deal presented by the Iraqi prime minister, calling the report “completely diversionary and misleading,” according to state media IRNA.

The NYT reported that the proposal was the only one on the table, and Tehran was not interested in a temporary deal which left the question of control of the strait of Hormuz unresolved, citing Iranian officials.

The IRNA report claimed the proposal was for a “temporary 10-day ceasefire”. Full details of the proposal have not been published.

“Iran has always regarded diplomacy as having intrinsic value,” an unnamed Iranian official said, according to IRNA. “The problem of the escalation of conflict in the region stems exclusively from the United States’ breach of its promises and violation of the commitments contained in the June 18 memorandum of understanding.”

Baghdad has also denied the NYT report. Ali al-Zaidi’s trip to Iran followed his recent visit to the White House where he met with Donald Trump.

The Iraqi prime minister’s media office said the “claims” in the report were “completely baseless and had no connection to reality”, according to a statement published by the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The office urged media outlets “to verify information, rely on official sources and refrain from circulating unsubstantiated reports or claims attributed to anonymous sources”.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned civilians in the Middle East on Friday to stay away from US forces, state media reported.

In an interview carried out by state TV, the IRGC said:

double quotation markWe warn the general public in countries where American soldiers are stationed to immediately stay out of a radius of 500 metres from the places where American soldiers are hiding, in order to be safe.

Jordan’s military said it intercepted seven missiles and six drones launched by Iran on Friday.

The military said the interceptions, performed by air defence systems and air force planes, “resulted in no casualties or material damage,” according to AFP.

Earlier on Friday, the Iranian army said it had launched drone attacks targeting US military personnel and military targets in Bahrain and Jordan after the US carried out its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran.
