US missiles struck targets across Iran on Friday after Donald Trump vowed “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen for extending the Middle East war to a second major shipping chokepoint, the mouth of the ⁠Red Sea.

The US Central Command said it targeted Iranian military command centres, communication networks, drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and maritime capabilities.

Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported that explosions were reported in Khondab, Khorramabad, Konarak and Jask.

Meanwhile, as Reuters reports, ​Iranian armed forces responded by firing a wave of retaliatory attacks on at US bases in neighbouring Arab countries and warning people there that they may strike non-military buildings used by US personnel.

The Iranian army said it used drones to target facilities in Bahrain and Jordan, with attacks also reported in Kuwait and Iraq.

It said Trump’s threats only strengthened its resolve.

title: How dangerous are wildfires and how can we stop them from getting worse?
excerpt:
The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet heats up, putting more people at risk

Fierce wildfires after back-to-back heatwaves have forced tens of thousands of people acr...
body_text:
The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet heats up, putting more people at risk

Fierce wildfires after back-to-back heatwaves have forced tens of thousands of people across southern Europe to flee their homes, while powerful infernos across Canada and the US choke big cities with thick smoke.

Wildfires directly kill hundreds of people each year. Though they may seem apocalyptic, the death toll is far lower than from floods, which kill thousands, and from heatwaves, which kill hundreds of thousands.

But when you factor in smoke, the human cost rises rapidly. The latest study estimates that the air pollution spewed by wildfires kills a staggering 1.5 million people each year. The toxic fumes can reach so far that tendrils of smoke from Australian bushfires have menaced South America, while smoke from Canadian fires – which regularly suffocate cities across the US – have fouled the air in Europe. Last year, a study attributed 22,000 early deaths in Europe to Canadian wildfire smoke in 2023, out of a total of 82,000 deaths.

Many things can spark a wildfire: natural causes such as lightning, faulty infrastructure such as downed power lines, or people behaving badly. Devastating blazes in recent years have been started by smokers tossing cigarette butts, tourists failing to put out campfires, and even arsonists intentionally setting nature alight.

But whether those sparks turn into small fires or raging blazes depends on the weather. Fires need hot, dry fuel to burn, and they spread further with strong winds.

Fossil fuel pollution has heated the planet by about 1.3C, raising the risk of prolonged heat that turns forests and grasslands into tinderboxes. In some regions, such as the Mediterranean, global heating is also fuelling droughts that dry out lush greenery.

Scientists have found that such shifts have made the wildfires that have happened this year in places including California, South Korea and Australia more likely – in some cases doubling the chance of extreme weather conditions that help fires spread.

Even as the planet has heated up, the area torched by fires has fallen. This is because people have taken nature that used to burn freely and turned it into farms or cities – in recent decades mainly in Africa – that stop the spread of flames. The latest models find land use changes and other human drivers have shrunk the burned area by 19.1% since 1900, while climate changes increased it by 15.8% – resulting in a small decline of 3.3% overall.

The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet bakes. Two separate indices of fire weather project a steady rise in the number of days with high fire danger as temperatures inch higher, a recent study found.

By the end of the century, the total burned area is projected to rise by 40% even in an optimistic scenario for cutting carbon pollution, according to a separate study. In a worst-case scenario, it is set to double.

The danger that wildfires pose to people and property can drop sharply by managing land better. This can include creating fire breaks to stem the spread of an inferno, stopping new settlement in places prone to fires, and even sending herds of goats into abandoned farmland to graze away overgrown vegetation.

In some places firefighters are trying the technique of intentionally burning land to avoid a buildup of fuel that could lead to catastrophic fires – a long-running Indigenous practice in Australia and North America that European fire experts are starting to adopt.

Not on its own. Land abandonment and fire suppression is a big contributor to the buildup of fuel that allows blazes in parts of the US and the Mediterranean to explode into mega-fires, but in Canada, most of the burning takes place in boreal forests that were never managed by humans. These fires are being intensified by rising global average temperatures that worsen the risk of severe fire weather.

If you live somewhere at risk of wildfires, put a plan together before disaster strikes. This could include identifying safe routes and nearby shelters, and packing an emergency bag. Some fire services recommend creating a safe zone around your home that is free from leaves and flammable materials.

Experts say you should vacate immediately if authorities tell you to – or if your home is at risk but warnings have not come. To avoid the smoke, keep windows closed and use respirator masks.

title: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed in West Bank shooting
excerpt:
It was the deadliest incident of its kind in the West Bank for months

At least four Palestinians and two Israelis have been killed in a shooting in the occupied West Bank - the deadliest single incid...
body_text:
It was the deadliest incident of its kind in the West Bank for months

At least four Palestinians and two Israelis have been killed in a shooting in the occupied West Bank - the deadliest single incident there in months.

There are conflicting accounts of the sequence of events in the northern village of Tal. Palestinians told the BBC that residents confronted Jewish settlers who were attacking them. An eyewitness said soldiers then arrived and started shooting.

Israel's military said it had responded to reports that hikers had been attacked. It said "terrorists stole the weapon" of a security guard and killed him.

It later said a soldier had also been killed, but did not give details. The IDF has not explained who killed the other Palestinians.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) says it is preparing for a major operation in the area and has cancelled soldiers' leave.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

Ahmed Zeidan, an eyewitness, told the BBC the latest incident began early in the morning, when locals in Tal rushed to confront about 30 settlers who were attacking Palestinian homes.

He said hand-to-hand clashes broke out in the presence of Israeli soldiers.

A local leader of the ruling Fatah party, Essam Saifi, told Reuters news agency that settlers opened fire before Israeli forces arrived and also started shooting.

He said two brothers and two of their cousins were among those killed. Palestinian officials said several other Palestinians were wounded.

The IDF said Palestinians began the attack.

It said soldiers had gone to Tal following a report of an attack on Israeli civilians who were hiking in the area. A security guard from a nearby settler outpost had gone to the scene and had his gun snatched by a Palestinian who used it against the Israelis, killing him.

Soldiers then "eliminated the terrorist who executed the terror attack", the IDF added.

It later said a 27-year-old soldier "fell during operational activity in the area of ​​the village". The circumstances of his death remain unclear.

The Israeli ambulance service said two Israelis were also wounded.

The Palestinian foreign ministry said it "condemns in the strongest terms the massacre" in Tal.

It said "the escalation of settler terrorism is a direct consequence of the protection, political backing, and complete impunity granted by the Israeli government and occupation forces".

"Official Israeli incitement continues to fuel and encourage these crimes, creating an environment in which settler violence flourishes without accountability," it added.

An AFP reporter at the site, south-west of Nablus, said roadblocks had been set up and troops were searching for additional suspects.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to act "with full force against the terrorists and those who orchestrate and sponsor them".

He called an emergency meeting with security officials, and reinforcements have been sent to the area, close to the settlement of Havat Gilad.

Since October 2023, 1,114 Palestinians have been killed there, the vast majority by the IDF, the UN says. It says at least 35 of the deaths have involved attacks by settlers.

The UN says 41 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law.

title: Purported Nancy Guthrie note includes unusual demand that breaks basic ransom rule: retired FBI negotiator
excerpt:
New excerpts from a purported Nancy Guthrie ransom note appear inconsistent with the kidnapping-for-ransom motive, according to retired FBI negotiator and supervisory agent Jason Pack.

The latest rev...
body_text:
New excerpts from a purported Nancy Guthrie ransom note appear inconsistent with the kidnapping-for-ransom motive, according to retired FBI negotiator and supervisory agent Jason Pack.

The latest revelations about the purported first ransom note in the Nancy Guthrie case appear inconsistent with a kidnapping for ransom, according to a retired FBI negotiator.

"The fact that they wanted to cut off communication quickly suggests that they may not have had kidnapping for ransom as a primary motive, even though that's what this says," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory agent. "It doesn't seem like how a usual kidnapping goes down."

He said typical kidnappers want to keep communication channels open to negotiate payment and maintain leverage over the victim's family, making the reported demand for no further contact highly unusual.

NEW DETAILS FROM NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMAND REVEALED, 'HER LIFE IS IN YOUR HANDS': REPORT

Savannah Guthrie will return to "Today" on Monday after a two-month absence since her mother, Nancy, went missing on Feb. 1. (Getty Images/Fox News Digital)

"The most telling sign is this no negotiation, no further contact line," Pack told Fox News Digital. "Genuine kidnappers wanna keep the line of communication open."

The sender did, however, incorporate known pressure tactics, including setting a deadline, making threats and telling the family that Guthrie knew what would happen if they failed to comply, Pack said.

But cutting off communication before the deadlines passed was also unusual, he added.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTE CLAIMED THAT SHE HAD DIED, BEEN ‘BURIED WITH NATURE,’ SOURCE SAYS

Annie Guthrie, her husband Tommaso Cioni, and Savannah Guthrie at their missing mother Nancy Guthrie's home on Monday, March 2, in Tucson, Arizona. (Fox News)

Guthrie was taken from her home in Tucson's Catalina Foothills neighborhood in the early morning hours of Feb. 1, according to the Pima County Sheriff's Department and the FBI. She has not been seen since, and no proof of life was ever provided.

In a second purported ransom note, the sender indicated Guthrie had died soon after she was taken and been buried "with nature."

New excerpts from what is reportedly the first note received by local media shed light on why Pack believes the communication departed from a traditional ransom demand.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTES DON'T MATCH SUSPECT'S BEHAVIOR, PROFILER SAYS: 'I DON'T BELIEVE THEY'RE REAL'

These two images were released by the FBI, recovered from Nancy Guthrie's Nest doorbell camera. It's unclear whether they show the same person. (FBI)

Briana Whitney, who was working for the Phoenix-based AZ Family news outlet when the case broke, joined "Crime Junkie" host Ashley Flowers on Wednesday to discuss the note her former outlet received. "Crime Junkie" declined to share copies of the text.

"Hello Savannah, we have your mother Nancy," she began, reading from what she said was the first note sent to local media. "She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom, and once payment is received, she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of seven days."

As previously conveyed by authorities, the sender gave two deadlines with increased money demands the longer it took.

"Once payment is received to the Bitcoin address below, she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop-off location back in Tucson," Whitney read. "If the payment is not received by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5 p.m., she will be killed. Your mother is aware of this, and her life is in your hands."

Deputies examine a flyer taped to Nancy Guthrie's mailbox on Sunday, Feb. 22, 2026. They were called to the scene after volunteer searchers and several streamers walked onto Guthrie's property with a shovel. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)

The sender left no room for further dialogue.

"It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible," the note reportedly continued. "You will not be able to contact me from here on out. There will be no negotiation. Do not play games. Law enforcement will not be able to help you."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

The note also included details that may have only been available to investigators and the suspect at the time, including the location of Guthrie's Apple Watch and details about the smashed floodlight in her backyard — but even that is not enough to pin down kidnapping for ransom as a motive, Pack said.

Savannah Guthrie poses alongside her mother Nancy Guthrie during a production break whilst hosting NBC's "Today Show" live from Australia. (Photo by Don Arnold/WireImage)

"The details about the security camera and the spotlight that was out, that proves that they know what the home was like, what the environment may have been like, but it's not a real proof of life," he said.

In most ransom kidnappings, he said, the abductors will want to prove they have possession of the victim and that the victim is alive.

"All these things put together don't seem really like they go with the kidnapping for ransom," he said.

Investigators appear to be split on the notes' authenticity. While one person has already pleaded guilty to sending an imposter ransom note to Guthrie's other daughter, Annie, and her husband Tommaso Cioni, that case is not believed to be connected to the notes sent to local media stations.

A well-wisher signs a banner that reads "Bring her home" and shows a photo of Nancy Guthrie, U.S. television journalist Savannah Guthrie's abducted elderly mother, at the KVOA newsroom, where Savannah worked earlier in her career, in Tucson, Arizona, U.S., Feb. 12, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)

"The FBI and its task force partners have received several ransom notes over the course of this investigation," the FBI's Phoenix office said in a statement in June. "Some have been deemed to be extortion attempts without legitimacy. Other ransom demands may potentially be legitimate and are still being investigated as such. This case continues to be investigated as a kidnapping for ransom case. The FBI has and will continue to offer all assistance possible in the investigation — however local authorities remain the lead."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Some investigators said they were confident that the ransom demands are all bogus, while others are cautious about reaching that conclusion while Guthrie's whereabouts remain unknown, federal law enforcement sources told Fox News and Fox News Digital. Still, the two notes that Whitney mentioned have been deemed potentially authentic by investigators and by the Guthrie family.

The only known suspect remains publicly unidentified — a masked intruder who appeared on Nest doorbell camera video that the FBI recovered with help from Google.

He is described as standing between 5 feet, 9 inches and 5 feet, 10 inches tall with an average build. He was wearing a black Ozark Trail backpack. It remains unclear whether he acted alone.

The sum of rewards in the case is over $1.2 million.

Anyone with information is asked to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Tucson's Crime Stoppers affiliate at 520-88-CRIME.

title: Confusing product recall adds to US cyclospora outbreak uncertainty
excerpt:
Explosive diarrhea infection detected in 41 states with at least 72 sickened by new, as yet unknown source of parasite

Confusion abounds in the cyclospora outbreak that has sickened thousands in at l...
body_text:
Explosive diarrhea infection detected in 41 states with at least 72 sickened by new, as yet unknown source of parasite

Confusion abounds in the cyclospora outbreak that has sickened thousands in at least 41 states, as officials identify a new cluster of cases and more potential products come under scrutiny.

The recall of products during this outbreak of explosive diarrhea has been an unusual one, complicated by poor communication, politicization and the delay of a new regulatory rule could have helped trace the cyclosporiasis outbreak faster.

At least 72 people have been sickened by another as-yet unknown source of cyclospora, and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is now tracing back to the potential contamination source, according to an update from the agency on Wednesday.

It joins another investigation, still ongoing, that led to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms, a mega-producer based in the US with facilities in Mexico.

Officials in North Carolina also identified parsley and cilantro, in addition to lettuce, as potentially linked to the state’s 561 confirmed cases.

“The amount of cases we’re having right now is incredibly high, and it’s clear that there’s multiple outbreaks happening all at once,” said Katelyn Jetelina, science communicator and founder of Your Local Epidemiologist. “The news of another cluster isn’t too surprising to me. What is is how little information was given. The communication just continually is falling short, which is leaving all of us on the outside to put these puzzle pieces together.”

With all clusters of cases, “the key question is whether the source can stop,” said Joshua Sharfstein, a public health professor at Johns Hopkins University and former principal deputy commissioner at the FDA.

If there was a confined burst of contamination, the outbreak could end soon; but if the soil or water is still contaminated, “then there’s a risk of ongoing contamination, and that’s kind of what FDA has to worry about,” he said. And “the ability to say all the downstream products – that has traditionally been very hard”.

A new regulation was supposed to help with all of that.

Last year, the FDA proposed the Food Traceability Rule in order to more quickly track and identify foods at high risk of being contaminated by foodborne pathogens – including iceberg lettuce.

“This is exactly the sort of gap that the food traceability list is meant to close,” Jetelina said.

The new regulation was required by the Food Safety Modernization Act of 2011, and it was finally set to go into effect in January.

“Probably the most important thing about that law was that companies like Taylor Farms have to recognize the risk and have these processes to address it,” Sharfstein said.

But food suppliers asked for more time, and it is now planned to take effect in early 2028.

These epidemiological investigations are particularly important since cyclospora is so difficult to detect in produce. Without the updated rule, traceback investigations can take days or weeks – which can allow an outbreak to spread even more.

The recall from Taylor Farms has been plagued with confusion and reversals. Last Thursday, businesses supplied by Taylor Farms learned they should not use the lettuce before the FDA’s announcements, according to reporting by Consumer Reports. Executives also met with the White House and the FDA to distance themselves from the cyclospora outbreak, according to reporting by the New York Times and Bloomberg.

On Friday, the FDA warned against eating shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia – but the agency did not identify the producer at that point, noting only that they were located in Mexico.

Taylor Farms posted to Facebook on Friday afternoon that none of their salads or kits were associated with the outbreak, the Times also reported; the post appears to be deleted now, with no posts visible on their page since 8 July. The Taylor Farms website still said there were no active recalls. “In the rare event a product does not meet these standards, we take immediate action to remove affected items from distribution and notify our customers,” the website said.

The recall was posted later that evening, noting that the potentially contaminated lettuce had been shipped as recently as Thursday.

The voluntary recall said that 27 states might be affected by the contaminated lettuce. And it took the unusual approach of not listing brand names, instead using internal product numbers – which appear to correspond with products sold in stores such as Walmart and potentially restaurants such as Subway. That greatly complicated the ability of stores, restaurants and customers to know which products were involved in the recall.

“The actual recall notice from Taylor Farms was incredibly weird, because you had to decode it,” Jetelina said.

On Saturday, the FDA added an update: lettuce that was not part of the recall had tested positive for cyclospora. But on Sunday, the FDA deleted that line and said the test was a false positive. The recall still existed, FDA officials told journalists on Monday – despite confusing messaging from the supplier.

“Today, FDA apologized to us,” a statement on the Taylor Farms website read on Sunday, despite no public information about an apology. The farm added that “at this moment, FDA has not identified a single positive product test result for Cyclospora.” On Monday, the producer clarified that the recall was still in effect and that they were no longer sourcing iceberg lettuce from central Mexico for this growing season.

Cyclospora is notorious for being difficult to detect in produce; it’s much easier to find in the feces of humans, in whom the parasite thrives. It’s also possible for contamination of all sorts to be temporary in produce, which means investigators sometimes never have laboratory confirmation of which product or products spurred an outbreak. But there are other ways to identify contaminated products, like epidemiological investigations, Sharfstein said.

A spokesperson for Taylor Farms told the Guardian they were undertaking an independent investigation of its central Mexico facility, but did not answer questions about executives’ meeting with the White House and FDA, or provide clarity on when they first learned their product might be contaminated.

“When questions were raised about the source of the recent cyclospora outbreak, we immediately removed all potentially implicated product from the marketplace, and out of an abundance of caution we issued an even broader recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from the region,” the spokesperson said.

US officials “remain focused on protecting the American people”, said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services. The administration has “mounted a robust, science-based response to this cyclosporiasis outbreak, working closely with health departments in all 50 states, rapidly identifying known sources, and ensuring Americans have the information they need to protect themselves,” she added.

Last year, Taylor Farms donated $1m to Maga Inc, a Trump-affiliated Super Pac, according to financial records obtained by Wired.

Potential political interference was also concerning, making it more difficult to trust what’s coming from officials and companies, Jetelina said. “Trust is everything. And trust is not declared; it’s demonstrated.”

She pointed to Taco Bell, which was “incredibly cooperative” and worked quickly to pull potentially affected products and trace them back to the supplier, Jetelina said. “I was very impressed with how quickly they owned this and came out and communicated and acted,” which she contrasted with a “more uncooperative” Taylor Farms, which appears to be slow-walking the response. “And the question is why, and why isn’t there more pressure from the federal government?”

Mega-producers can meet a lot of demand for food, Sharfstein said. “But if there is a problem, that problem can be pretty widespread.”

With cyclospora, washing doesn’t really help that much, unlike E coli or salmonella. “So we are relying on the regulatory and public health system to protect us,” Sharfstein said.

“You could call it the explosive diarrhea rule,” he added. “When you’re not having explosive diarrhea, you don’t realize that the regulatory and public health systems are protecting you. When you do have explosive diarrhea, you’re like, ‘What’s going wrong? And we need to invest in systems to keep us from getting exposed to diarrhea.’”

title: Mamdani warning to wealthy New Yorkers about 'fair share' sparks online firestorm: 'Full blown communist'
excerpt: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's "pied-a-terre" wealth tax on luxury properties ignites a contentious debate, drawing strong criticism from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin and hedge fund manager Bill Ackm...
body_text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's "pied-a-terre" wealth tax on luxury properties ignites a contentious debate, drawing strong criticism from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin and hedge fund manager Bill Ackman.

New York City socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing heat on social media after his post celebrating the state’s new pied-à-terre tax on New Yorkers with a second home.

"If you have a second home in New York City worth more than $5 million, check your mailbox when you’re back in the five boroughs — because you've got mail," Mamdani posted on X, touting the tax on specific second properties introduced by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul that he supported going into effect soon.

"Today, we sent notification letters to property owners, letting them know that our new pied-à-terre tax is coming soon," Mamdani continued. "The best city in the world deserves the best parks, libraries, and schools in the world. That's only possible when we all pay our fair share. "

As of Friday morning, Mamdani’s post had been viewed over 10 million times and conservatives on social media blasted the mayor and warned that the exodus of wealthy New Yorkers will only continue under this new plan.

HOCHUL CONFRONTED ON STUDY SHOWING MILLIONAIRE EXODUS IN NEW YORK CITY

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's video admitting that he lacks the legal authority to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did little to ease Jewish leaders' concerns. (NYC Mayor's Office via YouTube/Handout via Reuters)

"Never elect a politician who: (1) sees your money as his slush fund, (2) loves Karl Marx, or (3) uses French words like ‘pied-à-terre’ to disguise new, confiscatory taxes he wants to impose to redistribute wealth," Republican Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT) posted on X.

"Socialism - Florida’s best real estate agent," Republican Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) posted on X.

"NYC’s pied-à-terre tax hasn’t even started and brokers already say owners are calling to sell," GOP strategist and attorney Mehek Cooke posted on X. "Empty units don’t tip [doormen] or pay supers. You’re not taxing the rich. You’re firing the working class that depended on them. "

"More incitement," Judicial Watch President Tom Fitton posted on X. "Communist @NYCMayor celebrates a confiscatory tax targeted at a select few. "

MAMDANI SETS INTERNET ABLAZE WITH VIDEO EXPLAINING CAVE ON PLAN TO ARREST NETANYAHU: 'WHAT A JOKE'

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul speaks about the excitement of seeing the Buffalo Bills in Western New York for the next 30 years during the ribbon cutting ceremony for the new Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park on June 23, 2026. (Shawn Dowd/Rochester Democrat and Chronicle / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

"What will the excuse be when literally nothing improves after all these tax increases?" New York City Republican Councilwoman Vickie Paladino posted on X. "Will they just demand even more, or will they tell us to ignore our own eyes as they insist they’ve actually fixed everything? Both? "

"The condescension towards the people who already pay a ton of property taxes to NYC," Washington Free Beacon investigative reporter Chuck Ross posted on X. "He thinks you're an immoral person and worthy of mockery if you have a second home. ‘when you're back in the five boroughs.’"

"That's only possible when we all pay our fair share,’ says the man who’s literally lived off of taxpayer dollars for years, produces nothing, and is concentrating the burdens on others—others who’ve contributed exponentially more to the city in both taxes and charitable contributions than he could possibly hope to contribute in 10 lifetimes, I might add," Manhattan Institute fellow Rafael Mangual posted on X.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks at a rally in New York alongside 1199SEIU members and immigration advocates after the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can revoke protections for Haitians and Syrians. (Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)

"You can practically feel the glee emanating from this tweet so it's hilarious that people will still refuse to admit he's a full-blown communist," civil rights attorney David Pivtorak posted on X.

Mamdani’s support of the pied-à-terre tax on second homes worth more than $5 million has been a viral controversy for months and started when

In April, New York City Mayor Mamdani and Hochul unveiled the joint legislative proposal targeting luxury second homes worth $5 million or more. Known as a pied-à-terre tax, the annual surcharge is expected to generate an estimated $500 million from affluent out-of-state property owners.

Mamdani has previously said revenue from the tax would go toward initiatives such as free childcare, cleaner streets and safer neighborhoods.

Critics, including billionaire Ken Griffin whose luxury New York City home was featured in Mamdani's controversial video announcing the tax, argue the tax will only drive more wealthy New Yorkers out of the state and bring jobs and investments with them.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office for comment.

Fox Business's Kristen Altus contributed to this report

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Trump-fired US attorney launches unprecedented court fight after just 54 minutes on the job
excerpt: Chief legal correspondent Shannon Bream details the Supreme Court's latest rulings, including a decision in Trump v. Slaughter affirming the president's power to dismiss a Federal Trade Commission com...
body_text:
Chief legal correspondent Shannon Bream details the Supreme Court's latest rulings, including a decision in Trump v. Slaughter affirming the president's power to dismiss a Federal Trade Commission commissioner. However, in Trump v. Cook, the court states the president cannot unilaterally fire a Federal Reserve governor. These opinions shape executive power and independent agencies.

The Trump administration fired a newly sworn-in U.S. attorney just 54 minutes into his tenure.

Now, in what is believed to be the first lawsuit of its kind, he is fighting back.

Roger Rogoff was appointed to serve as the U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington last week after a panel of district court judges, among them Democratic and Republican appointees, unanimously decided that he should fill the vacant role. The Trump administration fired him just 54 minutes after he was sworn in, prompting Rogoff to file a lawsuit alleging that the Trump administration lacked the authority to remove him.

TRUMP ADMIN FIRES US ATTORNEY IN SEATTLE MINUTES AFTER HE WAS APPOINTED

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appears at a confirmation hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., July 15, 2026. (Eric Lee/Getty Images)

The legal challenge sets up a novel test of presidential power over court-appointed U.S. attorneys, pitting the Trump administration’s claim of broad removal authority against a federal law Rogoff says allows him to serve until a Senate-confirmed successor takes office. The outcome could determine whether presidents may dismiss judicially selected prosecutors at will — and potentially leave key offices under temporary leadership without seeking Senate approval.

Rogoff argues that, while the law allows the Department of Justice to appoint an interim U.S. attorney for 120 days, after that period has expired, the local district court retains the right to appoint a replacement "until the vacancy is filled," meaning that he can’t be fired until a permanent replacement is approved by the Senate.

Allowing the president to immediately remove any court-appointed U.S. attorney he opposed, according to Rogoff, would permit an administration to circumvent the Senate-confirmation process indefinitely.

"The district court did not coordinate with DOJ on this selection," a spokesperson for the agency told Fox News Digital of the firing. "Consistent with other firings of this type, this is wholly within the President’s authority."

TRUMP PICKS JAMES MCDONALD TO LEAD POWERFUL SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK AFTER JAY CLAYTON'S DEPARTURE

Judge Roger Rogoff spent 20 years as a state prosecutor and six as a federal prosecutor before becoming a state judge, and admitted he knew the administration might fire him immediately but did not reject taking on "the best job there is." (Ted S. Warren/AP)

Rogoff’s firing was the latest in a string of dismissals — such as those in New Jersey, New York and Virginia — where the Trump administration has removed U.S. attorneys very early in their tenure. Rogoff is unique in that he is the first to challenge his removal in court.

U.S. attorneys serve as the federal government’s chief prosecutors in their districts, overseeing criminal prosecutions and representing the United States in civil cases. They also direct local U.S. attorney’s offices and coordinate federal law enforcement priorities.

"District court judges can appoint a temporary U.S. Attorney, and POTUS can fire them," acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said on X shortly after the firing. "[Western District of Washington] judges abandoned the time-honored process of consultation with the administration so that the selected U.S. Attorney is qualified to serve in the administration."

TRUMP DOJ FIRES PROSECUTORS TIED TO FACE ACT CASES AFTER REPORT ALLEGES BIAS AND MISCONDUCT

A Department of Justice inscription is seen on the headquarters building in Washington, D.C., on October 20, 2022. (Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Several experienced federal attorneys, including many in U.S. attorneys' offices, have departed the second Trump administration, often going to work for Democratic-run states and taking north of a decade of legal experience with them.

In his complaint, Rogoff points to administration statements indicating that court-appointed U.S. attorneys who lack the president’s support will be removed.

Rogoff was appointed a King County Superior Court judge by Gov. Jay Inslee, D-Wash., in 2013 and worked in private practice after leaving the bench.

The White House referred Fox News Digital to the DOJ when reached for comment. Rogoff’s attorneys did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Bill Ackman reveals why he's not a 'fan' of Mamdani, doesn't rule out mayoral run against him
excerpt:
Billionaire Bill Ackman called New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's policies disastrous for New York in a podcast interview this week.

Billionaire Bill Ackman called out New York City Mayor Zohran Ma...
body_text:
Billionaire Bill Ackman called New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's policies disastrous for New York in a podcast interview this week.

Billionaire Bill Ackman called out New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday and labeled his policies a disaster for New York City.

"Money and Rehab" host Nicole Lapin asked Ackman if he was bullish or bearish on the socialist mayor.

"I'm not a fan," he responded. "He's very smart, very charismatic, very good at politics, but I think the decisions he's making are very bad for New York."

When asked if he'd consider running for mayor, Ackman said, "I would say possibly, but I think I could achieve a lot more by helping a very talented person do that job."

Ackman brought up Mamdani's video detailing a proposed tax on second homes worth more than $5 million. He filmed the video outside hedge fun CEO Ken Griffin's apartment.

Bill Ackman and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)

ZOHRAN MAMDANI FACES BACKLASH OVER 'CREEPY,' 'UNETHICAL' VIDEO FILMED OUTSIDE BILLIONAIRE KEN GRIFFIN'S HOME

"This is an annual fee on luxury properties worth more than $5 million, whose owners do not live full-time in the city. Like for this penthouse, which hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin bought for $238 million," Mamdani said in the clip.

Griffin sharply criticized the move, calling it a "personal attack" and a "profound lack of judgment" during remarks at the Norges Bank Investment Management 2026 Investment Conference in Oslo, where he questioned what he described as the "demonizing" of business leaders.

"I think he's scaring away, discouraging. You know, you saw the whole video, I'm sure, with Ken Griffin's apartment. Ken Griffin is a massive driver of New York City economic value, about to make a massive investment in New York City, and he has this major presence in Miami, and now he's increasing the presence in Miami and diminishing the presence in New York. That's a disaster," Ackman said in the podcast interview.

He said the many things Mamdani wants to fund and pay for require the revenue of people like Griffin.

"So, if you scare away Ken Griffin, we discourage the Ken Griffins of the world from being in New York City. it's a disaster for New York," Ackman added.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was elected in November 2025 and sworn-in as the city's first socialist mayor on Jan. 1, 2026. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

NEW YORK CITY LANDLORDS WARN AMERICAN DREAM IS SLIPPING AWAY UNDER SOCIALIST RENT POLICIES

Ackman said earlier in the podcast that he hoped Mamdani could be a better mayor but that he didn't feel that socialism was the answer.

The billionaire hedge fund manager took issue with several of Mamdani's policies, including the rent freezes. Ackman said Mamdani was right to address the housing affordability crisis in the city, but that his plan to freeze rent was not going to help.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"There are buildings in New York that are comprised of rent-stabilized units and where those people got a two-year rent freeze, and free market units where those people their rents had to go up in order for the landlord to cover their, you know, costs that have inflated because half his rent roll is fixed for the next two years," Ackman said. "I mean, that seems like an entirely unfair system."

Bill Ackman speaks during the WSJ D.Live global technology conference in Laguna Beach, California on Tuesday, Oct. 17, 2017. (Patrick Fallon/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

He said it was also discouraging development in the city, and said Mamdani wasn't doing anything to increase the housing supply, which Ackman argued would bring down the cost of rent.

"Developers are risk takers, and they're the last dollar in, and they're not going to risk their capital unless they believe it's a friendly environment for landlords," he added. "New York has become a very unfriendly environment for landlords."

Ackman did praise Mamdani for starting a "DOGE-like" savings effort and said he hoped it goes somewhere.

Mamdani's office did not immediately return a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

title: Maga influencer Laura Loomer reverses course on Ukraine after Kyiv visit
excerpt:
Rightwing provocateur meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who says he expects to meet Donald Trump in Washington next week

Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet Donald Trump in Washington next week, according to the ...
body_text:
Rightwing provocateur meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who says he expects to meet Donald Trump in Washington next week

Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet Donald Trump in Washington next week, according to the rightwing US influencer Laura Loomer, amid signs the White House’s traditional hostility towards Ukraine is beginning to crumble.

In an interview with Loomer, the Ukraine president said he will probably attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham and hold talks with Trump, which will take place as the latest version of the Russian sanctions bill makes its way through Congress.

Loomer interviewed Zelenskyy in the garden of the presidential palace in Kyiv – a remarkable move for the online provocateur who has previously minimised Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and amplified Kremlin propaganda to her nearly 2 million followers on social media.

This week, however, she performed a stunning about-turn. “Just experienced my first air raid in Ukraine. Sirens blaring. This is every day for every Ukrainian,” Loomer wrote on X. “I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. We need to have moral clarity.”

Loomer posted a photo of her one-on-one meeting with Zelenskyy as well as a clip from her interview with him in which she asks about his infamous confrontation last year with Trump and the US vice-president, JD Vance, in the Oval Office. No questions were off limits, she said.

In the clip, Zelenskyy said his relationship with Trump had significantly improved and describes their brief conversation in the Vatican in April 2025 as a “historic moment”.

“We changed the relations during 15, 20 minutes,” Zelenskyy added.

Writing on Truth Social, Trump praised Loomer’s interview, calling it “Very good!!!!”. Commentators in Kyiv said Trump’s message confirmed his administration’s once negative view of Kyiv was changing at a time when Ukrainian long-range drones are pummelling Russia.

Russia has continued to strike Ukraine, with a daytime ballistic missile attack on Friday killing six people in the Kyiv region and injuring dozens more. Another five people died when an air bomb hit the eastern city of Sloviansk.

Expressing support for US sanctions on Russia, Loomer said the Kremlin was a close ally of the Iranian regime. “Russia is funding Iran and providing them with explosives to murder US soldiers as Iran has called for President Trump’s assassination,” she wrote, arguing: “The United States needs to break Russia’s economy until they submit to peace.”

Loomer’s comments are a reversal for a woman who has spent years criticising US support for Ukraine’s defence, declaring it “a country full of
 Nazi apologists” – a claim used by Russia to justify its full-scale 2022 invasion – and “led by a Jihadi apologist”.

Her scepticism towards Kyiv has been shared by other major conservative
 influencers, including Tucker Carlson, a former Fox News host. The issue became a big point of contention between more traditional Republicans, such as Mike Pence, a former vice-president, and Trump’s Maga base.

Anton Gerashchenko, a popular blogger and former Ukrainian government adviser, described Loomer’s interview with Zelenskyy as “important and necessary”. “It records a public break with Russian narratives and propaganda by part of the Maga movement. We are seeing a shift in rhetoric regarding Russian aggression,” he said.

“It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are,” Zelenskyy’s office added this week. “It takes courage to come to Ukraine and not be deterred by Russian propaganda or air raid sirens. Thank you, Laura.”

Loomer also visited the Dormition Cathedral of Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, one of the country’s most significant religious landmarks, which came under Russian drone attack in June.

In a video recorded from inside the church, she accused Vladimir Putin of hypocrisy by portraying Russia as a pro-Christian nation – a perspective many US evangelicals appear to share. “I just don’t think that you should be allowed to say that you’re protecting Christianity if you’re trying to drone strike Jesus Christ,” Loomer remarked.

Loomer also met Ukraine’s chief rabbi, Moshe Reuven Azman, and toured a branch of McDonald’s hit repeatedly by Russian missiles. Loomer ordered a cheeseburger and sat demonstratively on an outside table in front of a wrecked building, in Kyiv’s much-bombed Lukianivka district.

On Friday, the chief rabbi wrote: “I had the honour of welcoming @LauraLoomer – whose views have a significant influence on the U.S. audience and who is well known for her close ties to President Donald Trump – to the Central Synagogue of Ukraine.

“The conversation was candid. I told her the truth about this terrible war – about the daily Russian shelling, the children and civilians killed, the destroyed cities and villages, and the pain that Ukrainian families endure every day.”

title: Secret Service offers glimpse into WHCA Dinner security after alleged Trump assassination attempt
excerpt: A judge expresses concerns over the solitary confinement of White House Correspondent's Association Dinner shooting suspect Cole Allen as he appears in U.S. District Court. New DOJ video footage revea...
body_text:
A judge expresses concerns over the solitary confinement of White House Correspondent's Association Dinner shooting suspect Cole Allen as he appears in U.S. District Court. New DOJ video footage reveals Allen in the Washington Hilton Hotel on April 24, the day before the attack, along with details of his extensive weaponry.

The Secret Service is giving a behind-the-scenes glimpse inside the strategy to protect President Donald Trump and guests at Friday night's rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) Dinner.

The originally scheduled event in April was done before it even started after a crazed gunman bolted through a security checkpoint and was later accused of trying to assassinate the 47th president.

"Our agency grows and adapts from every event we secure, and we have engaged with WHCA to ensure attendees are given timely information in the unlikely event on an emergency during the event," Anthony Guglielmi, Secret Service's communications director, told Fox News Digital.

Guglielmi noted that the Secret Service's protection plan worked during the April 25 dinner when agents stopped Cole Allen of California after he allegedly descended from the 10th floor of the Washington Hilton Hotel, where the dinner is historically held, and attempted to breach security barriers. He allegedly fired one shot from a shotgun before tripping and falling, after which he was quickly detained. One Secret Service agent was shot and sustained minor injuries.

FIRST ON FOX: WHITE HOUSE REVEALS WHO’S JOINING TRUMP AT CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER — AND WHO CAN’T ATTEND

Armed Secret Service agents stand on stage during a shooting incident at the annual White House Correspondents' Association Dinner at the Washington Hilton on April 25, 2026, in Washington, D.C. According to reports, President Donald Trump and other government officials were evacuated from the venue after gunshots. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The rescheduled dinner is set for Friday night at the Waldorf Astoria on Pennsylvania Avenue, which is housed inside the Old Post Office Tower and was previously owned by the president and called the Trump International Hotel. It's the first time in decades that the annual WHCA Dinner is not being held at the Washington Hilton.

Those attending the dinner will enter the ballroom through a door separate from the main lobby and entrance of the hotel.

"Guests will see a visible police presence around the Waldorf Astoria hotel and there will be enhanced traffic closures due to proximity to major thoroughfares," Guglielmi said. "All ticketed guests will go through airport-style magnetometer screening to enter the event."

"Roads immediately around the hotel will be closed Friday evening, and specifics about closures will be communicated in the coming days."

TRUMP URGES NEED FOR SECURE WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM AFTER DINNER SHOOTING, SAYS HOTEL SETTING ‘TOUGH’ TO PROTECT

Guglielmi added that exact arrival instructions will be communicated specifically to ticket holders, and that each ticket will be screened by event staff prior to Secret Service security.

Notably, the dinner is significantly scaled-back from the usual event, which typically hosts 4,000+ guests inside one of the largest ballrooms in the District of Columbia — second only to the convention center Marriott Marquis. The Waldorf Astoria ballroom can host a maximum of 1,300 people for tight banquet seating.

Armed Secret Service agents stand on stage during a shooting incident at the annual White House Correspondents' Association Dinner at the Washington Hilton in Washington, D.C., on April 25, 2026. President Donald Trump and other government officials were evacuated after gunshots were reported. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

At the dinner, Secret Service Police Officer Victor Gonzales, who was shot by the alleged gunman, will be awarded the President’s Award for Exceptional Service to the WHCA for his actions protecting Trump and event guests during the April attack.

"The WHCA is deeply grateful that law enforcement officials prevented the armed suspect from entering the ballroom," said Weijia Jiang of CBS News, who as president of the association presided over the April dinner.

"Officer Gonzales played a significant role when he ran toward danger so that thousands of others could make it home safely. His courage stemmed from a dedication to service, which we are looking forward to honoring this week."

WHCD SHOOTING SUSPECT PLANNED TO TARGET TRUMP OFFICIALS, MANIFESTO REVEALS

According to a court filing in the proceedings against Allen, the alleged gunman boarded an Amtrak train on April 21 after purchasing a one-way ticket from Los Angeles to the nation's capital, stopping in Chicago to change trains. While he rode, prosecutors say he "kept a running note on his phone of his observations and thoughts during his cross-country train journey."

His musings along the way, in tandem with what he wrote in a later manifesto, paint a picture of an unfocused person whose thoughts were "scattered," as one former FBI behavioral analyst said, despite the gravity of the situation.

A Secret Service agent fires at Cole Allen, suspected in the assassination attempt of President Donald Trump, at the White House Correspondents' Dinner on Saturday, April 25, 2026. (Obtained by The Washington Post)

While he traveled through the U.S. Southwest on the first leg of his trip, Allen made a note: "[t]he southwest desert in spring Distant wind turbines looming like snowy mountains across the hazy NM desert."

Of Chicago, where he would switch trains and board a second train to his final destination, Allen wrote that, "Chicago is cool; kinda like an Iowa small town was scaled up to LA size." Of the sliver of southwestern Pennsylvania through which he would pass, he wrote that the "woods are awesome (look like vast fairy lands filled with tiny trickling creeks in spring apparently."

Allen arrived in Washington, D.C., early in the afternoon on Friday, April 24. He spent about 30 hours in the city before initiating his alleged attack.

Law enforcement personnel detain Cole Tomas Allen, a suspect in the shooting incident at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner, in Washington, D.C., U.S. on April 25, 2026. (Donald J Trump via Truth Social/Handout via Reuters)

Surveillance video from the Washington Hilton hotel, also released by the Department of Justice, showed Allen apparently pacing through hallways, once entering the hotel's fitness center and taking a look around before hastily exiting.

Minutes before the attack, a pre-scheduled email from Allen was sent to his family and friends, explaining his actions, according to authorities.

He allegedly acknowledged that his mission would likely severely harm him at the least, but never stated that he was willing to die for his cause. His motivations were political, and he painted himself as a savior of the oppressed. He apologized profusely to family, friends and everyone he had come in contact with on his cross-country trek. He noted that there were certain people he hoped wouldn't be caught in the crossfire, and described himself as "friendly."

First lady Melania Trump and President Donald Trump attend the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner at the Washington Hilton in Washington, D.C, on April 25, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

Allen remains in federal custody in Washington, D.C., while awaiting trial on four charges.

Those charges are attempting to assassinate the President of the United States, discharge of a firearm during a crime of violence, transporting a firearm across state lines and assaulting a federal officer with a deadly weapon.

Fox News' Jake Gibson contributed to this report.

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Burnham urged to award £2.4bn military satellite contract to Airbus over US rival
excerpt:
Unite union leader says giving Skynet 6 WSS contract to Lockheed Martin would be a ‘massive mistake’

One of the Labour party’s biggest union backers has called for Andy Burnham to award a £2.4bn mili...
body_text:
Unite union leader says giving Skynet 6 WSS contract to Lockheed Martin would be a ‘massive mistake’

One of the Labour party’s biggest union backers has called for Andy Burnham to award a £2.4bn military satellite contract to the European manufacturer Airbus rather than a US rival, Lockheed Martin, amid concerns that as many as 600 jobs may be at risk.

Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said it would be a “massive mistake” to go for a US company over Airbus, which is headquartered in France but designs and builds satellites in Stevenage in Hertfordshire and Portsmouth in Hampshire.

The bid battle is likely to be seen as an early test of how Burnham’s pledge to use “public procurement to back British industry” will work. It will also be one of the first major spending decisions for the new defence secretary, Wes Streeting, as the UK tries to navigate the tricky relationship with the nationalistic US administration under Donald Trump, who wants other countries to buy more American kit.

The Skynet 6 wideband satellite system (WSS) will be two geostationary satellites to carry the UK Ministry of Defence’s most sensitive data. However, the union, which represents workers making the satellites, and the Labour MP for Stevenage, Kevin Bonavia, are putting pressure on the government to opt for Airbus to preserve existing jobs rather than choosing the US deal.

Lockheed Martin has promised to create about 500 direct jobs in north-east England, including an assembly facility in Durham, plus another 1,500 jobs in the broader supply chain. The potential for exports from the UK to other countries is thought to be a key part of its offer, as well as integration with the US military.

Critics of the Lockheed bid said the US company would rely on American intellectual property rather than using technology developed in Britain. Lockheed has pledged to keep any intellectual property it develops in the UK, and has already invested in a research partnership with Northumbria University in Newcastle.

Graham said: “Andy Burnham has said he is backing Britain and British jobs. The Skynet WSS contract could be the first test of this. These satellites have been designed and built in Britain for the last 20 years ensuring hundreds of skilled jobs in Stevenage and Portsmouth, as well as thousands more in the supply chain.

“Handing the British space industry over to the Americans in the first days of the new government would be a massive mistake, industrially and politically.”

Defence Eye, an industry publication, reported that the MoD was pushing to make a decision as soon as 1 August.

Senior defence industry insiders have said awarding the contract to Lockheed could make Airbus more likely to move its satellite construction elsewhere. They argue that the choice of a US system would be a fatal blow to efforts to export the British technology. The contract could also secure the facility during a planned merger of the space businesses of Airbus, France’s Thales, and Italy’s Leonardo.

Airbus and its predecessor companies have built the UK’s military satellites for decades, including the Skynet 5 system used by the UK’s armed forces. The first Skynet satellite was launched in 1969 (well before the use of the name for a hostile artificial intelligence in the 1984 film The Terminator).

Lockheed Martin, which also makes parts for the F35 fighter jet in the UK, declined to comment on the satellite competition. However, Rod Drury, Lockheed Martin’s vice-president for global business, said: “All our initiatives in the UK are based around UK government contracts, with a UK company, delivered predominantly through UK-based staff, leveraging the best of US-based tech and capabilities.

“We are always looking to leverage the best of local industry and academia, as evidenced through our Northumbria University relationship, as evidenced through the significant number of supply chain agreements we have utilising UK companies.”

Bonavia said: “This is a big opportunity for our new prime minister to back British manufacturing and sovereign capabilities, right off the bat.

“The defence investment plan is clear: we must back British industry. Design, manufacture and test of military satellites is one of the UK’s crown jewels of defence capability. Thousands of highly skilled workers in Stevenage and Portsmouth already have the expertise that keeps the UK at the forefront of satellite technology.”

title: 'Ransom Canyon' star Josh Duhamel says he'd rather put money into North Dakota after selling Los Angeles home
excerpt:
The "Ransom Canyon" star recently sold one of his Los Angeles homes, choosing instead to invest his money in his new homebase, Fargo, North Dakota.

Josh Duhamel is ready to set down roots somewhere o...
body_text:
The "Ransom Canyon" star recently sold one of his Los Angeles homes, choosing instead to invest his money in his new homebase, Fargo, North Dakota.

Josh Duhamel is ready to set down roots somewhere other than Los Angeles.

In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 53-year-old actor discussed season two of "Ransom Canyon," as well as his decision to sell his LA home following his move to North Dakota.

"Well, we still have a house in Los Angeles that we have because I have a 12-year-old son who goes to school there and will be there until he's done with school," he said. "So we go back and forth between Fargo, North Dakota and Los Angeles. The house that I just sold was the house that was sort of my transition space between when I got divorced and when I started a new family."

He explained that after "renting it for the last couple of years," he decided to sell it, adding, he realized he would "rather put that money in North Dakota."

Duhamel shared he would rather put money into North Dakota. (Tiffany Rose/Getty Images for Newport Beach Film Festival)

‘SOPRANOS’ STAR JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER FLED HOLLYWOOD FOR TEXAS WHERE SHE NO LONGER FEELS ‘WATCHED’

The "Life as We Know It" star sold the 3,310-square-foot $2.9 million home in Encino earlier this month, a little over a year after he spoke to Parade about his decision to move out of Los Angeles to spend time in Minnesota, living an off-the-grid lifestyle in a home he spent 15 years building.

"The closest store is 40 miles away," he explained to the outlet. "Once we get there, it's really about everybody taking care of each other — making memories, spending time with family and friends."

WATCH: Josh Duhamel would rather invest his money in North Dakota

Duhamel lives in Fargo, North Dakota, with his wife, Audra Mari, and their two kids – son Shepard, 2, and daughter Rocca, who is 2 months old – with his 12-year-old son, Axl, whom he shares with his ex Fergie, joining them from time to time. The family will often spend time at their off-the-grid cabin in Minnesota.

In addition to allowing his family to "get back to the basics," and his children to grow up exploring nature rather than being on their iPads all day, Duhamel says living an off-the-grid lifestyle in their Minnesota getaway has helped him prepare for his role in "Ransom Canyon."

Duhamel said living off-the-grid in Minnesota helped him prepare for his role in "Ransom Canyon." (Netflix)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I think that when I first met with April Blair, the showrunner, I was at my cabin, literally out there on my tractor doing something, and I was kind of in that headspace already," he said. "There are a lot of similarities. I don't have a horse, I don't have cattle, but I do have a lot of tractors, a lot of ranchy stuff out there, and I think that I sort of live this life, or something closely adjacent to it."

He added: "Anyway, so I felt like I really sort of understood the love of your land, the legacy, taking care of the people around you, all those things that I think are sort of the same themes as ranch life. And I think that that, they, do sort of inform one another."

The show is a neo-Western drama on Netflix starring Duhamel and Minka Kelly, and follows the lives of three rival ranching families in the Texas Hill Country.

WATCH: Josh Duhamel's off-the-grid lifestyle helped prepare him for his 'Ransom Canyon' role

In the show, Duhamel plays the owner of Double K Ranch, one of the biggest ranches in the canyon, who in season one is still grieving the loss of his wife and son, and is willing to do anything to protect his family's land and legacy.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Duhamel's character started a romance with Minka Kelly's character in season one of the show. (ANNA KOORIS/Netflix)

Season one of the show saw a budding romance between Duhamel and Kelly's characters, who plays his wife's best friend who has always had feelings for him.

"Constant sort of balance that we're trying to strike on the show in that I want to make sure that we keep it rough and sort of gritty and cowboy Western and then there's forces that want to pull it way into the romance, which I get," he said. "But it's finding that balance between the two so it's still a Western, and it still has that kind of gritty Western vibe."

"Ransom Canyon" season 2 is now streaming on Netflix.

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

title: Texas nun detained by ICE speaks out for first time: ‘It was very heartbreaking for me’
excerpt:
Sister Leticia Ugboaja says she went into a cold sweat as ICE officers approached her in McAllen on her way to church

A nun who was taken into immigration custody last month in Texas said on Thursday...
body_text:
Sister Leticia Ugboaja says she went into a cold sweat as ICE officers approached her in McAllen on her way to church

A nun who was taken into immigration custody last month in Texas said on Thursday that she went into a cold sweat as two armed men approached her while she walked to Sunday mass in her habit, thinking about the day’s Bible readings and carrying little more than her rosary and cellphone.

“Honestly, in that moment, I did not understand what was going on, what was happening to me,” Sister Leticia Ugboaja said at a news conference at Our Lady of Sorrows church in McAllen, Texas, on the US-Mexico border, where she spoke out for the first time since US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested her on 28 June.

Ugboaja’s attorney says she has for years been granted protection from removal to her native Nigeria because she was likely to face torture there.

Ugboaja, 56, was released several hours after being detained while on her way to church. Parish officials’ posting about her on social media brought attention to her case, and Congress members ultimately intervened on her behalf.

Donald Trump made mass deportations a central promise of his second administration, with his immigration crackdown leading to unusually aggressive tactics that have faced scrutiny.

Ugboaja, who has a check-in appointment with ICE on Tuesday, said she wanted to speak out to help others, and pleaded for people to have the chance to be heard before being taken into custody.

“There are many others in this same situation, people who have been given some form of protection under our laws, who have followed every rule asked of them, and who still live with uncertainty,” Ugboaja said.

While she’s grateful to those who helped her, she said, that “does not mean I can stay quiet about what happened to me, or about what is still happening to others”.

Her attorney, Carlos Garcia, sat next to Ugboaja at the news conference and provided details about her immigration case. He said that in 2019, an immigration judge denied her application for asylum but granted her protection from removal to Nigeria because she would probably be tortured there. Garcia said Ugboaja, who is a nurse, has complied with everything required of her and had permission to work in the US.

When ICE detained Ugboaja in June, she wasn’t given much explanation as to why she was taken into custody, her attorney said. But the US planned to remove her to a third country, he added.

The Trump administration’s third-country removal policy has been criticized by lawyers and human rights groups and has faced legal challenges. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has said the agreements allow people seeking asylum in the US to pursue protection in the other country, and that the agreements are used to try to address large backlogs in immigration courts.

The DHS and ICE did not respond to a request for comment on Ugboaja’s case on Thursday and did not respond to requests for comment after her detention in June.

Ugboaja is part of the Daughters of Mary Mother of Mercy and volunteered as an extraordinary minister of holy communion at Our Lady of Sorrows church, a spokesperson for the Diocese of Brownsville has said. Ugboaja is also a registered nurse at South Texas Health System and worked previously for 10 years as a certified nursing assistant in Edinburg, the spokesperson said.

Ugboaja said she had begged the arresting officers to let her attend mass and receive holy communion, but was told she could not.

“For me, a nun, not to go to mass on Sunday, not to receive communion, it was very, very heartbreaking for me,” she said.

title: Tanzanian lecturer arrested over anti-government protests charged with terrorism
excerpt:
Melkisedek Kaijage was among more than 130 people arrested earlier this month

A Tanzanian university lecturer who was arrested earlier this month over allegations of inciting anti-government protests...
body_text:
Melkisedek Kaijage was among more than 130 people arrested earlier this month

A Tanzanian university lecturer who was arrested earlier this month over allegations of inciting anti-government protests has now been charged with terrorism.

Melkisedek Kaijage, who works at the University of Dodoma, had appeared at a magistrate's court to request bail after spending 15 days in police custody when the charges were changed.

He was among more than 130 people arrested over planned protests calling for democratic reforms and justice for those killed in a post-poll crackdown last year. The 7 July demonstrations were banned and did not take place.

The academic will now remain in custody until his case goes to trial as terrorism offences are generally not eligible for bail.

Kaijage, who teaches political science and public administration, was not asked to enter a plea at Thursday's hearing as his terrorism case can only be heard by a higher court.

He was arrested a day after the planned nationwide protests and initially charged with inciting people to join them.

The authorities had deployed security forces across major cities in the East African nation on 7 July and warned that they would act against anyone accused of inciting unrest.

Prosecutors now accuse Kaijage of threatening to burn public buildings as part of intimidation tactics.

Under Tanzanian law, offences such as recruiting for, facilitating, harbouring or supporting terrorists or terrorist groups carry severe penalties. Individuals convicted of these offences may face prison sentences ranging from 10 years to life imprisonment.

Gerald Shija, chairman of the University of Dodoma Academic Staff Association (Udomasa), said Kaijage had been transferred from police custody to Isanga Prison in the capital, Dodoma.

Colleagues have described him as a respected lecturer whose popularity stems from his teaching rather than political activism.

His case comes amid a broader crackdown by the authorities on opposition figures and activists critical of President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

Last month, the government suspended political rallies across the country until further notice, saying the move was necessary to maintain security.

During the widespread protests that followed the results of the 29 October 2025 election, 518 people died from "unnatural causes", including 197 who were shot dead, according to a commission of inquiry established by President Samia.

The scale of the violence shocked a country that had cultivated an image of calm, consensus and stability for nearly six decades.

President Samia was declared the winner the poll with 98% of the vote, a result the opposition dismissed as a "mockery" of democracy after her two main challengers were excluded.

At the time, the president said the election had been fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the violence, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her.
