title: Singer Chris Brown pleads guilty to affray over London club confrontation
excerpt:
Other charges, including assault against Abraham Diaw, dropped as guilty plea averts trial

The American singer and actor Chris Brown has admitted attacking a man in a private members’ club in London ...
body_text:
Other charges, including assault against Abraham Diaw, dropped as guilty plea averts trial

The American singer and actor Chris Brown has admitted attacking a man in a private members’ club in London after playing a gig at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium in 2023.

Brown will be sentenced in October for what prosecutors called an “unprovoked attack” with a bottle on the music producer Abraham Diaw at the Tape club in Hanover Square, Mayfair.

Brown and his co-defendant and vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu had been facing trial later this year after pleading not guilty to more serious assault charges, as well as charges of possessing an offensive weapon – a bottle. On Friday, those charges were dropped as both men pleaded guilty to the less-serious offence of affray at Southwark crown court.

Prosecutors said Brown hit Diaw twice over the head with a glass bottle before Akinlolu joined in, punching the victim in the head. Diaw was also kicked while sitting on the floor, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said.

At a previous hearing, the court had been told Brown pursued Diaw through the nightclub during the attack on 19 February 2023. Diaw went to St Mary’s hospital in London with head and knee injuries.

Brown was arrested more than two years after the attack. Metropolitan police detectives detained him at 2am on 15 May 2025 at the Lowry hotel in Manchester where he was said to have arrived on a private jet for UK dates on his Breezy Bowl tour.

He was released from Forest Bank prison in Salford, Greater Manchester, six days later, and posted an Instagram story shortly afterwards referencing his upcoming tour that said: “FROM THE CAGE TO THE STAGE!!! BREEZYBOWL.”

On Friday, the senior crown prosecutor at CPS London South, Claire Campbell, said Brown and Akinlolu were guilty of a “vicious and unprovoked attack … in a crowded nightclub where Brown used a glass bottle as a weapon to strike the victim’s head twice”.

“This kind of violence is entirely unacceptable, and the Crown Prosecution Service will work tirelessly – with the police and partners across the criminal justice system – to pursue cases like this and prove that no one is above the law.”

Brown appeared for Friday’s hearing wearing a tan suit, gold-rimmed sunglasses and a St Louis Cardinals baseball hat. He was flanked by security guards as he arrived at court, where a small group of fans had gathered.

At earlier hearings, Brown had been ordered to pay a £5m security fee as part of his bail conditions, which also allowed him to go on a world tour as long as he surrendered his passport on arrival in each country. He was released on bail again on Friday.

It is the latest in a series of legal troubles for Brown – including previous instances of assault. In 2009, he was sentenced to five years’ probation and six months’ community labour for beating up his former partner, the pop singer Rihanna. Police investigating that incident described a brutal attack in which Brown hit, choked and bit Rihanna, as well as trying to to push her from a car they were in.

title: US summons Malaysia envoy over Israel policy
excerpt:
The US Department of State has summoned Malaysia’s ambassador to the United States over his country’s longstanding policy on Israel, state news agency Bernama reported.

Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mo...
body_text:
The US Department of State has summoned Malaysia’s ambassador to the United States over his country’s longstanding policy on Israel, state news agency Bernama reported.

Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said on Thursday night that Ambassador Muhammad Shahrul Ikram Yaakob told the US State Department that Malaysia’s policy on not recognising the state of Israel was not new.

“It has always been Malaysia’s policy. Our immigration policy does not recognise the State of Israel or the Zionist regime. This has long been our position,” Bernama cited Hasan as saying.

“There was an individual with dual citizenship, the US and Israel, who entered Malaysia using his US passport. However, subsequent checks revealed that he also held Israeli citizenship, and we asked him to leave.”

Malaysia does not have any diplomatic ties with Israel and has emphasised its support for the Palestinian cause and against Israeli actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

But the incident was triggered after the Network School, a “digital nomad” community founded in the country by US investor Balaji Srinivasan, came under fire when social media users claimed it included participants from Israel.

A probe into Network School followed, and while Malay authorities found that all participants had valid travel documents, the school was still shut down on Tuesday.

Later, eight US congressmen sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressing outrage over Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s plan to track any Israeli citizens in the country and immediately deport them.

However, on Wednesday, Ibrahim reiterated that Malaysia would continue to bar Israeli citizens from entering the country despite objections raised by the members of the US Congress.

Anwar added that Malaysia was guided by its commitment to defending the rights of the Palestinian people and opposing the “oppression, aggression and continued killing” of Palestinians in Gaza, Bernama reported.

“That will not deter us. They may issue threats, but I will firmly defend the rights of the Malaysian people and uphold the government’s decision to continue prohibiting the entry of any Israeli national into Malaysia,” he added.

The US congressmen urged the State Department to review economic and security ties with Kuala Lumpur.

They called for funding to the International Military Education and Training programme, which provides professional US training for Malaysian military personnel, to be cut off unless the decision is reversed within 15 days.

title: Connecticut Sun's Saniya Rivers melts down on social media over Caitlin Clark's scoreboard taunt
excerpt: Host of 'The Sage Steele Show' Sage Steele asserts the WNBA is mishandling generational talent Caitlin Clark. Steele critiques the league's consistently poor officiating, which has led to numerous unc...
body_text:
Host of 'The Sage Steele Show' Sage Steele asserts the WNBA is mishandling generational talent Caitlin Clark. Steele critiques the league's consistently poor officiating, which has led to numerous uncalled fouls against Clark and other players this season. She stresses that this continued neglect risks losing the WNBA's growing fanbase.

Connecticut Sun guard Saniya Rivers wasn't taking Wednesday night's loss quietly after Caitlin Clark and the Indiana Fever steamrolled the team 123-88.

After taking the loss and the taunting, Rivers took to Threads to defend her pride and insist she had zero regrets about jawing with Clark: "Girl idgaf if we're down by 50, I'm NEVER tolerating disrespect. As long as there's time left on the clock, ima keep hoopin. period."

Saniya Rivers #22 of the Connecticut Sun dribbles the ball during a game against the Indiana Fever on July 22, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind. (NBAE via Getty Images)

The whole dustup boiled down to one question: Did Clark pointing to the scoreboard during a 35-point blowout somehow cross the line?

CAITLIN CLARK PROVES THERE'S NO NBA 2K27 COVER CURSE AS FEVER SET FRANCHISE SCORING RECORD

With 28.8 seconds left in the third quarter and Indiana cruising 95-67, Rivers got in Clark's face after a routine foul and told her she was getting "locked up."

Meanwhile, Clark was busy hanging 27 points and 11 assists on the Sun on 8-of-13 shooting in just 27 minutes.

Clark didn't waste time arguing. She repeatedly pointed to the scoreboard in front of Rivers and barked, "Scoreboard!"

Connecticut Sun guard Saniya Rivers drives to the basket against Indiana Fever center Aliyah Boston on July 22, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

NBA'S ADAM SILVER PUSHED WNBA COMMISSIONER TO SUSPEND ALYSSA THOMAS FOR CAITLIN CLARK THROAT JAB: REPORT

Officials quickly stepped in anyway, issuing double technical fouls. The whistle did carry real consequences for Indiana, giving Clark her seventh technical of the season. Under WNBA rules, an eighth technical triggers an automatic one-game suspension without pay, leaving the league's biggest draw one whistle away from sitting out.

It has been another eventful week for Clark, who continues to rack up rivals on the court and critics off it. Rivers is simply the latest name added to that growing list.

USA Today columnist Nancy Armour recently drew widespread backlash after invoking Emmett Till in an opinion piece criticizing Clark and her fan base, another example of how even routine moments involving the Fever star quickly snowball into national talking points.

A referee steps between Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark and Connecticut Sun guard Saniya Rivers as they exchange words on July 22, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

While critics hyperventilate and opponents lecture about respect, Clark keeps selling out arenas, drawing record television audiences and giving people a reason to watch the WNBA.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

title: Boasberg delivers fresh immigration setback to Trump in free-speech clash
excerpt: A federal judge in Boston ruled against the Trump administration's $100,000 fee for H-1B visas, deeming it an unauthorized tax. The fee, which was significantly increased from a typical $2,000-$5,000,...
body_text:
A federal judge in Boston ruled against the Trump administration's $100,000 fee for H-1B visas, deeming it an unauthorized tax. The fee, which was significantly increased from a typical $2,000-$5,000, aimed to prioritize US citizens in the workforce. The administration is appealing the decision.

Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg has temporarily halted the Trump administration’s effort to deny visas to individuals it claims worked to perpetuate censorship against Americans.

Boasberg, who has been a major judicial antagonist across President Donald Trump's two administrations, handed down a decision earlier this month blocking the State Department from restricting visas for foreign officials and other foreign nationals considered responsible for or complicit in suppressing American free speech. He found that, while the federal government has a "legitimate interest in responding when foreign officials use sovereign power to suppress protected expression in the United States," it is possible that the government is engaging in viewpoint discrimination, and thus violating the First Amendment, through its policy.

"The policy, at its core, does not burden all speech about platforms, all research into content moderation, or all advocacy about online harms," Boasberg wrote. "It presses its enforcement thumb against one side of the scale: the view that platforms should do more to moderate content, label disinformation, restrict abuse, share data with researchers, or take responsibility for the harms their systems amplify."

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

U.S. District Judge James Boasberg is seen in an official portrait in Washington, D.C., on March 16, 2023. (Photo by Carolyn Van Houten/The Washington Post via Getty Images) ( )

"The Government, in other words, has not set itself against everyone who speaks about platform governance. It has set itself against those whose work favors more moderation rather than less," he added.

The State Department’s policy followed a Biden-era controversy where the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), which produced alleged "blacklists" of certain news websites, received funding from the federal government. Conservatives have argued that GDI’s ratings contributed to advertisers withholding revenue from conservative outlets and that federal support for the organization implicated free-speech concerns.

The State Department’s policy paused by Boasberg restricted visa access to individuals involved with GDI and similar organizations.

"The Trump Administration believes that aliens who are or were involved or complicit in censoring American citizens must face appropriate consequences," a spokesperson for the department told Fox News Digital. "An American visa is a privilege, not a right. Specific questions about this lawsuit should be referred to the Department of Justice."

DC APPEALS COURT ORDERS JUDGE BOASBERG TO HALT TRUMP CONTEMPT PROBE OVER DEPORTATION FLIGHTS

FILE - In this Sept. 22, 2014, file photo, a view of the E. Barrett Prettyman U.S. Courthouse in Washington. The American Civil Liberties Union is suing the Trump administration, claiming it is violating immigration laws and its own policies by detaining immigrants who have a solid case for seeking asylum in the United States. The ACLU said it was filing a lawsuit Thursday in U.S. District Court in Washington claiming that the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency is detaining many asylum seekers for months while they await hearings before an immigration judge. (AP Photo/Susan Walsh, File)

Boasberg has presided over several high-profile cases challenging actions by Trump’s second administration. He temporarily blocked the administration’s rapid deportation of Venezuelan migrants and ordered officials to preserve Signal messages in which senior national security officials discussed planned U.S. strikes in Yemen.

The clashes have made Boasberg a target of Trump, who called for his impeachment.

The Justice Department filed a misconduct complaint against him and accused him of overreach. Chief Justice John Roberts rejected impeachment as a response to an unfavorable ruling.

Boasberg was first nominated to the federal bench by President Barack Obama in 2010.

JUDGE ORDERS ICE TO FREE WISCONSIN MOSQUE LEADER OVER 'SUBSTANTIAL' FREE SPEECH CLAIM AFTER CRITICIZING ISRAEL

US Senator Eric Schmitt, Republican from Missouri, questions FBI Director Kash Patel during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on "Oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation" on Capitol Hill. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP) (Photo by JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images) (AFP via Getty Images)

"A visa is a privilege—not a constitutional entitlement," Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., wrote of the decision on X. "The First Amendment protects the American people’s right to speak. It does not require the American people to admit foreign actors who work to restrict that speech."

The case against the State Department’s policy was initially brought by the Coalition for Independent Technology Research (CITR), a nonprofit organization representing academics and journalists.

While Boasberg issued a stay temporarily preventing the State Department from enforcing its visa policy, he has not yet ruled on the merits of the case, meaning that the policy could still survive his court. Additionally, the State Department could still seek appellate review of his interim order blocking their policy.

CITR and the State Department did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

title: Bangladesh President Mohammed Shahabuddin resigns
excerpt:
Bangladesh President Mohammed Shahabuddin has resigned two years ahead the end of his full five-year term.

Shahabuddin, 76, cited health reasons for his decision on Friday. The move comes amid rising...
body_text:
Bangladesh President Mohammed Shahabuddin has resigned two years ahead the end of his full five-year term.

Shahabuddin, 76, cited health reasons for his decision on Friday. The move comes amid rising demand from opposition parties for him to step down.

“Recent medical examinations have diagnosed me with a condition known as Autonomic Neuropathy. Due to this condition, I occasionally experience momentary loss of consciousness,” Shahabuddin said in a statement released by his press secretary.

The speaker of the Jatiya Sangsad, the national parliament, will perform the duties of the president until a new one is elected, the statement added.

A new president must be elected within the next 90 days, according to the constitution.

“I am seriously ill … therefore, I am unable to perform my duty of the constitutional post,” Shahabuddin said in a letter to Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed on Friday.

Ahmed said he accepted his resignation, the Associated Press reported.

“According to the Constitution, the president’s resignation becomes effective upon submission of a signed letter to the speaker,” the president’s spokesperson, Sarwar Alam, said.

The resignation comes amid media reports that Shahabuddin spoke on the phone with ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who is living in India, during a visit by the former to the UK for medical treatment in May this year, according to Dhaka-based The Daily Star.

Shahabuddin has refuted the media report.

“I am suffering from various health complications,” he told The Daily Star when asked about the reason for his resignation. “I have nothing more to add at this moment.”

He had travelled to London on May 9 and returned on May 18.

Shahabuddin has been the president of the South Asian nation since April 2023. His term was meant to end in 2028.

He oversaw the country during a volatile period after Hasina was ousted in August 2024 by youth protesters and until a caretaker government was formed days later.

Hasina is currently living in exile in India’s capital, New Delhi, but is expected to return to Bangladesh in December, according to the Reuters news agency, which reported news of Shahabuddin’s expected resignation on Thursday.

His resignation leaves Hasina with no allies in high office five months before her planned return.

But as Bangladesh’s president, his role is largely ceremonial. While he is the head of state, the executive power rests with the prime minister and cabinet.

title: Ukraine’s pivot to warehouse strikes brings war closer to ordinary Russians
excerpt:
Kyiv’s attacks on Wildberries, country’s answer to Amazon, destroy goods made, sold, and bought by everyday Russians

Standing in front of a vast warehouse engulfed in flames outside Moscow, Tatyana M...
body_text:
Kyiv’s attacks on Wildberries, country’s answer to Amazon, destroy goods made, sold, and bought by everyday Russians

Standing in front of a vast warehouse engulfed in flames outside Moscow, Tatyana Mikhailova watched as her entire stock of 4,000 fur coats, bought months in advance for the winter season, burned.

“It’s not just a warehouse that’s burning,” Mikhailova said in a video she shared on Instagram. “It’s the time you’ve invested, the immense stress you’ve endured, your money, and your last bit of hope. All I feel is emptiness.”

Mikhailova is one of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of Russian entrepreneurs whose small businesses have been devastated by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes targeting warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s largest e-commerce company and the country’s answer to Amazon.

Ukrainian drones have hit at least nine Wildberries warehouses on four of the past seven days, striking logistics centres from southern Russia to the outskirts of St Petersburg, killing at least nine people and destroying inventory worth billions of dollars.

The attacks are a new phase in Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign. After months of targeting oil refineries and fuel infrastructure, contributing to shortages across Russia, Kyiv is turning its attention to logistics networks in an attempt to erode the sense of normality that has insulated many urban Russians from the realities of the war.

On Friday morning a warehouse in Shushary, a suburb of St Petersburg, caught fire after a drone strike, according to videos and local media, sending thick smoke across Russia’s second city.

Together, the targeted sites cover about 552,000 sq metres – roughly one tenth of Wildberries’ total warehouse capacity, according to calculations by the Kommersant business newspaper.

Losses at Wildberries have reached an estimated 170bn roubles (about $2.2bn or £1.65bn) in destroyed merchandise alone, according to Data Insight, a Moscow-based research firm.

Most of the losses fall not on Wildberries itself but on the independent merchants whose stock was stored in the warehouses.

Many vendors this week express their anger on social media that their inventories had been torched.

Maria, who handmakes postcards, lost about $8,000 of goods when drones struck Wildberries’ warehouse in Elektrostal, 58km (36 miles) east of Moscow. Days later, she lost the rest of her stock when a warehouse in Krasnodar, southern Russia, was hit.

In an interview with the Guardian, Maria said: “How can you run a business when all your company’s assets just go up in flames?”.

Maria, who asked for her surname to be withheld, added: “I’m raising a child on my own and I’ve lost everything. How am I supposed to stay calm? Yesterday you had a peaceful, normal life. You could make plans. Today I have nothing.”

Wildberries, founded by the self-made billionaire Tatyana Kim, has become one of Russia’s biggest business success stories.

The platform is particularly popular among lower-income Russians living outside Moscow and St Petersburg – a demographic that forms a central part of Vladimir Putin’s political base. Its vast network of collection points extends into small towns and villages, where they have become fixtures of everyday life.

But the sheer scale of Wildberries’ logistics network has now become a liability. With more than 200 warehouses and logistics centres scattered across Russia, protecting every site from swarms of cheap Ukrainian drones is virtually impossible.

Kim this week announced that the company had begun compensating some sellers, but merchants say the payouts amount to only a fraction of the value of the goods destroyed.

Anton Bryanski, who imports clothing from China, said he lost goods worth 4.6m roubles (about $59,000) but received just 19,000 roubles (about $240) in compensation.

“That’s less than 1% of the total losses,” he said.

Adding to sellers’ anger, Wildberries had changed its terms just 11 days before the first strikes, exempting itself from liability for goods destroyed in “force majeure” events, including drone attacks.

For many small entrepreneurs, the attacks are another blow in mounting economic hardships caused by the war, which has brought soaring inflation, higher taxes and rising costs as the Kremlin scrambles to finance its military campaign.

Ukraine has defended the attacks as legitimate military strikes.

In his nightly address on Saturday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy did not mention Wildberries by name but said Ukrainian forces had struck “major logistics facilities” used to transport sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment.

While Wildberries does not manufacture or sell weapons, the platform is used by soldiers and volunteers to buy equipment and goods used for the war. A Guardian review of the marketplace found thousands of listings for military-related goods, including body armour, first aid kits, field rations, drone goggles and drone components with potential battlefield applications.

The majority of products sold on the platform, however, are ordinary consumer goods. Wildberries built its business selling clothing, cosmetics and household items and remains central to everyday shopping for millions of Russians.

Analysts therefore say the campaign serves a broader purpose than disrupting military logistics.

Sergei Guriev, a Russian economist and the dean of the London Business School, told the independent Russian news outlet Meduza: “This is an attack that touches every Russian because people increasingly depend on e-commerce.

“The Kremlin has spent years trying to convince Russians that life continues as normal despite the war. It’s difficult to maintain that illusion when huge columns of smoke are rising over cities. These attacks are a double blow – to the military machine and to the image of normality.”

Putin has yet to comment on the attacks on Wildberries, but in recent weeks he has shown no willingness to abandon his maximalist war aims, insisting that the difficulties facing Russia are temporary.

Speaking to senior officials on Wednesday, the Russian president sought to project confidence in the country’s economic resilience. “Let me note at the outset of our meeting that the state of the Russian economy, and of its key sectors, remains stable despite external attempts to destabilise the fuel and energy sector and certain other industries,” Putin said.

title: Democrats accuse Trump of using forced labor as ‘convenient’ justification for tariffs
excerpt:
US president faced criticism from Democrats after officials announced tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on more than 80 countries

Donald Trump has been accused of using forced labor as “a pretext” to ...
body_text:
US president faced criticism from Democrats after officials announced tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on more than 80 countries

Donald Trump has been accused of using forced labor as “a pretext” to impose a fresh wave of tariffs on dozens of countries, as critics warned of higher prices for Americans.

The US president faced swift criticism from Democrats after his officials presented their latest effort to make his signature economic policy permanent following a string of high-profile legal setbacks. Some Republicans also expressed concern.

Hours before a temporary US duty of 10% on many countries was due to expire on Friday, the Trump administration announced new tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on more than 80 countries, including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and European Union members.

The new tariffs are being implemented under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to bypass Congress to instate tariffs designed to punish countries using forced labor to export goods to the US.

Trump “recognizes that decades of moral suasion have not eradicated forced labor from global supply chains”, said Jamieson Greer, his US trade representative, on Thursday, adding it was “well past time” that countries across the world eradicated the practice.

But as the US president continues to face questions over his controversial focus on tariffs, and the threat of higher prices, leading Democrats accused his administration of using forced labor to prop up their strategy.

“Today’s forced labor justification is too convenient to be taken seriously,” said Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the US House ways and means committee. “Forced labor is a real and pervasive problem in our supply chains and demands serious enforcement. It should never be cheapened into a pretext for a tariff policy built on dubious legal theories and personal grievances.’’

Trump’s trade strategy suffered a damaging blow in February when the US supreme court ruled 6-3 that many of his tariffs had been imposed illegally. His officials immediately announced another 10% tariff regime under another trade law that had never been used before, although these duties could only be imposed for up to 150 days – and expired after midnight EST on Friday.

This latest wave of tariffs is designed to replace the 10% regime.

Linda Sánchez, a California Democratic representative, denounced the administration’s justification for the new tariffs, writing on social media that Trump had gutted funding to combat forced labor at the Bureau of International Labor Affairs and rolled back worker protections domestically “while encouraging companies to profit off some of the world’s worst forced labor abusers through his proposed US-China Board of Trade”.

“If he was serious, he would not be applying the same tariff rate to China, one of the worst forced labor abusers in the world, as he does to countries like Australia,” wrote Sánchez. “Then again, unlike China, Australia, doesn’t manufacture any Trump corporation products.”

And Thursday’s announcement also renewed warnings around the impact on prices across the US, amid concerns over the cost of living.

Trump pledged to tackle affordability issues during his successful 2024 campaign to return to the White House. With those issues still a reality for many Americans, and after US inflation surged to a three-year high earlier this year, Republicans will fight to retain control of Congress in November’s US midterm elections.

Brendan Boyle, a Pennsylvania Democratic representative, cited an estimate by the Congressional Joint Economic Committee that US families have had to pay $3,500 more under Trump’s policies, adding that new tariffs would only cost them more.

“Federal courts have repeatedly struck down President Trump’s illegal and costly tariff taxes,” he said. “These new tariffs are more of the same: a nationwide sales tax that will make life even harder for families already struggling under the costs of Trump’s reckless war in Iran.”

A Harris Poll survey for the Guardian found earlier this year that 70% of Americans have reported paying more due to tariffs, and a majority of voters, including 60% of Republicans, say tariffs have had a negative effect on consumers.

Some Republicans applauded this week’s announcement, including Jason Smith, a Republican from Missouri and the chair of the House of Representatives ways and means committee, its chief tax-writing committee.

“True to its word, the Trump administration is fighting for American families, farmers and small businesses – as well as American values – when it comes to our trading relationships,” said Smith. “Holding accountable those countries that are not doing nearly enough to rid their supply chains of goods produced with forced labor is appropriate to address unfair trading practices that put American workers at a competitive disadvantage.”

But John Cornyn, a Republican senator from Texas, also raised concern about the effect of the tariffs on Americans. Cornyn is leaving the US Senate at this end of this term, after his Trump-endorsed rival, Ken Paxton, won the Republican nomination for his seat.

“There’s no question that tariffs on imports raise prices on American products,” Cornyn told The Hill. “So yeah, I’m concerned about that.”

title: Running out of time: SEC, Big Ten wait on 'Protect College Sports Act' revisions as August recess nears
excerpt: The Senate Commerce Committee has advanced a bipartisan bill aimed at reshaping college sports by establishing a nationwide NIL payout framework and limiting athletes to one penalty-free transfer duri...
body_text:
The Senate Commerce Committee has advanced a bipartisan bill aimed at reshaping college sports by establishing a nationwide NIL payout framework and limiting athletes to one penalty-free transfer during a five-year period.

TAMPA, FL - While the SEC was holding its annual kickoff to the upcoming football season this week in Florida, the bigger conversation was transpiring in Washington, D.C., around the 'Protect College Sports Act'.

After being passed through the Senate Commerce Committee in June, Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) are racing against time for the legislation aimed at creating guardrails around NIL, eligibility issues, transfers and even a conference realignment, with the SEC and Big Ten not providing their support for the bill in its current form.

CLOCK IS TICKING AS SENATORS TED CRUZ, MARIA CANTWELL PUSH FOR SEC, BIG TEN BUY-IN ON COLLEGE SPORTS BILL

The bipartisan bill was largely created to help navigate college athletics back into a realistic situation, and out of courtrooms. After years of lobbying Congress for help, which led to the SCORE Act being created before this latest bill, there is a growing dissension between parties on how much actual help is wanted at the federal level.

After meeting numerous times this week, the revisions currently being discussed have not been presented to either conference as of Thursday evening.

Obviously, time is of the essence, which Senate Majority Leader John Thune referenced to reporters on Thursday afternoon, with him mentioning that it doesn’t look as though it will reach the Senate floor before Congress goes on its August recess.

According to sources close to the situation in Washington, Senators Ted Cruz and Maria Cantwell are still working to get the bill to the Senate floor before the recess, while also continuing to work out revisions with the SEC and Big Ten regarding the legislation.

Also, there has been pushback on the thought that the bill is dead with the news that a vote would likely not take place in August.

"They're working on language through the night, and that's probably not how they'd be spending their Thursday night if there wasn't a chance," Sen. Maria Cantwell spokesperson Ansley Lacitis told Fox News/OutKick

GREG SANKEY ADDRESSES SEC BREAKAWAY TALK AS MICHIGAN TRIES TO STEAL SPOTLIGHT WITH AD WARDE MANUEL DECISION

SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey speaks during a roundtable discussion on college sports in the East Room of the White House on March 6, 2026, as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick looks on. The Trump administration hosted the event titled "Saving College Sports" with leaders from the Power Four conferences, media executives and former coaches. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Although the SEC and Big Ten conferences have repeatedly asked for congressional help, both feel as though the current bill is unfairly putting them in a corner, especially if the two are not allowed to add additional schools in the future.

In addition to previously reported issues, the section regarding the pooling of media rights has left a bad taste in the mouth of conference leaders from the SEC and Big Ten, with some voicing their displeasure that this current form would lead to them losing money on future television rights deals.

Senate advances landmark Protect College Sports Act, ignoring SEC and Big Ten opposition with clock ticking

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., attend a Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee roundtable on the Protect College Sports Act and collegiate athletics in the Russell Building on June 10, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

During an interview with OutKick on Wednesday afternoon in Tampa, where he was asked how real the August timeline is, SEC commissioner Greg Sankey pointed out that if this were to drag on until Congress returns, there would be more important issues to be discussed in the House and Senate.

"I consider it a milestone (August timeline), the August recess," Sankey noted. "Congress does return in September. Then once they’re through in September, you have budget battles, we've seen how those play out. So, it is important to try and keep moving, that has been a part of our communication, and there has been a lot of energy and effort expended by Senators, which we appreciate, to try and make adjustments.

"I think the reality is, if a bill is produced and advances, and it's eventually signed into law, the view will be we've solved those problems. And, Congress is going to move onto taxation, funding whatever, international issues. You just make a list, they have a lot of important issues, and they’re not coming back to close gaps or solve problems. That's why since the act was introduced, we've been focused on common sense adjustments to close the loopholes and make this manageable. There's energy and effort in that, but that doesn’t mean we're at the finish line yet."

If both felt as though the pooling of media rights was actually 'voluntary', which both Cruz and Cantwell have said is the case, then there would most likely be further support from conference members.

But, at the moment, the SEC and Big Ten are waiting to see if their input on changes to the bill would actually come to fruition, with revisions that neither side have seen as of Thursday evening, as previously reported.

There is no doubt in the eyes of conference officials and congressional leaders in Washington that work is being done to get this bill to the Senate floor.

The bigger issue was how senators were going to get such a complicated matter condensed into a bill that spans 100 pages, with issues that are running rampant across college athletics.

But, there was always going to be a problem with timing.

Also, when you add in the potential limiting of conference expansion and revenue-sharing, there was going to be roadblocks.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

While work continues on trying to get this legislation onto the Senate floor for a vote, with the House being a whole separate issue as midterms loom, even if the revisions are presented to congressional leaders, along with the SEC and Big Ten, it does not mean we are getting a signed bill.

But, by the time this makes the Senate floor, whenever that is, there will most likely be another lawsuit filed pertaining to a player's eligibility.

Or, as we like to call it in the college athletics world, 'Just a day that ends in Y'.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

title: British-born man living in US since age of nine held by ICE under threat of deportation
excerpt:
Connor Read, who is married and has two children, was apprehended in June during residency permit interview

A British-born man who has lived in the US since he was nine years old has been held in an ...
body_text:
Connor Read, who is married and has two children, was apprehended in June during residency permit interview

A British-born man who has lived in the US since he was nine years old has been held in an ICE detention facility for more than a month and a half under threat of deportation, it has been reported.

Connor Read, 29, was taken by ICE agents after he was invited to a green card (residency permit) interview in Tampa, Florida on 3 June, and separated from his wife, Jaelin, 25, and his twin sons Ryder and Ozzie, three.

Originally from Chatham in Kent, Read was brought to the US in 2007 as a child by his mother and stepfather. He attended American schools and only returned to the UK once.

According to the Times newspaper, he was subject to a removal order in 2011 but at the age of 16 was granted Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (Daca) status, a policy that provides deportation relief and work permits to eligible individuals brought to the US as children.

But while afforded the Daca protection, Read reportedly committed minor offences that led to him being deemed a “criminal illegal alien” by the Trump administration, including convictions for possession of narcotic equipment, possession of liquor and resisting an officer.

The Times reports that because of the narcotic charge, at the age of 22, Read was unable to renew his Daca status. He met Jaelin on a dating app in 2020, when his immigration status was unsettled. Having married, the couple attempted to apply for a green card.

On 3 June, Read was invited to attend a green card meeting at the federal immigration building in Tampa. In the interview room, four ICE agents arrested him and removed him from the building. Immigration officials told Jaelin Read that her husband would not be coming home.

He was taken to Pinellas county jail in Florida, where he spent eight days in a shared cell and was later flown to an ICE detention centre in Louisiana. He is appealing against his final removal order but has been warned a decision may not come for up to six months.

An ICE spokesperson told the Times: “Connor Michael Read, a criminal illegal alien of the United Kingdom, was arrested on 3 June 2026 by the ICE law enforcement in Tampa, Florida.

“His criminal history includes convictions for possession of narcotic equipment, possession of liquor and resisting an officer. He was issued a final order of removal issued by an Orlando, Florida immigration judge from January 2011.

“Read entered the United States on 21 November 2007, through the Orlando international airport as a non-immigrant with an F-2 visa, as a dependent of an F-1 non-immigrant student. Read’s status was contingent upon his parent’s status as a student. After a violation of the terms of their visa, Read was placed into removal proceedings.

“Under President Trump and [homeland security] secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the US.”

title: Trump’s new tariffs ‘a sales tax that will make life harder for Americans’, say Democrats – US politics live
excerpt:
Even some Republicans apparently expressing concern over measures against 85 countries

What to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countries

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog...
body_text:
Even some Republicans apparently expressing concern over measures against 85 countries

What to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countries

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump’s move to impose a fresh round of tariffs on more than 80 countries has drawn criticism from both Democratic politicians and his own allies.

Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, announced that the Trump administration “is imposing tariffs on more than 80 countries for their failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor”.

The tariffs will replace a 10% global duty that was due to expire for supposedly failing to crack down on forced labor. However, congresswoman Linda Sánchez, a California Democrat, denounced the pretext for the new tariffs as a sham.

“President Trump isn’t serious about combating forced labor. He’s trying to make an end-run around the Supreme Court and Congress to reimpose his illegal tariffs,” Sánchez wrote on social media.

double quotation markIf he was serious, he would not be applying the same tariff rate to China, one of the worst forced labor abusers in the world, as he does to countries like Australia. Then again, unlike China, Australia, doesn’t manufacture any Trump corporation products.

This is the same administration that gutted funding to combat forced labor through cuts to the Bureau of International Labor Affairs and rolled back worker protections here at home, while encouraging companies to profit off some of the world’s worst forced labor abusers through his proposed US-China Board of Trade.

We need to take forced labor seriously. But that includes addressing our problems here at home, including by taking on the export of goods made with American prison labor. Slapping more tariffs on every country that upsets the president isn’t the way to do it.

“Trump is hell-bent on raising your prices,” congressman Brendan Boyle, a Pennsylvania Democrat said in a statement on Trump’s lastest tariffs. “His new tariffs are a nationwide sales tax that will only serve to make life harder for Americans just trying to make ends meet.”

And even the president’s own allies have raised concerns over the latest round of tariffs, Politico is reporting.

One person close to the White House, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said:

double quotation markEverything that you do that’s not focused on affordability is not helpful. This might not be a negative five, but it’s a negative 0.5. Anything that you’re doing that is not on the plus side of the scale is a problem.

When you announce new tariffs, it’s not like, okay, well, let’s see what they do. It’s, ‘Oh crap, those are the bad things.’

Another White House source told Politico:

double quotation markI think Republicans are comfortable with the threat, even though that has some market impacts. But actual revenue coming away from people’s pocketbooks is not what Republicans are happy with.

Any conversation about tariffs, unless it’s reducing them, is a bad conversation for Republicans.

The government of Brazil has rejected the Trump administration’s claim that it, and 84 other nations, failed to enforce a ban on forced labor, and called the new 12.5% US tariff on imports from Brazil “completely arbitrary and unjustified”.

The Pentagon’s official online list of service members killed in the ongoing Iran war does not include the four soldiers who died during renewed fighting over the weekend, despite the fact that their names were included in a Pentagon press release on the formal transfer of their remains back to the United States on Wednesday.

The premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, said “it’s very hard to deal with President Trump when he changes his mind every single day. One day the prime minister [Canada’s Mark Carney] is with him side by side, and next thing you know, President Trump turns on him like a rabid dog.”

President Donald Trump ⁠will address the White House Correspondents’ Association at a rescheduled dinner later today, nearly three months after a shooting at the Washington Hilton hotel interrupted the event.

The black-tie gathering of journalists, politicians and administration officials ⁠was called off on 25 ⁠April after a ​man tried to force his way through a security checkpoint and fired a shotgun outside the ballroom where Trump and members of his cabinet were taking their seats.

The suspect, Cole Allen, pleaded ⁠not guilty in May to charges including attempting to assassinate the president. The dinner has been moved to the Waldorf Astoria hotel and will take place under heightened security.

Secret Service director Sean Curran told reporters that an ⁠advance team was implementing a comprehensive security plan at the hotel, Reuters reported.

“We do expect bad people to show up,” Curran said. “It’s just a reality ​of where we are, but we’re treating it no differently ‌than any other site that the ‌president goes to.”

The April incident occurred during Trump’s first presidential appearance at the correspondents’ dinner. He had boycotted ​the event in his previous years in office.

Just before a temporary levy on global imports was set to expire, the Trump administration issued a fresh wave of tariffs on more than 80 countries late on Thursday, ranging from 10% to 12.5%. The new tariffs take effect Friday morning.

It’s Donald Trump’s latest effort to continue imposing global levies without congressional approval, despite the supreme court ruling in February that found the US president had illegally used his executive power to implement his global trade policies. Trump has long maintained that the US has been paying more than its fair share in tariffs, and that increased duties are necessary to boost American manufacturing and jobs.

Here’s what to know about Trump’s latest round of tariffs:

Donald Trump has once again inspired anger and confusion in US allies and trading partners as he imposed a wave of tariffs on more than 80 countries, replacing an expiring global duty introduced earlier this year.

The new measures effectively replace blanket 10% tariffs that Trump imposed in February. The US supreme court ruled many of those were illegal. The new levies come in at between 10% and 12.5% on countries including the UK, Mexico, Canada, Australia, India, China and the 27 countries that make up the EU.

They are imposed under section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, and the Trump administration has said the new measures are due to the dozens of countries failing to enforce bans on goods produced by forced labor.

The imposition of the new tariffs led to Asian stock markets taking a hammering overnight. The Japanese Nikkei 225 fell 3.1%, while the Chinese SSE Composite dropped 1.4%.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index was the most heavily hit, down 11.4%, while the South Korean Kospi, which is dominated by its major semiconductor companies, slumped 6.2%.

It was more of a mixed picture in Europe as trading began on Friday, with the Stoxx 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropping 0.7% before steadying to a fall of 0.1%. France’s Cac 40 initially fell almost 1% before moving into positive territory, up 0.12%.

Similarly, Germany’s Dax fell 8% before erasing losses to climb 0.51%. In the UK the FTSE 100 index rose 0.28% in early trading. For many officials digesting the news on Friday, the US rationale was hard to swallow.

“You can’t say that ⁠for the European Union,” its foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said ​on the sidelines ‌of the Asean ‌meeting in Manila. “If you compare our ‌labour laws to the ones of the United States, I mean, we have paid vacations, we have very good labour conditions for our employees, so ‌it’s not really grounded.”

title: Trump’s latest tariffs put UK at disadvantage to EU, say experts
excerpt:
While overall levy for UK is unchanged, sectors not covered by Turnberry deal face tougher competition

Donald Trump’s latest round of tariffs has put UK businesses at a disadvantage against the EU ev...
body_text:
While overall levy for UK is unchanged, sectors not covered by Turnberry deal face tougher competition

Donald Trump’s latest round of tariffs has put UK businesses at a disadvantage against the EU even though the overall tariff for British goods has not changed, experts have said.

In the levies, announced late on Thursday and said to be aimed against countries that engage in forced labour, the EU’s previous 15% near blanket tariff is reduced to 10%, the same level as the tariff deal struck by Keir Starmer and Peter Mandelson last year.

The UK welcomed the deal, announced by the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, and said there was “no change” to the headline 10% tariff or preferential rates in the car, pharmaceutical and aerospace sectors concluded in the UK’s economic prosperity deal (EPD).

The new measures for the EU will replace the tariff in the Turnberry deal concluded at the US president’s Scottish golf course last year.

An EU spokesperson said the deal “establishes an all-inclusive tariff rate of 10% for the EU, and reintroduces the additional tariff exemptions for the EU, such as cork and diamonds, on top of those on aircrafts and parts, generic medicines, and active ingredients”.

The Turnberry deal meant no tariffs could be added to the 15% blanket levy. The reduction to 10% effectively puts the EU at an advantage for sectors not specified in Starmer’s deal, such as bikes, clothing, chemicals, beverages or gifts.

However, in a fillip for Andy Burnham, a deal cutting US tariffs on Scottish whisky to zero is expected to be announced later on Friday, giving the UK an advantage over Irish and French spirits rivals, which attract a 10% duty.

William Bain, the trade policy director for the British Chambers of Commerce, welcomed the fact that there was no change on the headline 10% rate for the UK but said some sectors, such as clothing, have lost their comparative advantage against the EU.

A British knitted jumper, for example, which attracted a 12.5% tariff, would be imported with an additional EPD tariff of 10%, bringing total levies to 22.5%. An EU jumper could now be sold into the US at an all-inclusive rate of 10%.

“Clearly there is a difference between how the UK has been treated today and how the EU has been treated today. And that is undeniable,” Bain said.

“Negotiations have to go on between the UK and the US over this. At the chambers network we want to see a path to lower tariffs,” he added.

The GMB trade union said the new tariffs were “ill-judged, potentially catastrophic for business and likely to utterly fail in their stated aim”.

Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, the GMB national secretary, said: “The EU now has a better trading relationship with the US than we do – which undermines the so-called ‘special relationship’.”A government spokesperson said: “There is no negative change to the tariff rate facing UK businesses as a result of this announcement. Our agreement with the US remains in place, and today we see an improvement to our trading terms with zero tariffs on whisky and medical technology.

“We take forced labour very seriously to ensure that in global supply chains UK businesses are not complicit. The US has recognised the steps the UK is taking, which is why there are no additional tariffs for the UK under this announcement.”

An EU spokesperson said: “We did not agree with the premise of this investigation on forced labour. And we had communicated this, also to our US counterparts.”

Trump is expected to announce more tariffs under section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act. With hints of retaliation over the EU’s decision to impose a €890m (£760m) fine on Google earlier this week and a threat to impose 100% tariffs on pharma, this would hit Ireland, Germany and Belgium hard.

title: Jennifer Sey reveals alleged communication with Sophie Cunningham amid recruitment pitch for XX-XY Athletics
excerpt: Jennifer Sey, the founder of the activist sportswear brand XX-XY Athletics, says she first received a DM from Sophie Cunningham in 2024, as she is now trying to court the WNBA star as a brand ambassad...
body_text:
Jennifer Sey, the founder of the activist sportswear brand XX-XY Athletics, says she first received a DM from Sophie Cunningham in 2024, as she is now trying to court the WNBA star as a brand ambassador.

Jennifer Sey is ready to make Sophie Cunningham the face of XX-XY Athletics — and says she would "give my right arm" to convince the WNBA star to leave Adidas for her brand.

Sey, the founder and CEO of the pro-women’s sportswear brand, told Fox News Digital she has wanted to sign Cunningham since the Indiana Fever star privately praised XX-XY Athletics’s viral "Dear Nike" campaign in 2024.

"She’s the perfect person for us," Sey said. "We have wanted to work with her for such a long time."

WHITE HOUSE DEFENDS WNBA STAR SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM AFTER SHE SPEAKS OUT IN SUPPORT OF PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS

"It’s not just that she’s a fantastic athlete and she’s a currently competing professional athlete," she added. "She’s just got such an incredible personality. She’s fun and she’s funny and she’s tough and she says what she thinks, and that’s what we’re all about."

Sey revealed that she first opened communication with Cunningham after XX-XY Athletics released its "Dear Nike" in October 2024. The ad challenged the sportswear giant to take a public stand against biological males competing in women’s sports, and generated more than 10 million views.

Sey claims Cunningham liked and commented on the original ad, then sent Sey a private direct message on social media praising it. But Sey said she did not see the message for months because it landed in a folder for messages from accounts she did not follow.

FEVER GUARD SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM'S VIRAL FINGER-POINTING MEME REACHES WWE

"She liked it and commented on it. She actually wrote me a DM on Instagram, which I didn't see for months because I'm a moron and I never check the little tab from unknown people," Sey claims.

"Cause there's just so many in there, I just never look, and I didn't follow her. I didn't know who she was. And then a few months later, and she was kind of taking off at this point as Caitlin [Clark]'s defender... I checked that random tab from unknown DMs and she had DMed me about the ad, that she really liked the Dear Nike, and I was like, 'Oh my gosh, I should have... How did I miss this? I should have responded months ago.'"

Fox News Digital has reached out to Cunningham's representatives for comment.

Cunningham is already under contract with Adidas, which is preparing to release her first publicly available player-exclusive shoe Friday. The Adidas Crazy Energy "Sophie Cunningham" PE will retail for $120. It is a Cunningham colorway of an existing Adidas model, not a signature shoe created exclusively for her. Adidas recently unveiled the Crazy Energy line.

But Sey hopes Cunningham will eventually defect from Adidas.

"I would do anything within my power to get her to defect from Adidas and come to work with us," Sey said. "I don’t know that Sophie is likely to do that, but I would give my right arm to have her do it."

Sey criticized Adidas for not publicly endorsing Cunningham’s position in the days since the WNBA star made her position public.

"Adidas is not a brand that supports women," Sey said.

Sey also pointed to Adidas’ 2023 Pride campaign, which featured a male-presenting model wearing a swimsuit sold in the women’s section. Adidas said at the time that the collection promoted LGBTQIA+ advocacy and self-acceptance. Sey also criticized the company’s sponsorship of the Boston Marathon, whose rules permit transgender athletes to qualify in their gender category, although eligibility for prize money is governed by World Athletics standards.

"Even now, when she’s getting a lot of heat, it’s not like Adidas is coming out and saying, ‘We stand with Sophie. We agree women’s sports must be protected,’" Sey said. "They’re silent."

"They just want to capitalize on sassy Sophie who points," she added. "They don’t want to actually stand with her when she says something that makes people angry."

Still, Sey praised Adidas for not dropping Cunningham as a client since she's made her statements.

"It says something is shifting in the culture about this issue. They’re not dropping her," Sey said.

Sey conceded that XX-XY could not match the financial resources of Adidas. But she said her brand could offer Cunningham something the global sportswear company could not: top billing and unconditional support.

Sey previously served as Levi Strauss & Co.’s chief marketing officer and global brand president. She said she personally negotiated celebrity partnerships while at Levi’s and often sold potential ambassadors on the relationship rather than the biggest possible check.

"I wasn’t offering the most money," Sey said. "I was offering the best partnership."

Asked how much she would offer Cunningham, Sey declined to name a figure.

"I would pull together as much money as I could to pay her, to make her a favorable deal, but I’m not going to pretend like I can pay what Adidas can pay," Sey said. "We’re going to be more fun to work with."

"She’s not going to be a third-rate athlete on our roster. She’s going to be number one," Sey added. "And she’s going to be able to say whatever she wants, and we’re going to have her back."

Sey is also pitching Cunningham on something bigger than a traditional endorsement.

After the WNBA Players Association declined to allow its group licensees to commercialize Cunningham’s viral pointing image, Sey posted a silhouette modeled on the pose. The union called the image "derogatory," according to an initial report, but later explained that it generally avoids monetizing confrontations between its members. It clarified that Cunningham remains free to license or create her own products.

Sey offered to produce a hoodie featuring the silhouette and give Cunningham all the proceeds. She now envisions using it as the logo for a Cunningham line under XX-XY, similar to how Michael Jordan’s Jumpman pose became the symbol of Jordan Brand.

"Sophie can have her own brand like Jordan with us, and that’s the logo," Sey said.

"That should be the logo for the XX-XY Cunningham collection."

Cunningham’s profile has risen sharply since she joined Caitlin Clark and the Fever in 2025. She became known as Clark’s on-court defender, then turned into one of the WNBA’s most recognizable personalities after her prolonged finger-pointing exchange with Phoenix Mercury veteran DeWanna Bonner went viral in June.

The 29-year-old guard is also enjoying one of her most efficient seasons. Cunningham entered the All-Star break averaging 9.3 points while shooting 47.4% from the field and 42.9% from 3-point range.

Her growing popularity has extended beyond basketball. Cunningham recently appeared as a guest ring girl at UFC 329 and has built her image around an outspoken, humorous and combative personality.

She then waded into one of the most divisive issues in women’s sports.

Cunningham told ESPN this week that she wanted to protect girls who "shouldn’t have to go against biological men" in sports or share locker rooms with them. She later doubled down, calling her position "common sense" while insisting she does not hate transgender people.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"I said what I said," Cunningham told reporters Wednesday. "I think it’s really important to protect children, and that’s little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

The Fever responded by saying its players have the right to their own views.

"Our players are thoughtful adults with their own perspectives and voices, and those views are their own," the organization said. "We are committed to welcoming fans from every background and treating everyone with respect, and that’s what guides us as an organization."

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: Australia World Cup star Volpato faces speeding, cocaine charges
excerpt:
Cristian Volpato, who represented Australia at the World Cup, has allegedly tested positive for cocaine and was also charged with speeding, New South Wales state police have said.

They said the 22-ye...
body_text:
Cristian Volpato, who represented Australia at the World Cup, has allegedly tested positive for cocaine and was also charged with speeding, New South Wales state police have said.

They said the 22-year-old Volpato, who switched allegiances from Italy to Australia before the World Cup, was allegedly clocked at 50km (30 miles) an hour over the designated speed limit when police stopped him on Sydney’s Anzac Bridge early on Friday morning.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test which returned a positive result for cocaine, police said in a statement.

Volpato made three appearances for the Socceroos at the latest World Cup.

The forward represented Italy at youth level but never appeared for the senior national side.

He began his youth career with Sydney United, Sydney FC and Western Sydney Wanderers.

Volpato’s big break came when Roma signed him in 2020. He moved to Sassuolo in 2023, where he established himself as a Serie A player.

His final appearance for Italy came at under-21 level in 2025. Volpato had previously been linked with a switch to Australia ahead of the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

title: Citizens Bank cuts ties with ICE prison contractors after months of activist pressure
excerpt: Fox News legal analyst Gregg Jarrett tells Lawrence Jones that banking discrimination for political or religious purposes is illegal. Jarrett asserts that federal and state laws protect consumers, mak...
body_text:
Fox News legal analyst Gregg Jarrett tells Lawrence Jones that banking discrimination for political or religious purposes is illegal. Jarrett asserts that federal and state laws protect consumers, making it unlawful to close accounts based on political or religious beliefs, unless criminal activity is suspected. He warns of civil enforcement actions, including significant financial penalties, for banks and their officers.

Citizens Bank is ending its financial relationships with two of the nation's largest private prison companies following months of protests over their role in operating ICE detention facilities, though the bank insists the decision was driven by changing business conditions rather than political pressure.

The Rhode Island-based lender said it will wind down its lending relationships with CoreCivic and GEO Group, companies that have operated immigration detention centers under federal contracts. Activists who had urged customers and municipalities to cut ties with the bank hailed the move as a victory, while Citizens said the companies' financing needs had changed because the federal government plans to acquire some detention facilities.

"Over the past year, we have been targeted by several activist groups regarding our relationships with two private prison operators, CoreCivic and The GEO Group," Citizens Bank said in a July 17 announcement. "To date, we have refrained from commenting directly given our commitment to maintaining client privacy. However, given recent developments, we feel it is appropriate to comment at this time."

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PLANS NEW ICE HOLDING FACILITY NEAR LOUISIANA DEPORTATION FLIGHT HUB

This Wednesday, Aug. 28, 2019, photo shows the Adelanto U.S. Immigration and Enforcement Processing Center operated by GEO Group, Inc. (GEO) a Florida-based company specializing in privatized corrections in Adelanto, Calif.

"GEO has been a client of the bank since 2018, and CoreCivic has been a client since 2011," the announcement continued. "Among the services these companies offer is the operation of prisons under service contracts with the federal and various state governments. This includes contracting with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to operate detention facilities for those individuals scheduled for deportation. Both companies also own various facilities in addition to their service contracts."

Citizens said it decided to end its lending relationship with CoreCivic and GEO Group because recent federal purchases of correctional facilities have reduced the companies' capital needs and changed how they finance their operations. The bank said the decision was driven by those business changes, not by any concerns about the companies or their business practices.

"Citizens has been disappointed that the activists have dragged it into what is largely a political matter," the bank’s announcement continued. "Public characterizations of Citizens by activist groups, including as it relates to our commitment to immigrants and to communities, do not reflect who we are or the record we have built. Citizens is deeply committed to serving our customers, colleagues, and communities."

SOROS-BACKED NONPROFIT ACCUSES NJ GOV SHERRILL OF SPREADING 'MAGA PROPAGANDA' ON ICE DETAINEES

An exterior view of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) administrative office and processing center on June 28, 2025. (Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

The bank also highlighted its broader community investments, saying it supports 140 nonprofit organizations that serve immigrant communities, logged more than 265,000 employee volunteer hours last year, has staff serving on more than 1,000 nonprofit boards, and provided $2 billion in community development financing for affordable housing and local economic development.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesman for CoreCivic said that the company "is a lawful business that has served government partners at the federal, state and local levels, under administrations of both parties, for more than 40 years. Our financial position is the strongest it has been in the company's history and we value very much our diverse set of financial partners that help support the company's capital needs."

NEW YORK TIMES TORCHED FOR ‘FALSE’ REPORTING ON ICE INVESTIGATIONS, OUTLET FIRES BACK

Police officers patrol outside of Delany Hall, an immigrant detention center in Newark, N.J., on May 13, 2025. (Stephanie Keith for Fox News Digital)

It added, "We remain focused on delivering safe, high-quality services for our government partners and delivering quality outcomes which is where we believe our emphasis should be."

Fox News Digital contacted Citizens Bank, which referred to its July 17 statement. Fox News Digital also reached out to ICE and GEO Group for comment.

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

These alleged accomplices are accused of helping deputy-dubbed "master manipulator" Isabelle Rose Johnson, 38, steer clear of cops; she's been on the run for several weeks.

Johnson, of Florida, is accused of killing Jason Coulthart, 43, whose body was found buried in a shallow grave on a Florida property on June 25. He was last seen alive on May 24.

Jason Christopher Coulthart, 43, was found buried in a shallow grave at a property in Niceville, Florida. He leaves behind a son. (Walton County Sheriff's Office)

FLORIDA WOMAN ON THE RUN AND WANTED FOR MURDER RELIED ON NETWORK OF ALLEGED ACCOMPLICES TO EVADE CAPTURE: COPS

Bobbie Jean Wagstaff, Isabelle Johnson's roommate, is charged with accessory after the fact to first-degree murder and possession of methamphetamine after investigators alleged she helped conceal the killing of Jason Coulthart. (Walton County Sheriff's Office)

A witness in the same report said, "She killed the victim by placing a zip tie around his neck." The same witness went on to say, "She covered the body with cement so that the dog would not dig it up again."

ALABAMA MOTHER SENTENCED TO LIFE FOR HIRING HITMAN TO KILL HER CHILD'S FATHER OVER CUSTODY DISPUTE

Johnson's possible motive for the alleged murder? The report says the witness told investigators "he was aware of her 'getting rid' of a boy because he was 'aggravating and irritating her.'"

Alleged accomplices 4 & 5: In another report, more alleged helpers were arrested for assisting Johnson.

The report also includes a string of text messages between Morris, White and another suspect, aforementioned Leaverton, that investigators say show them coordinating Johnson's whereabouts, discussing her backpacks and referencing efforts to help her.

In one alleged text exchange, Morris texted Leaverton, "Why is Harley on our couch?" before following up with, "More importantly, when are you coming to get her?"

"Harley" is one of the aliases that Johnson has been using, according to the sheriff's office, along with "Jessica Elaine Bowman" and "Denise."

Isabelle Johnson is wanted for murder and investigators say she has been on the run for weeks, relying on help from alleged accomplices to stay hidden from cops. (Walton County Sheriff's Office)
