The duties, ranging from 10% to 12...
body_text:
The US is imposing new tariffs on around 60 trading partners accounting for the vast majority of its imports over claims they failed to properly stop forced labour.

The duties, ranging from 10% to 12.5%, target key economic partners – including the UK, China, EU, Canada, Japan and India. They come in on Friday, as a temporary 10% tax on foreign goods introduced earlier this year expires.

The move is the latest escalation in the global trade war reignited by US President Donald Trump when he returned to office last year.

The US Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that many of the tariffs imposed globally under emergency powers were illegally enacted.

So the president has since sought other legal avenues to pursue his flagship trade policy.

It was last month that the White House first proposed a series of 10-12.5% duties on goods arriving to American shores from dozens of countries over concerns they were not doing enough to tackle forced labour.

On Thursday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, acting under Trump's direction, said those duties would now take effect.

"Today's action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere," his statement said.

Greer invoked Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which governs US trade enforcement of practices that burden or restrict American commerce.

Earlier this week the Trump administration invoked a different statute, Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, to impose 50% tariffs on products from Canada.

On Thursday, the Office of the US Trade Representative said the latest tariffs were being imposed on partners "for their failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labour".

The new duties apply to the top 60 US trade partners covering 99.4% of US imports, it added.

The office said Trump in his second term had made adoption of a ban on imports made with forced labour a "critical" part of reciprocal trade agreements with other nations.

It said so far 10 trading partners had agreed to enact such a ban in these agreements, and other countries had enacted bans in response to its investigations in recent weeks.

Trading partners that have "made commitments to adopt, and effectively enforce" bans on forced labour imports will be subject to a 10% tariff, while those that have not will have the higher 12.5% rate, the office added.

Greer said in his statement he was "encouraged by the trading partners who have moved quickly to adopt forced labour import prohibitions, and look forward to ensuring their effective enforcement".

Trump has long argued that tariffs protect American workers, create more manufacturing jobs and boost the US economy.

After returning to the White House last year, Trump imposed tariffs of up to 50% on global trading partners on what he called "Liberation Day".

He said the measures were aimed to address what he saw as decades of unfair treatment of the US by countries around the world.

In February, the US Supreme Court struck down those tariffs and said that the president had exceeded his authority as he had not gained approval from Congress.

Tens of billions of dollars have since been refunded to companies that paid the levies.

But the White House has since looked at alternative ways to impose import duties, including a sweeping 10% levy as part of a temporary solution that is set to expire on Friday.

Washington has also imposed a slew of other tariffs on countries like Brazil and Canada.

The US and China have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.

Economists have warned that higher tariffs can make everyday goods, like coffee and microwaves, more expensive. Because taxes are paid by importing companies, those businesses often pass the extra costs on to shoppers through higher prices.

The president has also used the duties to press other countries, such as Mexico, on non-trade issues, like labour rules.

Business groups and affected countries are expected to push back on the latest tariffs.

Many trading partners are already weighing potential legal challenges or retaliatory duties in response.

The administration is also preparing for further action.

The US trade representative is currently investigating 16 countries – accounting for the vast majority of US imports – over claims of manufacturing overcapacity, which could pave the way for additional duties later this year.

Carney looking at 'all options' as Trump announces 50% tariffs on Canada

US announces new tariffs over forced labour concerns

title: Qantas tests new ultra-long-range Airbus in 17,000km direct flight from France to Melbourne
excerpt:
Airbus A350–1000ULR becomes most watched plane on flight tracking websites as Qantas tests new aircraft for its Project Sunrise

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breakin...
body_text:
Airbus A350–1000ULR becomes most watched plane on flight tracking websites as Qantas tests new aircraft for its Project Sunrise

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Qantas’s new ultra long-distance aircraft has landed on Australian soil for the first time on Friday after a 19-hour test flight from France.

The Airbus A350-1000ULR, designed for Qantas to complete some of the longest commercial flights in the world, set off on a nonstop journey from Airbus’ manufacturing facility Toulouse, France on Thursday, destined for Melbourne.

The planes have been designed to fly up to 22 hours nonstop for the company’s Sydney to London direct route, expected to start in October 2027.

The test flight has attracted attention from transport enthusiasts, with more than 67,000 people following its almost 17,000km path on flightradar24.com on Friday morning – the most-watched flight globally on Friday.

The air traffic website indicates the flight departed Toulouse at 7.33am on Thursday, local time.  It landed in Melbourne just over 19 hours later, at 10.46am, local time.

In a statement, Qantas said four Airbus flight test pilots and five flight test engineers were operating the model’s test. They and the aircraft will stay in Melbourne over the weekend then depart for Toulouse on Monday, with two Qantas pilots joining them on board.

Qantas’ chief technical pilot, Alex Passerini, told Channel Seven on Friday the return flight would take 23 hours, as the crew tested systems from fuel transfer to air conditioning.

Passerini said crews would be able to take regular rest breaks on the plane, aligned with the airline’s “data-driven” systems.

“Everyone’s going to get tired,” Passerini said.

Qantas said the plane in flight was the first of its model to take to the skies. The A350–1000ULR was first flown on 2 June, for three hours 43 minutes over France and the French Atlantic coast, and has since undergone extensive testing.

The test model is not carrying Qantas’s official white and red livery. It has a tan exterior carrying company branding, with Qantas logos on its wingtips.

The company said the first A350-1000ULR painted in the Qantas livery, named Vega, is still on the assembly line and will be delivered to Qantas in April 2027.

The A350–1000ULR’s extra 20,000-litre fuel tank enables it to fly ultra long-haul routes of almost 10,000 nautical miles (18,500km), according to Airbus. Qantas in June said it was buying 12 aircraft with 238 seats rather than the 300-plus seats on other A350-1000 models.
  Qantas’s Project Sunrise plans for nonstop services between Sydney and London have been delayed multiple times in previous years.

In November 2025, the company said the service would start in the first half of 2027, with Airbus set to deliver the first specially configured A350-1000ULR by late 2026. But Airbus in June revealed the first aircraft would be delivered in April 2027, pushing back the start date again.

Qantas had previously mentioned Melbourne and Brisbane, along with Sydney, as planned hubs for direct flights to London and New York City. The company’s latest announcement in June did not mention those cities but officials have indicated Qantas would adjust its routes based on customer demand.

title: Scottie Scheffler addresses growing rivalry between Rory McIlroy, Bryson DeChambeau after The Open
excerpt:
Ned Michaels explains the friction that has been growing between Rory McIlroy & Bryson DeChambeau

The Open Championship just closed out the 2026 major championship season, and somehow one of the most...
body_text:
Ned Michaels explains the friction that has been growing between Rory McIlroy & Bryson DeChambeau

The Open Championship just closed out the 2026 major championship season, and somehow one of the most unexpected winners in recent memory, Ryan Fox, hasn't been the story.

Instead? It's once again Bryson DeChambeau. DeChambeau was a lightning rod for criticism ahead of The Open when analysts Nick Faldo and Brandel Chamblee had harsh words for his approach. Faldo said he lacked the "strategy" to succeed in links golf, that he hits driver as far as he can and hopes for the best instead of trying to "thread" it down the fairway.

Chamblee had a broader complaint: He believes DeChambeau has spent more time chasing YouTube golf star Grant Horvat than trying to run down the best in the world, Rory McIlroy and Scottie Scheffler. So how did Bryson respond? In the most Bryson way possible.

BRYSON DECHAMBEAU CLAPS BACK AT NICK FALDO, OTHER CRITICS, AFTER -3 ROUND AT THE OPEN: 'INCREDIBLY STRATEGIC'

Bryson DeChambeau celebrates winning the 2024 U.S. Open at Pinehurst Resort in North Carolina. (Jim Dedmon/USA TODAY Sports)

He immediately put himself in contention with a strong 3-under 67 first round. Afterward, he said in his media appearance that he had been very "strategic" when playing Royal Birkdale, a clear response to Faldo. Round two, however, was where he really became the center of attention.

After the round was completed, a seeming 4-under 66, rules officials brought DeChambeau back to the fifth hole, where they assessed him a two-stroke penalty for improving the area around his backswing. DeChambeau was furious, and apparently threatened to withdraw from the tournament in protest.

Some players, like Xander Schauffele, came to his defense. Scottie Scheffler also was adamant that the 32-year-old is not a "cheater."

One player who didn't come to his defense? Rory McIlroy. McIlroy was clear in his post-round comments that he doesn't care for DeChambeau and believed he deserved the penalty.

Rory McIlroy of Northern Ireland plays his tee shot on the 7th hole during the third day of the British Open Golf championships at Royal Birkdale golf club in Southport, England, Saturday, July 18, 2026. (Peter Morrison/AP)

"I won’t pretend to be up here and defend Bryson," he told reporters during the tournament. "I’m not particularly fond of him. I think a lot of it is performative. I think a lot of it’s for attention.

"To hold the tournament hostage like that and to have all of us — players, volunteers, everyone — waiting on him to depart, I didn’t feel like it was a great look," McIlroy said.

BRYSON DECHAMBEAU DETAILS THE TWO COMPLICATED HURDLES IN HIS WAY OF A POTENTIAL PGA TOUR RETURN

"I think there’s no doubt that he improved the line of his backswing," he added. "Again, it’s like, whether it was careless or whether it was intentional, I don’t think it matters. Hopefully, it was careless, but I think the two-shot penalty was justified, for sure."

This marked the latest entry in the budding rivalry between the two big names and big personalities in professional golf. They're on opposite sides of Ryder Cup battles. DeChambeau was one of the earliest and largest stars to depart for LIV Golf, while McIlroy became a sort of player spokesman defending the PGA Tour. McIlroy has never done a full 18-hole match on YouTube, while DeChambeau's made his channel into a behemoth, filming rounds with President Donald Trump and many others.

Ahead of this week's 3M Open at TPC Twin Cities in Minnesota, Scheffler was asked whether he believes the rivalry is good for golf, and gave a typically incisive answer.

"I think golf's different in a sense of a lot of other sports because my biggest rival week in and week out is the golf course that we're playing," he told the media. "I mean, I could never stop somebody from doing anything in golf. I felt like when I played basketball there would always be rivalries in basketball because you're going to play defense against a person and that is much more personal in a sense like because I'm actively trying to stop...like if you and I were going to go out and play one-on-one, it would turn into a rivalry because I'm actively trying to stop what you're doing.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"But in golf, we're always competing against ourselves on the golf course. I've never been a big fan of personal jabs. I don't think that rivalry is a big thing in golf just because, like I said, my biggest rivalry week in and week out is the golf course."

There have been a few instances of McIlroy and DeChambeau facing off with a tournament on the line, though they've never gone head-to-head in a Ryder Cup. Most of the rivalry seems to be McIlroy disliking Bryson for either his personality or his departure for LIV, and DeChambeau playing into it, because as he's put it, "rivalries are good" for golf.

(Left) Rory McIlroy watches his shot from the ninth tee during the second round of The Open Championship golf tournament at Royal Birkdale in Southport, England. July 17, 2026. (Right) Bryson DeChambeau looks on from the first green during the first round of the U.S. Open golf tournament in Southampton, New York, on June 18, 2026. (Bill Streicher/Imagn Images; Bill Streicher/Imagn Images)

Which is what makes the rivalry so fascinating. It's not competitive, it's personal. Scheffler and McIlroy have faced off in Ryder Cups, for example, yet there seems to be only mutual respect between the two.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

One thing is certain, though: 2027 will be a fascinating season in the golf world. Between the potential collapse of LIV Golf, the (mostly) iconic venues hosting major championships and yet another Ryder Cup where both are guaranteed selections, this time back in Europe, there'll be plenty of opportunities for Rory and Bryson to face off.

title: Timothy Olyphant revealed the surprising truth behind his computer-free lifestyle

Timothy Olyphant revealed he had to resurrect an old computer in an attempt to log on to the "SmartLess" podcast. Ultimately, he wou...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Timothy Olyphant revealed he had to resurrect an old computer in an attempt to log on to the "SmartLess" podcast. Ultimately, he wound up using a friend's office to make the interview happen.

"I needed a computer," Olyphant, 58, told hosts Jason Bateman, Will Arnett and Sean Hayes. "I guess you can't do your show if you don't own a computer."

As the hosts pressed him, Olyphant doubled down on his surprisingly low-tech lifestyle.

JENNIFER GARNER KEEPS HER KIDS OFF SOCIAL MEDIA: 'FIND SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE' IT'S GOOD FOR TEENS

Timothy Olyphant revealed he doesn't own a computer, telling the hosts of the "SmartLess" podcast he had to dig out an old desktop and eventually use a friend's office just to join the interview. (Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images)

"I got like a, you know, I got a phone and I got a thing," the "Justified" star said. "That's all you gotta do."

"I don't buy it," Bateman questioned. "You don't have, and you being an artist, you don't have an iPad with one of those little, one of those little stylist pen thingies?"

The "Five-Star Weekend" actor then explained that while he technically owned a desktop computer, it had been sitting unused long enough to become a project in itself.

"We went… I had a… we went and got out an old desktop computer that we still have in the house and plugged it in and started it up, and they were all USB things."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Timothy Olyphant said he has no interest in owning a computer, insisting a phone is all he needs despite questions from "SmartLess" hosts Jason Bateman, Will Arnett and Sean Hayes. (Alberto Rodriguez/Variety via Getty Images)

The aging machine proved to be another obstacle. After digging out the outdated desktop and getting it running, Olyphant joked that appearing on the podcast required far more effort than expected.

"There's a lot of sacrifices that went into this guys," he admitted. "And don't get me wrong, I appreciate ... I'm super honored, and it is a pleasure to be here. I'm a big fan. I listen – I don't listen – but I read the transcripts. And the show's very good. Very, very, very good."

Bateman wasn't ready to let the conversation go, continuing to question Olyphant's aversion to computers.

"But wait, but Tim, you've never been tempted to buy a laptop or a desktop just to see the landscape out there, like all the different sites you can go visit to expose yourself to?" Bateman said.

Timothy Olyphant surprised the "SmartLess" hosts with his low-tech lifestyle, explaining he doesn't own a computer and had to resurrect an old desktop before appearing on the podcast. (Kevork Djansezian/NBCU Photo Bank)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Bateman then shifted the conversation to artificial intelligence, wondering whether Olyphant had any interest in the technology despite avoiding computers.

"All this talk about AI and stuff. Not curious to see what the fuss is about?" the "Arrested Development" actor added.

"But you can do all that on… on the little phones," Olyphant emphasized.

Neal McDonough, Timothy Olyphant and Walton Goggins arrive at the premiere of FX Networks and Sony Pictures Television's "Justified" on Jan. 10, 2012. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

Olyphant landed his breakthrough role in 1999 with the cult crime comedy "Go." His performances in "Deadwood" and "Justified" cemented his star status. His other notable works include "Santa Clarita Diet," "The Mandalorian," "The Book of Boba Fett" and "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood."

title: India ‘cockroach’ activist Sonam Wangchuk ends hunger strike as protests spread
excerpt:
Sonam Wangchuk halted strike amid concerns about ‘possible violence’ in India as protest movement urges demonstrations across country on Friday over police brutality

Indian “cockroach” activist Sonam...
body_text:
Sonam Wangchuk halted strike amid concerns about ‘possible violence’ in India as protest movement urges demonstrations across country on Friday over police brutality

Indian “cockroach” activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a 26-day hunger strike on Friday over an exam paper scandal that has spiralled into a wideranging youth-led protest against Narendra Modi’s government, with protesters continuing to call for the education minister to resign.

Wangchuk said on social media that he ended the hunger strike in Delhi in the presence of two federal ministers at the urging of scores of members ⁠of parliament, and after “a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country”. He did not elaborate on the talks but promised to lay out details in a video soon.

Protests under the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) ​movement have called for nationwide demonstrations on Friday ‌in solidarity with students who alleged police brutality during a march on parliament on Monday by tens of thousands of people, even as Modi’s government urged them to join talks.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke thanked Wangchuk for his “courage and sacrifice” and said the protests would continue until minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. “We won’t let Sonam ⁠sir’s sacrifice go in vain,” he added in a video message.

The CJP ​movement wants Pradhan to step down over exam paper leaks that affected 2 million students in May and have been linked to several student suicides.

Late on Tuesday, Pradhan, in his first comments since demands for his resignation were made, said the government was committed to addressing concerns and reforming ​exams.

The protests have drawn tens of thousands on to the streets, and represent the biggest youth challenge to Modi since he came to power in 2014. ‌Opposition parties have echoed the youth movement’s demands and have ‌disrupted the monsoon session of parliament that began this week.

After Wangchuk ended his hunger strike, Modi urged the activist to follow doctors’ advice and regain the weight he has lost.

Thousands of people remained at the Jantar Mantar protest site on Thursday afternoon, carrying anti-government posters and chanting slogans amid heavy security deployment. The protests have shut metro stations and mobile internet services and curtailed business in central Delhi.

Protests also have spread to other cities, including Ranchi, Pune, Thiruvananthapuram and Kolkata, local media reported.

Authorities in Delhi shut down 16 metro rail stations on Thursday in and around the central parts of Delhi where the protesters have remained camped, inconveniencing thousands of commuters.

The government also ordered telecom firms to block mobile internet services in the area, sources told Reuters, a move that not only ‌affected protesters but also stopped shops and restaurants receiving digital payments by phone.

The measures ​are widely seen by human rights groups as an attempt by authorities to curb protests and prevent any fresh outbreak of violence.

Earlier on Thursday, Modi said that special courts would be set up to prosecute those behind exam paper leaks, his first public response to the crisis. “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future ⁠of our youth!” Modi posted online.

But the CJP rejected the proposal, saying what courts do after paper leaks is just one aspect of the problem. “But ​Modi-ji, tell us why are paper leaks happening in this country in the ​first place?” CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka said, using the Hindi honorific.

“Fast-track ​courts are set up in this country for every other issue, but whether those fast track courts have actually solved those issues – you know the answer to that question, ​and so do we.“

Later in the day, Modi ‌said on social media that the government ​would announce more strict actions against paper leaks at ​a cabinet meeting on Friday.

Top Bollywood stars, including Salman Khan, Alia Bhatt and Kareena Kapoor, supported the protesters via social media posts, saying it was heartening to see students come together to fight for a cause.

title: Megan Rapinoe blames Trump for US Mens soccer team losing 'underdog' vibe in World Cup
excerpt:
Former U.S. women's soccer team star Megan Rapinoe said President Donald Trump was the reason the U.S. men's soccer team lost their underdog edge in the World Cup on "The Daily Show."

Megan Rapinoe p...
body_text:
Former U.S. women's soccer team star Megan Rapinoe said President Donald Trump was the reason the U.S. men's soccer team lost their underdog edge in the World Cup on "The Daily Show."

Megan Rapinoe put blame on President Donald Trump for the U.S. mens soccer team's World Cup loss on Tuesday, saying the president's involvement killed the team's underdog vibe in the tournament.

"The Daily Show" host Desi Lydic asked Rapinoe about the red card given to U.S. player Folarin Balogun in their Round of 32 match, which was eventually suspended. Trump admitted to calling FIFA President Gianni Infantino to ask for a review of the red card.

"How do you think that affected the men's team?" Lydic asked Rapinoe.

"Certainly not well, it didn't give them the boost, maybe, that they were thinking it would or that Trump was hoping that it would," she responded. "I don't know. It seemed like it kind of like, threw them off their game."

FOLARIN BALOGUN ADMITS THAT RED-CARD REVERSAL AFFECTED USA WORLD CUP TEAMMATES: 'A LOT OF OUTSIDE NOISE'

Former professional soccer player, Megan Rapinoe, attends the game between the Seattle Storm and the Indiana Fever at Climate Pledge Arena on June 24, 2025, in Seattle, Washington. (Alika Jenner/Getty Images; Rob Newell - CameraSport via Getty Images)

"But it didn't go well. They had, like, such a good vibe," she added. "I feel like they had, like, the underdog kind of vibe going. And then you-know-who got involved, and everyone was like, nope. No. We don't like it. And then, obviously, Belgium was like, 'No, we absolutely can't lose to this team now.'"

Rapinoe, who won two World Cup titles with the women's national soccer team, said she didn't know the rules and wasn't a referee.

"No other president in history could have pulled off the historic feat that President Trump delivered for the American people and the world. Thanks to his bold vision and decisive leadership, the 2026 FIFA World Cup generated billions of dollars in revenue, created a massive economic boost across host cities, and delivered a safe, secure, and seamless experience for millions of fans and athletes from around the globe. It will undoubtedly go down as one of the greatest and most successful sporting events in history," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Rapinoe said during her podcast "A Touch More: The Beautiful Game," that Trump's involvement was a distraction.

LA GALAXY COACH GREG VANNEY SAYS TEAM USA WAS 'TOO NAIVE,' EXPLAINS CHRISTIAN PULISIC'S STRUGGLES

President Donald Trump and FIFA president (Fédération Internationale de Football Association) Gianni Infantino talk in the Oval Office of the White House after signing an executive order for a task force related to the FIFA World Cup, in Washington, D.C., on March 7, 2025. (Jim Watson/AFP)

"I think the distraction got to the team for sure in some type of way. Whether it was, you know, this red card situation, whether it was being in a public discourse with this president, all of the, you know, shenanigans and chaos that comes with the feelings on both sides of that. Whether you agree with it or not it's — it's just like it's a lot to contend with," Rapinoe said.

"So, not only does this team not have like a core of older players who are used to that, but none of these players talk about anything ever, like for the most part," she continued.

"I think in men's football, just like in general, there's not a lot of players who are choosing to use their platform or to, you know, broaden their scope of pressure and responsibility," she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Former U.S. women's national team player Megan Rapinoe gave her take on the U.S. men's team's World Cup loss to Belgium. (Soobum Im/USSF/Getty Images)

The U.S. men's national team lost to Belgium in the Round of 16 match following the red card controversy.

Balogun told CBS after the loss that there was a lot of outside noise leading up to it.

"My initial reaction was I was happy to be back in the team, but when I kind of started to reflect, I knew it was going to cause a lot of controversy, and I could almost see within my teammates a bit of nerves, because it is something that is so unique," Balogun told CBS in mid-July.

"The closer we got to the game, I tried to just focus as best as I could, but it was difficult. A lot of outside noise and that’s hard to avoid," he added.

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

title: Ex-Denver Nuggets star Ty Lawson hurls 'white b---h' insult at cop after Tito's vodka theft arrest
excerpt:

body_text:

Ty Lawson made millions of dollars during an eight-year NBA career. Last week, a $34 bottle of Tito's vodka led to his arrest.

Instead of showing remorse, the former Denver Nuggets guard went on the attack, repeatedly calling a Castle Rock Police Department officer a "white b*tch" during his arrest before later claiming on social media that he was the victim.

Arron Afflalo and Ty Lawson of the Denver Nuggets react in the first half alongside Kobe Bryant of the Los Angeles Lakers in Game 7 of the Western Conference quarterfinals of the 2012 NBA playoffs on May 12, 2012, at Staples Center in Los Angeles. (Getty Images)

Interim head coach Melvin Hunt leads Ty Lawson and the Denver Nuggets against the Milwaukee Bucks at Pepsi Center in Denver, Colo., on March 3, 2015. (Getty Images)

The bottle of vodka was worth $34. Lawson was booked into Douglas County Jail on a shoplifting charge.

JAMES HARDEN ARRESTED IN HOUSTON ON MISDEMEANOR WEAPONS CHARGE AFTER NBA PLAYOFF EXIT: REPORT

According to the arrest details, Lawson smelled strongly of alcohol during his arrest on July 16. He allegedly took the bottle of Tito's while intoxicated and was later found by officers sitting at a nearby restaurant.

The retired NBA player then took to social media to defend his behavior, instead launching into a familiar "America is racist" rant on X.

Ty Lawson #3 of the Denver Nuggets controls the ball against the Atlanta Hawks at Pepsi Center on March 11, 2015, in Denver, Colo. The Nuggets defeated the Hawks 115-102. (Getty Images)

SHAQUILLE O'NEAL SAYS HE DOESN'T TEXT NBA PLAYERS PAST OR PRESENT BECAUSE 'THEY'RE A--HOLES'

From 2009 to 2015, Lawson was a key piece of the Denver Nuggets' backcourt. He also played on Roy Williams' NCAA championship-winning North Carolina team in 2009.

Lawson also spent time alongside Chauncey Billups in Denver. Billups is currently under federal scrutiny amid allegations involving illegal high-stakes poker games.

title: UN envoy for Yemen ‘alarmed’ by Houthis’ Red Sea attacks, calls for talks
excerpt:
The United Nations envoy for Yemen has warned that renewed attacks by the Houthis on Red Sea shipping risk dragging the country back into full-scale war.

Hans Grundberg said in a statement on Thursda...
body_text:
The United Nations envoy for Yemen has warned that renewed attacks by the Houthis on Red Sea shipping risk dragging the country back into full-scale war.

Hans Grundberg said in a statement on Thursday that he was “alarmed” by the resumption of attacks by the Houthis, known as Ansar Allah, on commercial vessels, and called for talks to resolve the country’s crisis.

“Escalatory actions risk putting Yemen on a path toward further confrontation, drawing the country deeper into an already volatile regional environment, and deepening the suffering of the Yemeni people,” Grundberg said.

“It is still possible to change course and move towards negotiations that address Yemen’s political, economic and security challenges and put the interests of its people at the centre. A negotiated political settlement in Yemen would also contribute to greater stability in the region.”

The war in Yemen has been largely paused since 2022, but the political deadlock between the Houthis, who control the capital, Sanaa, and the internationally recognised government continue.

The Houthis said on Wednesday that they struck two Saudi oil tankers, the Encelia and the Layla, with missiles and drones, their first attack since announcing a blockade of Saudi-linked shipping on July 20.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the vessels were hit “for their violation of the blockade decision issued by the armed forces”.

The Houthis had imposed the blockade in retaliation for the July 13 bombing of Sanaa airport’s runway, which Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it carried out to stop an Iranian aircraft landing. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, the government’s main backer.

The Houthis, who are allied with Iran, also fired missiles into Saudi Arabia, targeting an airport.

The maritime campaign has caused at least five tankers to change course to avoid the Bab al-Mandeb Strait off Yemen’s coast. The disruption has helped push the price of Brent crude oil above $100 a barrel.

Yemen’s civil war has ground on for nearly 12 years since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, driving the internationally recognised government to Aden and drawing in a Saudi-led coalition.

The US-Israel war on Iran has threatened to reactivate ground fighting between the two sides, plunging the country into deeper strife.

The UN estimates that 22 million Yemenis need aid this year, with 18.3 million suffering acute food insecurity – not having enough to eat.

The UN warning on Thursday came as the United States carried out its 12th consecutive night of strikes on Iran in a war that has already disrupted shipping through another global chokepoint, the Strait of Hormuz.

US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that Washington would hold Iran responsible for further Houthi attacks on shipping, calling the group a proxy of Tehran and threatening retaliation against both.

“Major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis,” he wrote on Truth Social.

title: Dem’s stunning ideal standard for immigration detention conditions resurfaces amid Texas senate bid
excerpt: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton joins Will Cain to discuss Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's campaign. Paxton argues Talarico's current border security messaging contradicts his past voti...
body_text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton joins Will Cain to discuss Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's campaign. Paxton argues Talarico's current border security messaging contradicts his past voting record in the Texas House. They also compare Talarico's significant fundraising to Paxton's, highlighting the close race in Texas.

During a 2019 interview following a visit to border enforcement, James Talarico, candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, said he gauged the suitability of immigration detention facilities based on how he would treat his own family.

"I think I was struck by the conditions these folks were being held in," Talarico said.

"When I first walked in, I looked at one of the security monitors and saw these things strewn around the floor, and I realized they were human beings being held in these tiny rooms. The standard I use is: would I allow my child, my parent, my grandparent to be held in one of these facilities? And the answer, after my visit, was a resounding no," Talarico said.

His resurfaced comments continue to raise questions about his views on border policy as he looks to flip a Republican-held Senate seat in Texas.

PROGRESSIVE TALARICO KNIFES BIDEN'S OPEN BORDER, TRIES MODERATING STANCE ON KEY ISSUES IN TEXAS SENATE RACE

Texas state Rep. James Talarico, D-Austin, a Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, speaks at a primary election watch party Tuesday, March 3, 2026, in Austin, Texas. (Eric Gay/AP Photo)

During his campaign, Talarico has drawn scrutiny for walking a tightrope between traditionally Democratic criticisms on President Donald Trump’s border enforcement measures and appearing too soft on border policy.

Like progressives in the party, Talarico has called on lawmakers to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), has characterized voter ID requirements as a method to rig elections and, in the past, even criticized President Barack Obama’s record on immigration.

In one 2019 remark, Talarico famously called Obama the "deporter-in-chief."

His past comments have left some observers believing his record makes the case for him.

"There is a very concerning pattern with James Talarico siding with pedophiles, criminal illegal aliens and cartels while slandering the brave men and women of law enforcement who keep Texans safe," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement, referring to detentions highlighted by the Department of Homeland Security.

ICE ARRESTS 15 ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS WITH CONVICTIONS INCLUDING HOMICIDE, RAPE AND CHILD SEX CRIMES OVER WEEKEND

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Baltimore Field Officer director Matt Elliston listens during a briefing, Monday, Jan. 27, 2025, in Silver Spring, Md. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)

"Talarico is a true radical and fully committed to defunding the police, knocking down President Trump's border wall and welcoming millions of illegal aliens into America," Kraft added.

At the same time, Talarico has voiced concern about the government’s effective use of resources on the border and whether its investments are being reflected in its detention operations.

He raised the issue in the 2019 interview.

"How are we spending close to a billion dollars every year on border security when these border patrol agents told us firsthand they didn’t have the resources, basic logistical items that would help the situation better for them and for the people being held?" Talarico said.

Talarico argued that poor standards don’t speak to individual facility needs but rather reflect broader problems with immigration enforcement.

"This is not a matter of some bad apples at a Border Patrol station. This is a systemic problem that even the Border Patrol agents identified as something morally wrong and something that needed to be solved," Talarico said in an interview.

"I believe this is a statewide problem; this is a stain on all of our reputations. It violates a lot of the values we have as Texans."

Texas spent roughly $800 million on border security in 2019, according to the state’s legislative budget board.

TALARICO MAKES STUNNING CLAIM ABOUT WHY HE THINKS TEXAS ELECTIONS AREN'T 'FREE AND FAIR'

A cactus and sign mark the entrance to the Eloy Detention Facility for illegal immigrants on July 30, 2010.

When pressed for more details about Talarico’s ideal detainment conditions a reality, his campaign pointed to his border security plan he recently unveiled.

"James supports stronger border security and safe, secure, and humane detention facilities. He’s the only candidate in this race to unveil a border security agenda endorsed by Republicans and Democrats that will add more border patrol agents and improve technology at the border to better detect threats. For too long, both parties have failed our border communities by grandstanding on the issue instead of finding real solutions. James is running for Senate to keep our country safe by deporting criminals instead of locking up moms, babies and small business owners who have been contributing to our economy for decades," a campaign spokesperson said.

Having secured the Democratic nomination, Talarico will face Republican nominee Ken Paxton in the Nov. 3 general election.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump expands voluntary pledge to blunt AI-driven utility bill surges
excerpt: US President Donald Trump’s administration has said it will expand a voluntary pledge seeking to shield consumers from the energy costs of the rapid expansion of data centres, mostly used by artificia...
body_text:
US President Donald Trump’s administration has said it will expand a voluntary pledge seeking to shield consumers from the energy costs of the rapid expansion of data centres, mostly used by artificial intelligence companies.

The White House announced on Thursday that it would add state governors and electricity companies to the agreement, first announced with tech and AI firms in March. But the US administration stopped short of any enforceable protections.

The White House called the expansion of the pledge “historic”, saying 200 additional utilities, data centre developers and states would join it.

The pledge is a “public commitment that hyperscalers, AI companies, and the utilities and data-center developers behind them will build, bring, or buy every kilowatt their facilities need — and cover every dollar of the infrastructure that delivers it”.

It says consumers would not foot the bill for AI’s energy needs.

In remarks about the pledge at the Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday, Trump called on the gathered executives and governors to sell the public on data centres, stressing that the cities and towns that have them will be “rich.”

“You have to convince your community. You can’t fight it. You have to go with it,” Trump said.

“If you don’t take all that money, somebody else is going to take it. You might as well do it yourselves.”

The US president has been a strong advocate for AI, which has become an enormous source of investment and a key priority for the country’s powerful tech sector. Trump has approached the sector, which includes some of his close allies, with a light regulatory touch during his second term.

But increased electricity demand from AI data centres could spur an increase in monthly utility bills between 15 and 40 percent by the year 2030, according to an analysis by the consulting and technology services company ICF.

A May Gallup poll suggested that seven out of 10 people in the US oppose the construction of AI data centres in their area, with about 48 percent saying they were strongly opposed. Slightly more than 25 percent said they favoured such efforts, with only 7 percent saying they strongly favoured them.

Concerns over the impact of such centres on the cost of utilities, such as electricity and water, are commonly cited as reasons for opposition, along with quality of life concerns and scepticism about the benefits of AI.

Some elections across the country have seen AI data centre construction emerge as a prominent issue, but the industry has pushed forward with plans to rapidly scale up infrastructure for the technology.

A poll from Johns Hopkins University in June suggested that Americans strongly favour greater regulation of AI, and about 60 percent of respondents said they expected AI to increase inequality over the next decade.

Four in 10 respondents said that AI companies stand to increase their power the most from the expansion of the technology, while just one in 10 said that individuals would gain the most.

title: Carly Pearce says she doesn't want children and calls her first marriage a 'start-up marriage'
excerpt:
Country star Carly Pearce explained how her heart condition diagnosis reshaped her workout routine and helped her prioritize long-term health over intensity.

Country star Carly Pearce has revealed th...
body_text:
Country star Carly Pearce explained how her heart condition diagnosis reshaped her workout routine and helped her prioritize long-term health over intensity.

Country star Carly Pearce has revealed that kids are off the table.

Earlier this week, Pearce responded to a fan on TikTok who asked her if she was still deciding on children and if she would ever remarry. Pearce was married to singer Michael Ray for a year before they divorced in 2020.

"Maybe some of you out here are like me. I always feel bad saying that I actually don't want children. I love children, I love my friends' children, I'm a great aunt. But, it was never my dream," the 36-year-old said.

Carly Pearce says she doesn't want to have children. (Gilbert Flores / Penske Media via Getty Images)

Pearce went on to explain that her dream was always to pursue country music and live on the road.

COUNTRY SINGER RAELYNN FILES FOR DIVORCE FROM ARMY VETERAN HUSBAND AFTER DECADE-LONG MARRIAGE

"I think we should normalize people that truly know they don't wanna have kids. I don't think it should be for everyone just because society tells us to," Pearce stated. "So, I don't want children and I'm totally okay with that."

Pearce addressed the fan's second question about marriage and said she "absolutely" wants to get married again. The "truck on fire" singer said that she would never let her past sway her away from marriage.

"So what I was divorced. It was my start-up marriage and now I get to have the real one," Pearce ended her video.

Michael Ray and Carly Pearce were married for a year before their divorce. (John Parra/Getty Images for Sandals)

Fans were supportive of Pearce's decision in the comment section of her TikTok.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"People who don’t want children shouldn’t have children. More power to you!" one user wrote. Another added, "You should not feel bad!"

"It is totally ok that is not your dream! Be you!" another user wrote. "You should never feel bad. Women are validated so much by how they serve others as a wife, mother, etc. than just the person they are," another TikTok user commented.

Carly Pearce said she always feels bad when she says she doesn't want children.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Pearce and Ray began dating in 2018 after Pearce made the first move by messaging him on social media. Their whirlwind romance quickly progressed, with the couple getting engaged in December 2018 and marrying in a Nashville-area ceremony in October 2019. Less than a year later, however, Pearce filed for divorce in June 2020, citing irreconcilable differences, and the divorce was finalized that September.

Carly Pearce and Jordan Karcher went Instagram official in 2025. (Carly Pearce Instagram)

Since her divorce, Pearce has had a few relationships, including her current relationship with entrepreneur Jordan Karcher, founder of Grounds & Hounds Coffee Co. The couple went Instagram official in July 2025.

Janelle Ash is an entertainment writer for Fox News Digital covering Hollywood, celebrity culture and breaking entertainment news through exclusive reporting, interviews and in-depth storytelling.
